📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Former NASA astronaut Victor Glover has flown in combat, performed four spacewalks and strapped himself to the top of rockets launching into space. But before embarking on his historic Artemis II journey around the moon, he faced something even more difficult: a conversation with his four daughters.

Speaking alongside former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife, Canary Islands, on Oct. 18, Glover opened up about the challenges of preparing his family for his riskiest mission yet.

"This is maybe the greatest challenge of my astronaut career," Glover noted.

Glover joined NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen aboard NASA's Artemis II mission, which released on April 1, 2026, marking humanity's first crewed journey to the moon since Apollo 17 in 1972.

But preparing for the historic journey wasn't just about mastering the spacecraft and executing the mission successfully. It also meant making sure his family was ready for what lay ahead.

When Glover first traveled to space aboard SpaceX's Crew-1 mission in 2020, his children were much younger and he and his wife, Dionna, made a conscious effort to prepare them for his time in space.

"We decided, as a parental unit, Dionna and I, that we were going to put as much effort into making sure our family was ready as NASA was putting into making sure I was ready to be a crew member," Glover explained.

The family visited NASA's Kennedy Space Center, toured the launch pad and crew quarters and even planned when Glover would call home from the International Space Station. But by the time Artemis II came around, things were different. All four of his daughters were now adults, and preparing them for his journey around the moon meant discussing the mission's risks, including the possibility that he might not return home.

Glover recalled his wife telling him something he described as maybe the scariest thing he'd ever heard.

"You should have this talk with our daughters.".

And although he knew she was right, it wasn't an easy conversation to have.

"We did, and it did not go well in my opinion," Glover admitted. "Well, it's not about going well. The talk needed to be done, just because it's hard.".

The following day, Glover sent his daughters and wife a poem, Live Your Life, by Chief Tecumseh.

The poem helped Glover express something he had struggled to put into words during their conversation: why he believed the risks of traveling to the moon were worth taking.

Recent findings suggest that "It was a very tough conversation, but they understood that I know this is risky. I wasn't just telling them Dad's risking his life. There's a real point to this and there's a reason to take this risk," Glover explained. "This poem helped me to say it in a way that I didn't have words for.".

In a recent development, after traveling around the moon and returning safely to Earth, one moment stood out above all others. When we asked Glover in a separate interview at Starmus on Oct. 20, which moment from Artemis II he would most like to relive, he answered immediately.

"It's the true, ultimate mission accomplishment. Just 'we did it.' We survived. My family is relieved, and there's just nothing like it," Glover explained. "There's nothing like coming home. There's nothing like returning to Earth.".

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

According to recent reports, daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#24314. NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1192 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that organic carbon has been confirmed in two ancient Martian rocks examined by NASA's Perseverance rover, adding an important fresh piece to the puzzle of whether Mars once supported life.
  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery builds on NASA's September 2025 announcement that Perseverance had identified a potential biosignature.
  • The study was co-led by Ashley Murphy, a postdoctoral researcher at the Planetary Science Institute, and Kyle Uckert, Deputy Principal Investigator of the SHERLOC instrument.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that organic carbon has been confirmed in two ancient Martian rocks examined by NASA's Perseverance rover, adding an important fresh piece to the puzzle of whether Mars once supported life. Even more surprising, the material was found just beneath the planet's surface, where harsh conditions can destroy organic compounds.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery builds on NASA's September 2025 announcement that Perseverance had identified a potential biosignature. A potential biosignature is a substance or feature that could have formed through biological activity, although other explanations are possible. Now, research published in Science Advances provides definitive confirmation that the same two rocks, located in Mars' Bright Angel formation, contain organic carbon, an essential component of life. The findings also offer a clearer picture of the material's characteristics and how it may have been preserved.

The study was co-led by Ashley Murphy, a postdoctoral researcher at the Planetary Science Institute, and Kyle Uckert, Deputy Principal Investigator of the SHERLOC instrument.

NASA's Perseverance Rover Detects Complex Organic Carbon.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate the rocks, researchers used the Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman & Luminescence for Organics & Chemicals (SHERLOC) instrument mounted on Perseverance's robotic arm. The instrument examined several rocks in the Bright Angel formation within Jezero crater, where the rover also collected a sample from a rock named "Cheyava Falls.".

SHERLOC uses a technique called Raman spectroscopy, which shines laser light onto a material to identify and map its minerals and organic compounds without damaging the rock.

The measurements revealed macromolecular carbon (MMC), a form of carbon consisting of large, interconnected networks of carbon atoms. This type of material is also found in rocks on Earth and in meteorites. Importantly, it can form through biological activity or through chemical processes that do not involve life, so its presence alone cannot establish that Mars was once inhabited.

The surrounding geology offers additional clues about how the material reached these rocks. Billions of years ago, water flowed through a river channel into Jezero crater, carrying sediment that gradually settled on the bottom. Over time, those fine particles hardened into the mudstone formations Perseverance is now exploring.

Sources indicate that researchers detected the carbon within these ancient sediments and alongside carbonate and sulfate minerals that developed later as water altered the rocks. This distribution raises the possibility that organic material entered or formed within the rocks during at least two separate periods of Mars' geological history.

"While the specific formation mechanism of the MMC detected in the Bright Angel mudstones remains unknown, this is still one of the most exciting findings to date," Murphy said.

Organic Carbon Survives Just Beneath Mars' Harsh Surface.

Sources indicate that one of the most striking results concerns where the organic carbon was found. The material survived only a few microns below the exposed Martian surface, at a depth smaller than the thickness of a sheet of paper. This is the shallowest detection of macromolecular carbon ever reported on Mars.

That location makes the finding particularly unusual. Mars' surface is exposed to radiation, sunlight, and chemically reactive substances that can break down organic molecules. Scientists would generally expect these conditions to make long-term preservation especially difficult so close to the surface.

In a recent development, "The Martian surface environment includes radiation and chemical oxidants that are destructive to organics, and terrestrial laboratory simulations have shown that the survival time of organics in Martian-like conditions -- especially at or near the surface -- depends on factors such as the type of organic molecule and the surrounding minerals," Murphy said. "The MMC detected in the Bright Angel mudstones is either resistant to degradation and/or has been sufficiently shielded by other minerals, such as clays, or iron-rich Martian soil.".

In other words, the carbon may have survived because of its own chemical durability, protection provided by surrounding minerals, or a combination of the two. Understanding how it endured could help scientists determine where similar organic compounds might remain preserved elsewhere on Mars.

Ancient Martian Lakes and Rivers May Have Been Rich in Organic Material.

The findings also suggest that organic carbon may not have been confined to a single region of ancient Mars.

Perseverance collected the Bright Angel sample more than 2,000 miles from Gale Crater, where NASA's Curiosity rover previously detected organic compounds. Finding organic material at such widely separated locations suggests that the chemistry associated with life's building blocks may once have been common across the Martian landscape.

In a recent development, "It is encouraging for Martian habitability," Murphy mentioned. "This indicates that billions of years ago, organics may have been more than just locally present and may have been more widely available in ancient lakes and rivers on Mars.".

The possibility of widespread organic material is significant because ancient Mars once had environments containing liquid water. If organic compounds were also broadly available, some of those lakes and rivers may have offered crucial chemical ingredients for life.

Recent findings suggest that however, discovering those ingredients does not mean that living organisms were present. Organic carbon can be produced without biology, and scientists still need to determine exactly how the material in the Bright Angel rocks formed.

Could Martian Rocks Preserve Evidence of Ancient Life?

Determining whether the Bright Angel formation contains fossilized microorganisms remains beyond the capabilities of the rovers currently exploring Mars. Neither Curiosity in Gale Crater nor Perseverance in Jezero Crater carries the large, energy-intensive laboratory equipment needed to conclusively distinguish fossil evidence of ancient life from geological processes.

According to recent reports, perseverance was designed to search for potential biosignatures, including features like those identified in the Cheyava Falls rock. From that perspective, the discovery represents a "resounding win for Mars science," Murphy remarked.

Sources indicate that the next major step would be to examine Martian samples using the more sophisticated instruments available in laboratories on Earth. Such equipment could reveal details too small or chemically subtle for the rover's instruments to resolve, helping researchers determine whether biological processes or nonliving chemistry produced the organic carbon.

Sources indicate that if samples from the Bright Angel formation eventually reach Earth, scientists hope to study their minerals and organic compounds with much greater sensitivity and resolution. These investigations could help explain how the macromolecular carbon formed, how it survived, and what its presence reveals about the distribution of organic material across Mars.

It has been revealed that murphy continues to collaborate with the SHERLOC science team as Perseverance explores the Martian surface. Her research also includes studying Earth materials that resemble Martian rocks and using Raman spectroscopy to improve how scientists interpret the measurements returned by the rover.

Murphy's work on SHERLOC Instrument Mars 2020 was supported through JPL Subcontract No. 1641753 to the Planetary Science Institute.

#24313. Sunrise on the Reaping review: The biggest and boldest Hunger Games yet

Sunrise on the Reaping review: The biggest and boldest Hunger Games yet

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that are you looking for a movie to thoroughly wallop you?
  • Sources indicate that based on Suzanne Collins' second prequel novel following The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping once again rewinds the clock on Panem to the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell.
  • Sources indicate that the question here is not whether Haymitch will survive the games.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that are you looking for a movie to thoroughly wallop you? To leave you emotionally battered, physically exhausted, and full of despair and hope at the same time? Then allow me to prescribe a healthy dose of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, the sixth film in the Hunger Games series.

Sources indicate that based on Suzanne Collins' second prequel novel following The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping once again rewinds the clock on Panem to the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell. These are the biggest Hunger Games yet, with 48 tributes instead of the standard 24. Among them is Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), future mentor to series protagonists Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark.

Sources indicate that the question here is not whether Haymitch will survive the games. We know, by virtue of the entire original trilogy, that he does. But before he was the cynical, heavy-drinking, lone wolf victor audiences met in The Hunger Games, he was an optimistic 16-year-old with a caring family, a loving relationship, and a solid community in District 12. So the real question of Sunrise on the Reaping becomes, what broke that young man down so thoroughly? The answer is, unsurprisingly, bleak as all hell. But director Francis Lawrence executes it in thrilling (if occasionally overstuffed) fashion, with a Hunger Games sequence that blows series-high Catching Fire's own games out of the water, and a dogged focus on the philosophical themes at the core of Collins' work.

This being a Hunger Games movie, there are certain key beats it needs to hit. First, tributes need to be reaped. In this case, District 12's motley crew is made up of Haymitch, Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), and Louella McCoy (Molly McCann). From there, the tributes must go to the Capitol and witness its gaudy depravity for themselves. They get makeovers, train, give interviews, and eventually make their way into the Capitol's ultimate death trap.

In a recent development, viewers have seen these beats before in The Hunger Games and Catching Fire. They also witnessed a deliberately scaled-back version in prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which established the Games' evolution from what was essentially a run-down cage match to a glossy propaganda spectacle.

After sending us through three very different Hunger Games, how can the franchise create a latest variation on the same brutal theme? First, by making Sunrise on the Reaping a heist movie. Granted, Haymitch and his allies aren't actually trying to steal anything from the Capitol. Rather, they're trying to break the arena and send a clear message. For that, Haymitch gets roped into a scheme cooked up by former victor Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) and his son, District 3 tribute Ampert (Percy Daggs IV). With a complex series of moving parts, Ampert and Haymitch's plan captures the essence of a dangerous heist, and Lawrence delivers the suspense to match.

In a recent development, then, there's the arena. If you thought Catching Fire's clock was a sadistic marvel of game-making, not to mention a visual feast thanks to its tropical jungles and beaches, get ready for a level up. The arena for the Second Quarter Quell is a technicolor nightmare. Lush flower beds and crystal clear streams hide poisonous underbellies. Swarms of beautiful birds and butterflies will kill at a moment's notice. Even an idyllic, snow-capped mountain hides explosive horrors. Thankfully, Sunrise on the Reaping is actually colorful to match, its eye-popping hues reminding blockbuster filmmakers everywhere that yes, vibrancy is still possible!

That vibrancy in Sunrise on the Reaping extends to the broader world of Panem itself, which has taken on a distinctive '70s look. The Capitol is awash in glitzy psychedelics, a far cry from the post-war dilapidation of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. As the Games have grown more extravagant, so, too have the Capitol citizens. Take District 12 escort Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close, almost unrecognizable under prosthetics and an uncanny tape facelift). She is the pinnacle of excess, from her visible cosmetic work to her neon fashion. Close is chewing so much scenery she could probably devour the entire arena, but it's exactly what the role calls for: ridiculous pomp, circumstance, and venomous hatred for the Districts.

It has been revealed that drusilla is one of the fresh characters introduced in Sunrise on the Reaping. However, a massive chunk of the film's supporting cast is made up of familiar figures from the original trilogy: Capitol insider Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons); master of ceremonies Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin); former victors Beetee, Mags (Lili Taylor), and Wiress (Maya Hawke); stylist Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning); and of course, President Coriolanus Snow (Ralph Fiennes). Their non-stop introductions give Sunrise on the Reaping an unfortunate case of prequel-itis, even if they play key roles in the story. Their presence also means the involvement of many new Capitol characters feels muted. Billy Porter's snake-loving stylist Magno Stift gets short shrift (and even shorter screen time), while his helpers Proserpina (Iris Apatow) and Vitus (Edvin Ryding) might as well be afterthoughts.

Thankfully, the District 12 newcomers fare far better. As Haymitch's great love Lenore Dove, Whitney Peak is a radiant beam of rebellious wisdom. Elsewhere, each of the tributes buck misconceptions about them to reveal their true mettle underneath. Maysilee may seem stuck-up and aloof at first, but Grace swiftly unleashes the ferocious survivor in her. Wang brings kind courage to oddsmaker Wyatt, and McCann is steely sweet as Louella.

Industry observers note that leading it all is Zada, who does an admirable job making Haymitch his own, all while balancing Harrelson's mannerisms from the original trilogy. Put them saying "sweetheart" side by side and tell me that's not the same character, years apart.

According to recent reports, sunrise on the Reaping works hard to build out this captivating fresh version of Panem and the Games, but once it starts really playing in that sandbox, you're in for wave after wave of brutality. It's almost impressive how, after five books and six movies, the Hunger Games franchise can still find new ways to up the emotional pain of watching children fight to death under the thumb of an authoritarian regime. You'd think we'd already hit that peak with Rue's death in the first Hunger Games, and yet!

No spoilers, but let's just say I hope Zada's contract included a bonus for each time he had to cradle the body of a dear ally and tearfully beg them to stay with him. That his performance and the film never feel stale as they go through the motions of helpless grief time and time again is a testament to how distinct each of Haymitch's relationships feel.

But while Sunrise on the Reaping is arguably the Hunger Games at its most tragic, it's also the franchise at its angriest. Every instalment in the series has critiqued the Capitol, but Sunrise on the Reaping puts a laser focus on the mundane machinery that keeps these systems of power in place. As the film opens, we see Peacekeepers and Capitol staffers performing administrative tasks for the Reaping, like putting up barricades and placards dictating where children should stand. Elsewhere, the propaganda machine chugs along, with cameramen like Plutarch always finding the perfect shot to tell the Capitol's story. (And always knowing which context to leave out to make the Capitol look its absolute best.).

According to recent reports, throughout, though, Sunrise on the Reaping also turns its lens on Panem's citizens, asking why they allow themselves to be ruled by such a horrific regime. Collins opens Sunrise on the Reaping with several epigraphs, including two from Scottish philosopher David Hume, the first of which details his thoughts on implicit submission. The film takes that message to heart, repeatedly questioning what leads the many not to rise up against the few that govern them. Why do District 12's citizens stand mutely by while Drusilla and Plutarch re-stage a key moment from the Reaping ceremony? Why do armed tributes not turn on the unarmed Peacekeepers who oversee them at training? Sunrise on the Reaping doesn't take a subtle approach — at one point Plutarch straight-up states "no more implicit submission" — but then again, it's also vital to see a blockbuster not sand down the novel's overt messaging.

It has been revealed that it's also vital for a film this heavy to have hope, and almost miraculously, Sunrise on the Reaping, does. The film emphasizes the fact of its title: that for Haymitch's whole life, the sun has always risen on the Reaping. But as Lenore tells him, just because that's the way things have been for so long doesn't mean they'll be that way forever. (Their conversation remixes the novel's second epigraph from Hume.).

Anyone who's watched or read the original Hunger Games series knows that Panem will one day see a world where the sun doesn't rise on the Reaping. It'll just take a lot of work and sacrifice to get there. In Sunrise on the Reaping, we get to witness the first sparks of that eventual reunion. Knowing where Haymitch's story ends turns his tragedy into a bittersweet bridge to the future, making Sunrise on the Reaping a perfect bookend to the Hunger Games franchise as it stands. (At least, until Collins decides to return to Panem.).

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters Nov. 20.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • To children, though, the videos are a portal into a temporary bliss state so powerful that many parents have come to view Accurso as a quasi-­mythical figure.
  • Accurso speaks in a singsong voice when she’s performing in her trademark denim overalls and bubblegum-pink shirt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rachel Accurso, better known by her stage name Ms. Rachel, specializes in making videos for babies and toddlers. She started as a DIY creator on YouTube, working with her musician husband Aron and shooting around Newly introduced York on a shoestring budget. To an adult with a fully formed frontal lobe, her videos can be, well, a bit much: a whole lot of close-ups on Accurso’s mouth making shapes, cutesy stomp-clap sessions, and winsome nursery rhymes.

To children, though, the videos are a portal into a temporary bliss state so powerful that many parents have come to view Accurso as a quasi-­mythical figure. She has racked up billions of views and gained so many fervent fans that she inked a juicy deal with Netflix last year, cementing her status as the biggest star in digital children’s entertainment. This fall, she released her first album, I’m So Happy, and she sells a slate of branded toys and picture books. But when people look back on 2026, they’ll likely remember Ms. Rachel for something unrelated to her kid-centric empire: offering an example, for adults, of how to be a good person.

Accurso speaks in a singsong voice when she’s performing in her trademark denim overalls and bubblegum-pink shirt. The former preschool music teacher started out hoping to create videos to help her son communicate, focusing on sign language, repetition, and other strategies employed by language development specialists. The saccharine voice is part of it. Research indicates that speaking in high-pitched, rhythmic patterns best spurs imitations from kids.

But this cotton-candy tone belies the convictions that drive Accurso professionally and personally. She is perhaps the single staunchest celebrity advocate for children and has faced fierce criticism for her advocacy on behalf of Palestinian kids. On her show, she has featured children like Rahaf Saed, a toddler who became a double amputee after an Israeli air strike hit her home in Gaza. At an awards ceremony, Accurso wore a dress embroidered with artwork from Gazan children. Recently, she pledged $1 million to the Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund; she’s gone so far as to insist that all of her collaborators speak on the glitch and has called out celebrities who fail to do so.

It has been revealed that she’s often compared to Mr. Rogers, but Accurso is as much an inheritor of Jane Fonda’s activist mantle. Blowback to her advocacy has been intense—pro-Israel groups have accused Accurso of antisemitism. One of these groups even wrote to Florida’s attorney general, asking for Accurso to be investigated as a potential “foreign agent” spewing “Hamas-aligned propaganda.” None of this has deterred her from speaking out. “I would risk everything, and I will risk my career over and over to stand up” for kids, she said in a radio interview last year.

Accurso’s willingness to duke it out doesn’t end with Gaza. She has weathered right-wing ire for employing nonbinary performer Jules Hoffman, for celebrating Pride Month, and for speaking out against ICE. She helped draw attention to the plight of a nonverbal 5-year-old imprisoned at a South Texas detention center by featuring a Zoom call with him on her social media. An immigration lawyer saw Accurso’s post and connected with the boy’s family, helping secure his release. “We need to put children’s lives and human lives before our hesitations,” Accurso said in an interview about her activism around ICE detentions. “I just urge everyone, especially those with huge platforms and privilege, to speak out.” For her efforts, Fox News described Accurso as “really sinister.”.

Industry observers note that talk to anyone who has encountered Accurso in person and they’re likely to share a glowing story about how lovely she is. I’ll add mine to the pile. A few years ago, when I interviewed her for a story about YouTube and children’s television, I was bleary-eyed on Zoom after a long night with a teething baby. I mentioned that my then 1-year-old adored her videos, especially a song she sings about hopping bunnies, and that I’d sung it to him at night. A few weeks later, I got an email from Accurso. It had a video attached; she’d made my son a personalized sing-along, making sure to say his name repeatedly during the Bunny Hop song so he knew it was something special, just for him.

What did we miss? Tell us about your favorite moments of 2026 in the comments below.

#24309. Superheated magma could fuel towering lava fountains

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1190 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Superheated magma could fuel towering lava fountains

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Why do some volcanoes send towering fountains of lava into the sky while others release molten rock in much calmer eruptions?
  • An international research team led by The University of Manchester investigated volcanic material from the 2021 Tajogaite eruption on La Palma, Spain.
  • Superheating occurs when magma reaches temperatures above those at which its crystals would normally remain stable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why do some volcanoes send towering fountains of lava into the sky while others release molten rock in much calmer eruptions? Scientists have discovered that a hidden effect of extreme heat inside magma may help explain these striking differences.

An international research team led by The University of Manchester investigated volcanic material from the 2021 Tajogaite eruption on La Palma, Spain. Their findings reveal that a process known as "superheating" can dramatically slow the formation of crystals inside magma as it travels upward toward Earth's surface.

Superheating occurs when magma reaches temperatures above those at which its crystals would normally remain stable. The researchers found that this extra heat can keep magma relatively fluid for much longer than expected, potentially allowing it to rise rapidly and produce spectacular lava fountains.

The discovery, published in Nature Communications, offers new insight into a long-standing question in volcanology: How does magma's temperature history influence the way a volcano erupts?

How Extreme Heat Changes Magma Deep Inside Volcanoes.

Sources indicate that magma is a mixture of molten rock, gases, and sometimes solid crystals beneath Earth's surface. Once it emerges from a volcano, it is called lava. Although temperature and chemical composition are key in determining how magma behaves, the new research suggests that the heating it experienced before an eruption can also make a major difference.

Under normal conditions, crystals begin forming as magma cools. This process often starts around tiny existing crystals that act as "seeds," providing surfaces on which additional crystals can grow.

Superheating can disrupt this process in two notable ways. First, sufficiently high temperatures can dissolve the microscopic crystal seeds that would otherwise encourage latest crystals to develop. Second, the heat changes the internal structure of the molten material, making it more uniform and less favorable for new crystal formation.

These changes matter because crystals affect magma's viscosity, which describes how easily a substance flows. As more crystals develop, magma generally becomes thicker and more resistant to movement. This can influence both its speed of ascent and the way trapped volcanic gases escape.

Lead author Dr. Barbara Bonechi, Research Associate at The University of Manchester, explained:.

"The history of crystal and bubble growth can dramatically control how a magma erupts, in particular as more crystals grow, they eventually have a dramatic effect on magma viscosity. Until now, we did not fully understand the dynamics of crystal growth for magmas that received an injection of superheat just before ascent. But using our exciting and newly developed X-ray transparent pressure vessel combined with synchrotron X-ray microtomography, we can actually observe these processes 'in situ'.".

Scientists Discover an Eight-Hour Delay in Crystal Formation.

To investigate what happens inside superheated magma, the researchers recreated volcanic conditions in the laboratory using material collected from the Tajogaite eruption. The magma involved in that eruption may have experienced superheating before reaching the surface and while rising through Earth's crust.

The team conducted experiments under carefully controlled temperatures and pressures designed to reproduce conditions encountered by magma underground.

Industry observers note that at Diamond Light Source, a major scientific research facility, the researchers used synchrotron X-ray microtomography to watch crystals develop in real time. This advanced imaging technique uses extremely powerful X-rays to examine the internal structure of materials in three dimensions without having to cut them open.

A specially developed pressure vessel that allows X-rays to pass through it made these observations possible while the magma was subjected to volcanic conditions.

The team also performed complementary experiments in Prague, where samples could be examined over longer periods outside the real-time imaging setup. Together, these approaches allowed the researchers to observe how different heating conditions affected the timing of crystal formation.

The results revealed a remarkable difference.

Magma that had not undergone superheating began producing crystals after approximately 20 minutes. However, when magma was subjected to strong superheating, the beginning of crystallization was delayed for more than eight hours.

This substantial delay suggests that intense heating can leave magma without newly forming crystals for far longer than scientists might otherwise expect, with potentially notable consequences for volcanic eruptions.

Why Superheated Magma Could Produce Towering Lava Fountains.

The researchers next explored how these laboratory findings might affect real volcanoes.

They incorporated the measured delays in crystal formation into computer models that simulate how magma rises through Earth's crust. These models account for changes in magma properties as the molten material moves toward the surface.

The simulations revealed two very different possibilities.

Sources indicate that when superheating delays crystallization, magma can remain relatively fluid as it rises. Because it encounters less resistance to flowing, it may travel upward more rapidly, potentially creating conditions that favor dramatic lava fountains.

These spectacular eruptions occur when escaping volcanic gases propel molten rock high above a vent, producing jets and fountains of glowing lava.

In contrast, magma that begins crystallizing earlier becomes more viscous and tends to ascend more slowly. This slower movement gives volcanic gases additional time to escape, favoring gentler eruptions in which lava flows out onto the surface rather than being thrown high into the air.

Such behavior is known as an effusive eruption, a type of volcanic activity characterized primarily by flowing lava.

The findings suggest that even when volcanic systems have similar characteristics, differences in their earlier heating histories may help explain why their eruptions look and behave so differently.

A Newly introduced Clue for Predicting Volcanic Eruptions.

Understanding what happens to magma before it reaches the surface is essential for assessing volcanic hazards. Scientists monitor signals such as earthquakes, ground deformation, and volcanic gas emissions to identify changes within active volcanoes.

It has been revealed that however, predicting exactly how an eruption will unfold remains difficult. Two volcanoes with seemingly similar magma compositions and gas conditions can still display markedly different eruptive behavior.

The new research suggests that the effects of superheating and the timing of crystal formation deserve greater attention in volcanic forecasting models.

By accounting for these previously underappreciated processes, researchers may eventually be able to better interpret volcanic monitoring data and assess whether rising magma is more likely to produce vigorous lava fountains or gentler lava flows.

The results do not mean that magma temperature alone determines how explosive an eruption will be. Instead, they identify another notable piece of the complex physical processes that shape volcanic activity.

Recent findings suggest that co-author Dr. Margherita Polacci, Senior Lecturer in Volcanology at The University of Manchester, highlighted the potential importance of the findings for understanding volcanic hazards:.

Industry observers note that "Current volcanic hazard models typically focus on magma chemistry, gas content and pressure changes. This work suggests that pre-eruptive thermal history and crystallization kinetics may also play an vital role in controlling magma ascent and eruptive behavior, with implications for volcanic hazard assessment.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that with seven wins from eight nominations, Tame Impala was no deadbeat at the 40th annual ARIA Awards, presented Wednesday evening (Nov. 18) at Sydney’s Hordern Pavilion. Explore Tame Impala See latest videos, charts and news.

See latest videos, charts and news.

Recent findings suggest that kevin Parker’s psychedelic pop outfit snagged the biggest honors on the night, including album of the year for Tame Impala’s fifth studio album, Deadbeat; best solo artist; and song of the year for “Dracula.” On winning solo artist, the Western Australian singer, songwriter and multi-instrumentalist used the moment to unfurl the joke that was on everyone’s mind. ARIA has now put the argument to bed that, yes, Tame Impala is a one-man band. Actually, it’s not so clear-cut. Tame Impala has, in fact won for best group at the ARIAs on three occasions, in 2013, 2015, and 2020. Related Noah Kahan Reacts to 2027 Grammy Nominations Snub: 'I Was In My Feelings for a Sec' 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Revs Its Engines & Leads 2026 Game Awards Nominations: Full List Cody Johnson on Why He's Skipping 2026 CMA Awards: 'Going 100 MPH All the Time Isn't Healthy'.

Industry observers note that by snagging album of the year for Deadbeat, a record that went to No. 2 on the ARIA Albums Chart in 2025, but missed out on the crown and got a lukewarm review from some armchair critics, Parker got the last laugh. “I’m so grateful,” he remarked. “There are so many great f—ing Australian artists and so many great nominees.” Deadbeat “got off to a rocky start, to be honest…but I’m so proud of it. It’s getting the respect that it deserves, I think.”.

As previously reported, Tame Impala collected the second annual Global Impact Award presented by Spotify. Savage Garden’s Darren Hayes was on hand to present the honor. “I’m so proud to be an Aussie artist, always,” Parker remarked. “Whenever I go overseas, I feel like I wear a badge on my shirt.” And, he noted, he’s “one of the lucky ones,” an artist who’s had an international career and just this week collected four Grammy Award nominations.

According to recent reports, another artist enjoying a global career is Ecca Vandal. As the Glastonbury Festival 2027 lineup dropped with her name on it, the Australian punk rock artist was converting four of her seven ARIA Award nominations, including the Michael Gudinski breakthrough artist, best independent release and best alternative release, in respect to her sophomore album Looking For People To Unfollow. “Not sure what breakthrough means,” she mentioned after snagging the award named after Michael Gudinski, the late, great Mushroom Group founder, but “the biggest breakthrough for me was realizing I didn’t need to be anybody but myself.” The rising star also gave a shout out to those people who said “no” along the way, a burn which forced her to “dig deeper.” The naysayers, “you did me a really major favor.”.

After collecting their first-ever ARIA No. 1 in August with their self-titled fifth album, DMA’S won a brace of ARIA Awards, including best group, while G Flip was also a two-time winner on the night (best video and best Australian live act).

K-pop superstars BTS won for most popular international artist, beating the likes of Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo and Olivia Dean. Other winners included Bluey (best children’s album), Ninajirachi (Porter Robinson, for best dance/electronic release), Donny Benét (best jazz album), Emma Donovan (best blues & roots album) and Karnivool (best hard rock/heavy metal album).

According to recent reports, if music was the glue that connected the night, artificial intelligence — or rather, the threat of it to the creative community — was the theme. On each industry table, reminder of the “Not AI’s to Take” campaign, while presenters including Spiderbait’s Kram, Tim Minchin, Tash Sultana and Elton John shared their thoughts on the matter. Sultana, the singer, songwriter and guitarist, offered a poem as she presented the independent category: “roses are red, violets are blue, if you support AI music, f— you.”.

In a recent development, ARIA doesn’t support it. Earlier this year, the trade body announced it would ban from its official charts those recordings that featured mostly AI-generated music.

Performers at the 2026 ARIA Awards included Genesis Owusu; Blusher; Ecca Vandal; 3%, Scribe and Fred Leone; BOY SODA; and 2026 ARIA Hall of Fame inductees Spiderbait, which closed out the show with a medley of their hits including “Calypso,” “Buy Me A Pony” and “Black Betty.”.

Among record labels, it was an especially solid outing for Sony Music which had its fingerprints on 18 of the 30 awards.

Industry observers note that “What a night,” remarks ARIA CEO Annabelle Herd. “I am absolutely in awe of the incredible power of human artistry and Australian music. Tame Impala capping a sensational year on the world stage by sweeping the night on home soil, Ecca Vandal making her ARIA performance debut and walking away with four awards… then Sir Elton! I couldn’t be prouder to be the CEO of ARIA. Congratulations to all of our winners and a huge thank you to every artist who performed, you blew us away.”.

It has been revealed that the ARIAs, the Australian recorded music industry’s flagship awards ceremony, is supported by Destination NSW, in partnership with Spotify, and beamed out live on Paramount+ and broadcast on 10. Performances and moments will be available on the @ARIA.official YouTube channel.

Despite restrictive abortion laws, Poland's 'Abortomat' — a locker that dispenses abortion pills — helps women who want to end a pregnancy

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.
  • It has been revealed that known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk.
  • Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.

It has been revealed that known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.

Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.

In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.

Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, showed DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.

Recent findings suggest that inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.

In a recent development, the "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.

Parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.

"When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," noted Wydrzynska.

In a recent development, women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.

According to recent reports, in 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.

Recent findings suggest that because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.

Wydrzynska remarked she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.

Dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, mentioned the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated.".

She mentioned that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.

"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she remarked.

The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.

"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," mentioned Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.

Wydrzynska said anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.

At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan.".

"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she noted.

Earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.

Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.

Sources indicate that "I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she remarked.

In a recent development, "I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.

Another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, said they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.

In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.

Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.

It has been revealed that "I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she stated.

After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.

Afterwards, Tusk mentioned abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.

In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.

One reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.

The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.

Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.

According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents noted they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.

Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • "We know that more and more people — more and more creators — are kind of multidisciplinary, especially for folks who are maybe video first and then they have to worry about audio second," Steve Marek, Associate Product Manager at Shure, noted in a briefing with Mashable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that spatial audio is having a moment in the creator-verse. Just last month, Sony introduced its ECM-AX10 spatial audio mic, and now Shure is entering the category with its USB-C MV360 and MV360+ spatial audio microphones.

"We know that more and more people — more and more creators — are kind of multidisciplinary, especially for folks who are maybe video first and then they have to worry about audio second," Steve Marek, Associate Product Manager at Shure, noted in a briefing with Mashable. "So, we know that there's room for that industry to grow.".

Marek said, "We really wanted to think of this as a microphone that people can grow with," and that rather than having five different audio recording tools, creators can do everything with the MV360 and have flexibility with their audio output.

Recent findings suggest that the MV360 retails for $349 and is available now. The microphone kit comes with the USB-C mic, a tripod, a cold shoe mic clip, a 5/8-inch mic clip, a phone clamp, two USB-C cables, a carrying case, and a foam windscreen. The microphone also has an onboard 3.5mm headphone jack.

Recent findings suggest that the MV360 features four capture modes: mono, stereo, immersive binaural, and auto tracking. The latter uses virtual microphones that steer toward the loudest sound source and is ideal for recording podcasts, interviews, or moving subjects. Regardless of capture mode, you'll get a ready-to-use two-channel audio file that requires no post-production work — though it is compatible with editing apps and devices should you want to adjust or edit.

The MV360 can be as simple or as complex as you want. If you're a skilled audio engineer, you can mix to your heart's desire. Or if you've never seen audio software in your life, you have perfectly good sound straight from the mic.

Recent findings suggest that the MV360+ is not available yet, but will be the more advanced option geared toward field recordists, videographers, and VR storytellers. It'll pair with DSLR cameras, action cameras, and 360 cameras. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

In a recent development, shure's MOTIV app is where you can set your capture mode and edit audio that you've recorded. There are plenty of presets and adjustable settings that you can play around with, too. Slide the level adjuster to capture every minor sound for ASMR or to avoid audio spiking. You can even select where the microphone is oriented in relation to the subject — whether it's facing up, down, or on its side. There's a little diagram in the app that shows a sound heat map, so you can see exactly from which direction sound is hitting the microphone.

You can record and edit directly in the app. And one really cool feature is that you can move "virtual microphones" after you've already recorded to better boost directional sound.

Industry observers note that I received a test unit of the MV360 microphone ahead of its launch and have had a chance to play around with it a bit. It sounds great for unboxing videos — it picks up on all the crispy sounds without sounding blown out. I tested some whispering ASMR, and I was able to boost the audio levels in the companion app before recording to really pick up on every minor sound. I will be using this as an excuse to buy a bunch of weird candy from Five Below to further test the microphone's ASMR-ability, so stay tuned for that. We'll have a full review of the MV360 coming later.

Recent findings suggest that my only minor frustration with the microphone is how bulky/heavy it is. With pocket mics, like the DJI Mic Mini, there's a small receiver that you plug into your phone. The MV360 plugs directly into your phone or computer via USB-C, so it's tethered to your recording device. Clamping my phone and the mic to the tripod was just a little clunky when oriented in portrait mode. But its heft also makes sense, considering how much more advanced the audio recording is compared to small creator mics.

Also, I love that Shure includes a tripod with the MV360, but I found myself reaching for my personal tripod for most of my recordings.

Neither of those are reason enough to discredit the microphone at all — just some minor learning curves.

The MV360 is available now from Shure and third-party retailers like Amazon for $349. The MV360+ will be available in early 2027 for $449.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Justin Devenny's equaliser in Budapest took Northern Ireland into Nations League A for the first time.

Speaking before his side ground out the required point against Hungary to seal top spot in Nations League Group B2, Northern Ireland's Trai Hume told reporters that automatic promotion had not been the most immediate aim coming into the campaign.

Two years ago, this side were a League C team, battling to return to the second tier from a group containing Belarus, Bulgaria and Luxembourg.

Fast forward 24 months and a League A place was secured on the final night of an unbeaten campaign that had looked a serious challenge. Prior the trip to Georgia in September, Northern Ireland had a record of played 10, lost eight and drawn two at this level.

Recent findings suggest that across six games in eight weeks, the side won three and drew three, conceding just once along the way. Justin Devenny's brilliant equaliser in Budapest on Tuesday secured the draw required to top the group and earn promotion to the top tier for the first time.

"It's a great feeling for us," stated manager Michael O'Neill.

"In a way, we sort of set out when we came into this level of competition first of all to try and stay in it. Obviously to do that, you have to, you have to be in the top two positions.

"We knew that would help us potentially with the draw for Euro 2028, but to come away unbeaten, to to finish top and to give the performances we've given against some very good teams, it's very encouraging.".

Northern Ireland draw with Hungary to seal Nations League promotion.

Watch: Devenny the hero as NI earn promotion.

Belief and bench help NI scale fresh heights.

With such a young team on the international stage, there will always be more intangible markers of progress too.

It is perhaps easy to forget that not so long ago Pierce Charles' shot-stopping was being questioned as a weaker part of his game when compared to his range of passing.

Quite apart from a penalty save from Georgia's Khvicha Kvaratskhelia to start the group, the Queens Park Rangers loanee made momentum-changing stops from Georges Mikautadze in Tbilisi and Danylo Sikan against Ukraine in Belfast last week.

All three of the Ruairi McConville-Tom Atcheson-Ciaron Brown defensive triumvirate have enhanced their reputations too, while, perhaps not yet in a first-choice XI, Patrick Kelly, Terry Devlin and Brodie Spencer feel increasingly trusted members of a deepening pool of players.

O'Neill may have only made nine changes to his starting teams across the six games, but it felt notable how often those coming in did not look out of place.

The bench then made a huge impact in the draw that sealed promotion with two players at opposing ends of the experience spectrum, Josh Magennis and Kieran Morrison, to the fore.

"We have a squad now where I think the younger players are coming in and making an impact straight away," said O'Neill, who still has the likes of Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard to come back into his squad.

"Which is a real positive, particularly if you look at the likes of Tom and Ruairi, but also Kieran Morrison and Ceadach [O'Neill] coming in and getting minutes early in their international careers.

"I just think that like the the squad is still very much still in development, we we still have areas where we still need to improve.".

The next staging post for this Northern Ireland team is the Euro 2028 qualifying draw in Belfast on 6 December.

They will be among the second seeds thanks to their top-two Nations League finish and, depending on whether they land in a four or five-team group, could face qualifiers as early as March next year.

Not only did their Nations League performance win promotion to League A and a place with Europe's elite, it has also all but guaranteed a play-off for the Euros if the qualifying campaign does not go to initiative.

"The great thing is we finish on a high and the players go back to their clubs now, they have to deal with a lot of football, they're all playing and demanding leagues," added O'Neill.

"Depending on the draw, we might come in in March and have friendly games which might be a nice thing for us to have.

"But we can just go in and see what the draw brings in December and then we can sort of plot the next 12 months.".

After a string of impressive performances in the past three months, they will do so with serious momentum.

Breaking: Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1091 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, physicists have captured an extraordinary quantum phenomenon in which electrons appear to leap across energy gaps that would normally be off limits.
  • The effect is similar to stepping into an elevator and watching the floor display change from "1," "2," and "3" directly to "20." Instead of traveling through the seventeen floors in between, you somehow arrive at the twentieth floor.
  • It has been revealed that these unusual events are known as Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, physicists have captured an extraordinary quantum phenomenon in which electrons appear to leap across energy gaps that would normally be off limits. Using a upcoming type of slow-motion electron camera, researchers were able to watch these incredibly fast movements in graphene, revealing how powerful electric fields can drive electrons between different energy states.

The effect is similar to stepping into an elevator and watching the floor display change from "1," "2," and "3" directly to "20." Instead of traveling through the seventeen floors in between, you somehow arrive at the twentieth floor. Although this sounds impossible in everyday life, electrons can make comparable jumps in the quantum world.

It has been revealed that these unusual events are known as Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions. Physicists have long suspected that they could become increasingly important in high-speed semiconductor electronics, but observing exactly how they unfold has been a major challenge.

Industry observers note that now, researchers from the University of Regensburg, Philipps-Universität Marburg, and Forschungszentrum Jülich have directly tracked these transitions in graphene, a material made from an extremely thin layer of carbon atoms. Their findings, published in Nature, provide a detailed look at how electrons respond to intense electric fields generated by light.

How Electrons Cross Forbidden Energy Gaps.

In semiconductors and similar materials, electrons are restricted to particular ranges of energy called energy bands. Between these bands are regions known as forbidden energy gaps, where electrons cannot ordinarily occupy stable states.

Under normal conditions, electrons tend to remain within their existing energy bands. However, the researchers observed something very different when they exposed graphene to intense pulses of light. The electric field accelerated the electrons and caused some of them to switch from one energy band to another, crossing the intervening gap through a quantum mechanical transition.

To capture these movements, the scientists developed an experimental technique that combines advanced laser technology with electron microscopy. This allowed them to examine electron behavior on timescales far too short for conventional imaging methods.

A Slow-Motion Camera Reveals Quantum Jumps.

In a recent development, "If you want to know who has won a race, you have to watch all participants," explains Vincent Eggers, first author of the study. "Likewise, we must observe as many electrons as possible at one time to catch those that undergo a quantum mechanical transition while moving.".

The key instrument is a photoemission momentum microscope. Rather than producing an enlarged picture of a material's surface, as a traditional microscope would, it measures the energies of electrons and how they are moving. Researchers then use this information to create detailed maps showing how electrons are distributed across different energy states.

One of the biggest technical obstacles was combining these measurements with powerful light fields that oscillate at extremely high speeds. The team needed to drive the electrons into motion while simultaneously recording how their energies and movements changed.

It has been revealed that "Our team worked on this experiment for many years. Now, we can track electrons moving across the entire energy landscape of a solid in real time," notes Rupert Huber.

Ulrich Höfer, a collaborator on the project and a pioneer in ultrafast electron spectroscopy, describes the excitement of witnessing the effect firsthand.

"Being able to observe such a fundamental quantum mechanical process during our first measurement campaign was a very special moment for us - it was also made possible by the samples we used.".

Ultra-Pure Graphene Makes the Discovery Possible.

According to recent reports, the experiment depended on exceptionally pure graphene samples manufactured at Forschungszentrum Jülich. These specially prepared carbon layers were only one atom thick and had to be nearly flawless for the measurements to work.

Industry observers note that "These precision experiments require material that is nearly perfect at the atomic level. This ensures that impurities do not obscure the delicate quantum dynamics of the electrons. Another notable factor for the study was the use of "rotated" graphene, a specialty from Jülich, which allows the quantum dynamics to emerge particularly clearly," emphasizes Stefan Tautz from Forschungszentrum Jülich.

The carefully engineered material made it possible to distinguish the delicate quantum effects from interference caused by imperfections in the graphene.

What the researchers saw was remarkable. When exposed to sufficiently strong light fields, electrons crossed the forbidden energy gap with a transition probability reaching 100 percent.

In a recent development, this result highlights one of the most surprising features of Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions. Electrons can move between energy states with very high probability even when those states are separated by a substantial energy gap.

Sources indicate that the crucial factor is how quickly the electrons approach the gap under the influence of the electric field. This makes the process fundamentally different from conventional quantum tunneling, in which particles pass through a barrier in physical space.

A Latest Path Toward Light-Controlled Electronics.

Beyond revealing a fundamental quantum phenomenon, the newly introduced imaging technique could help scientists understand what prevents electrons from moving in a controlled and predictable way.

The graphene experiments have already provided an important clue. Although the electrons initially move in an orderly fashion, their interactions with the material's crystal lattice gradually disrupt that motion. Understanding these effects could help researchers develop more precise ways to control electron behavior.

Industry observers note that this knowledge is particularly valuable for future electronic technologies that could use the extremely rapid oscillations of light to direct electrons instead of relying entirely on electrical voltages. Such approaches could open latest possibilities for manipulating electronic properties at exceptionally high speeds.

The researchers also expect their method to work with many other quantum materials, allowing scientists to investigate previously inaccessible electron dynamics and potentially discover newly introduced ways to control them.

As Giacomo Inzani from the University of Regensburg explains, the achievement marks the beginning of a much broader exploration.

It has been revealed that "Our experiment opens a panoramic window into the quantum world. Now, we can follow in real time how electrons move through the energy landscape of a material. And this is just the beginning. Our method can be applied to many other quantum materials, opening up completely latest possibilities for controlling their electronic properties selectively with light.".

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a sea of Israeli flags, Yiftach Golov holds one that looks a little different.

Among the hundreds of thousands of protesters who took to the streets for the 13th week in a row on Saturday, Golov hoists a brown flag that represents a group called “Brother and Sisters in Arms.”.

They are veterans – many, like Golov, from elite forces – who now feel they are fighting on a newly introduced battlefield: To save Israeli democracy.

“We believe this is our responsibility to go once again called to the flag of the nation to stop this madness to defend Israel,” Golov said, as he weaved his way through the protesters on Tel Aviv’s Kaplan street, between the high-rises that house many of Israel’s high tech companies.

It has been revealed that during the second intifada, in the early 2000s, Golov served in a special forces reconnaissance unit. He was never before particularly political, focusing more on getting his PhD in biophysics from Tel Aviv University.

But when the protest movement against the Israeli government’s judicial overhaul blueprint began in January, Golov attended one a demonstration and soon became one of thousands of veterans, and now military reservists, who have taken up the cause as their newly introduced mission.

Some, including elite Air Force reservists, have taken it a step further, threatening not to heed the call to train or even serve in protest of the government’s aims planned judicial changes, which would give the governing parties more control over Israel’s judiciary.

It has been revealed that others have taken to becoming some of the most active organizers and demonstrators. Last week, a group from Brothers and Sisters in Arms protested by carrying a figure wrapped in the Israeli flag on a stretcher, the way they would carry a wounded comrade off the field.

While Golov says he has not taken the drastic step to refuse service, he understands the motivation.

“We’re fighting for justice and liberty, just like the American story, that’s the values that that are being represented symbolized back when we look at our flag, that’s something that was lacking lacking for the last few decades. So basically, we reclaim the flag,” he remarked.

Palestinian taxi driver recounts surviving attack by right-wing protesters.

In a recent development, fellow members of the group, all wearing brown shirts with the organization’s logo, come up and say hello. They’re sprinkled all throughout the protests. One is even leading the “Pink Front,” a group of coordinated drummers who look like they are dressed for a rave, and often lead the chants at the protests.

According to recent reports, they’re using skills they learned in the military – how to organize, how to mobilize – now for the protests. But more importantly, they say they have the same type of motivation.

Sources indicate that “The very deep feeling that you are part of something bigger than yourself, that (you’re) allowed to sacrifice anything that is needed, whether it’s your career, health, seriously mental health,” Golov said. “We all have a mission, you’re willing to do it at any cost. You’re very determined, you know that you are on the right side, you’re carrying the torch of light. That keeps us being highly motivated despite the fact that we’re not sleeping for days.”.

Israel’s protest movement is made up of many disparate groups, but the pressure from Israel’s much vaunted veterans has been seen as a key to moving the needle.

Last Monday, after weeks of sustained protests and the largest general strike in Israeli history, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu unveiled a pause to the legislation, to allow time for negotiations with the opposition.

But despite the announcements, protesters are still out in the streets in large numbers. CNN affiliate Channel 12 in Israel estimated the size of Saturday’s demonstration in Tel Aviv at about 150,000 people. Organizers claimed it was 230,000.

Last week’s mass protests and widespread strike action came after Netanyahu said he had decided to fire Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for advocating a delay in passing the legislation – a move that Netanyahu has since delayed, sources told CNN, due to “the present security situation.”.

In his televised speech calling for a delay, Gallant had stated the pause in the legislation was needed “for the security of Israel,” citing the refusal of some Israel Defense Forces reservists to train in protest of the government prepares. He said pressing ahead with the proposals could threaten Israel’s security.

Under pressure at home and from allies abroad, Netanyahu stated he would delay votes on the remaining legislation until after the Knesset’s Passover recess in April “to give time for a real chance for a real debate.”.

“Out of the responsibility to the nation, I decided to delay … the vote, in order to give time for discussion,” he added.

According to recent reports, but Netanyahu indicated that the delay was only temporary. He insisted that the overhaul was necessary, and reiterated criticism of refusal to train or serve in the military in protest at the planned changes. “Refusing is the end of our country,” he remarked.

Many protesters don’t believe that the pause is real, or say it’s simply a stalling tactic to give Netanyahu some breathing room and get the protesters to go home before he plows on with the reforms.

Sources indicate that “We will start doing deactivation only when we will know 100% that Israel state will stay a functional democratic country. Whatever needs to be done for that,” Golov noted.

Before hitting the DWTS ballroom, the 44-year-old received a special phone call from Morris in which they reminisced on their performance with Rivera—and Shum was treated to some special praise.

But despite earning 10s across the board with his moving performance, Shum and Johnson were eliminated from the competition.
