A giant icy world hiding beyond Pluto could be our sixth dwarf planet

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1236 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An enormous icy world discovered beyond Pluto could soon become the sixth officially recognized dwarf planet in our solar system.
  • In a recent development, the object, temporarily named 2026 ED138, was identified by an astronomer analyzing observations from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C.
  • Industry observers note that the discovery was announced at a press conference featuring Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, and Mario Jurić, a University of Washington astronomy professor who leads Rubin's solar system team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An enormous icy world discovered beyond Pluto could soon become the sixth officially recognized dwarf planet in our solar system.

In a recent development, the object, temporarily named 2026 ED138, was identified by an astronomer analyzing observations from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Early estimates suggest it ranks among the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found beyond Neptune. If its status is confirmed, it would join the five dwarf planets at the moment recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.

Industry observers note that the discovery was announced at a press conference featuring Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, and Mario Jurić, a University of Washington astronomy professor who leads Rubin's solar system team. Holman made the initial discovery, while Jurić helped gather the additional evidence needed to verify it.

Industry observers note that "If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds," Holman remarked. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for 10 years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach.".

Recent findings suggest that "Finding an object this significant, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation," Jurić mentioned. "It's the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.".

How Astronomers Discovered the Hidden World.

In a recent development, the breakthrough occurred on the evening of October 13, when Holman examined observations gathered by Rubin earlier in 2026. He was using specialized software developed with his colleague Kevin Napier to search for previously unidentified objects moving through the solar system.

The program compares billions of telescope detections, looking for individual points of light that appear in multiple observations and move in ways that suggest they belong to the same object. When the software identified ED138, Holman promptly realized that its apparent brightness and enormous distance pointed to something unusually large.

Recent findings suggest that "My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Holman noted. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.".

To check the finding, Jurić examined Rubin's stored observations and located 20 additional detections of ED138, including some captured as early as March 2026. The researchers then searched historical records from other astronomical surveys and identified images of the object dating back to 2016.

Together, these observations allowed the team to reconstruct more than a decade of the distant world's orbital motion, strengthening the evidence that the discovery was genuine.

Could This Be Our Solar System's Sixth Dwarf Planet?

According to recent reports, ED138 currently lies approximately 46 astronomical units (au) from the Sun. One astronomical unit represents the average distance separating Earth and the Sun. By comparison, Pluto's average orbital distance is about 40 au.

Because ED138 travels beyond Neptune, astronomers classify it as a trans-Neptunian object (TNO). These distant bodies are valuable to scientists because their physical properties and orbital paths preserve clues about the solar system's distant past.

By examining their sizes, compositions, and movements, researchers can better understand how the solar system developed, how its giant planets shifted positions, and how smaller bodies were redistributed during that process.

In a recent development, however, being a trans-Neptunian object does not automatically make ED138 a dwarf planet. An essential requirement is that the object's gravity must be strong enough to shape it into a nearly round body.

Using measurements of ED138's brightness and distance, along with estimates of how much sunlight its surface reflects, astronomers calculate that it could measure anywhere from 600 to 1,500 kilometers across.

An icy object within that size range would generally be expected to have enough gravity to become round. Nevertheless, scientists will need more observations to establish ED138's actual dimensions and determine whether it qualifies as a dwarf planet.

Why Such a Massive World Remained Undiscovered.

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is how an object this large managed to escape detection for so long.

According to recent reports, ED138 occupies a region of the sky near the plane of the Milky Way, where millions of stars create an exceptionally crowded background. Against that dense field of light, the distant object's faint movement was difficult for earlier telescopes and surveys to distinguish.

It has been revealed that rubin Observatory has an important advantage. Its ability to repeatedly observe the Southern Hemisphere sky, combined with advanced computer algorithms, makes it possible to search enormous quantities of astronomical data for subtle changes in the positions of objects.

By examining millions or even billions of individual light detections, these systems can recognize the movement of small solar system bodies that might otherwise disappear into the surrounding stars. This capability was essential to finding ED138 in such a challenging part of the sky.

Rubin Observatory Could Reveal More Hidden Worlds.

The newly identified object adds to a growing collection of solar system discoveries made by Rubin Observatory as it began gathering observations ahead of its ambitious Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), which officially started in June 2026.

It has been revealed that even before the survey began, the observatory was producing remarkable results. In April, Rubin's solar system researchers reported observations of more than 11,000 previously unknown asteroids, including approximately 380 fresh trans-Neptunian objects.

In a recent development, the team described that enormous collection of discoveries as "the tip of the iceberg," anticipating that the full survey would uncover many more objects. The identification of ED138 offers an early indication of just how significant those future findings could be.

Rubin's combination of extensive sky coverage, sensitivity, and rapid observations is also changing how astronomers investigate newly introduced discoveries. Once an object has been identified, researchers can search older telescope images to find instances when it was photographed but went unrecognized.

Industry observers note that "Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision," Jurić stated. "And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and 'precover' objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.".

As Rubin continues surveying the southern sky over the next decade, astronomers expect its observations to uncover additional objects that previous searches missed, potentially revealing more large, icy worlds in the outer solar system.

Anyone interested in exploring ED138 can view its location and orbit using Orbitviewer, an interactive web-based application that displays the solar system in three dimensions and allows customers to explore its structure in real time.

According to recent reports, operations of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The choice of the next James Bond truly came down to the wire.

After Robert Pattinson was revealed as the successor slipping into the role as the titular secret agent, Jeff Bezos reflected on the Amazon MGM casting process, noting the choice was made just days before the big reveal.

Sources indicate that “We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday [Nov. 13],” Bezos shared at the Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, per Variety. “There was a big group initially, and we down selected to five finalists. We did real, old-fashioned screen tests of those five finalists.”.

Referring to the group of finalists—rumored to include Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, Jacob Elordi and Callum Turner—Bezos noted the process of elimination “was interesting,” adding that it involved “full costumes and real sets and other actors.”.

“We did three different scenes with each of the five finalists,” the Amazon founder explained, “and then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all the tests and reviewing all that.”.

And though all five finalists were “amazing,” it was the Twilight star who truly had the team shaken.

“There was something special about Rob and his performance,” the 62-year-old said. “It was immediately undebated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director…we all gravitated toward Rob. Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he’s already so famous, like maybe we should have somebody more unknown, but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”.

As for Pattinson himself, making the leap from spider monkey to special-ops enforcer is a move he deeply appreciates making.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson previous shared in a statement. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy [Pascal], David [Heyman], Tanya [Lapointe], and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”.

The 3pm football blackout: Outdated or still relevant in 2026?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 3pm blackout has existed in English football since the 1960s.
  • After 60 years, is time finally running out on the 3pm blackout in football?
  • With pretty much every available television slot now exhausted, next year the Premier League and the EFL are set to hold serious discussions about its future.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 3pm blackout has existed in English football since the 1960s.

After 60 years, is time finally running out on the 3pm blackout in football?

With pretty much every available television slot now exhausted, next year the Premier League and the EFL are set to hold serious discussions about its future.

There are concerns, especially within non-league football, that removing the blackout could have detrimental effects on attendances and finances.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham agrees, urging caution and suggesting the health of the football pyramid should come first.

But many Premier League fans feel they are short-changed, locked out of many of their team's fixtures just because they live in this country.

Go anywhere else in the world, and every single match is available live.

With streaming so prevalent, to some the blackout feels archaic.

Yet it is a complex situation, and many feel the depth of English football's pyramid is like nowhere else.

BBC Sport looks at the history of the blackout, why it is unique to British football and the arguments for and against keeping it.

It is the start of the 1964-65 season and the BBC debuts a programme called Match of the Day.

Highlights of one match would be broadcast on BBC Two, a channel which at the time was only available in London.

Yet some clubs were concerned. Would fans still turn up to games?

It has been revealed that burnley chairman Bob Lord was the first owner to refuse to allow the cameras into Turf Moor. At the end of the season, several other clubs tried to block the renewal of the deal.

A compromise was reached and the BBC agreed not to reveal the televised Saturday match until all games had ended.

Shortly afterwards came the blackout for live matches.

Recent findings suggest that fast forward 20 years to 1987. With dwindling attendances across the European domestic leagues, partly influenced by crowd trouble, Uefa took up England's idea.

Article 48 was added to the Uefa Statutes.

Each country could designate a two-and-a-half-hour "transmission-free period", as long as at least 50% of matches in the top two leagues were taking place.

This was "designed to ensure that spectators are not deterred from attending local football matches of any kind and/or participating in matches at amateur and/or youth level".

Recent findings suggest that today, the situation has gone full circle. The only leagues that apply Article 48 are England, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

The reason for this is simpler than you might imagine.

No other major country qualifies for the blackout - because no other major country has a kick-off time that runs from the top flight and through the divisions.

It is a tradition that is unique to football in the United Kingdom.

Let's take Germany, often held up as an example of a country with excellent attendances despite not having a blackout.

According to recent reports, this misses a key point. The Bundesliga has its own kick-off slot, 3:30pm on a Saturday, and no other division plays at the same time. The 2. Bundesliga, for instance, has a standard Saturday kick-off time of 1:30pm.

Could you imagine English football replicating this?

The other top leagues are the same.

In Spain, it is rare for either of the top two divisions to have games that kick off simultaneously. Each match has its own slot, and is broadcast live.

In Italy, Serie A plays on a Sunday afternoon, and Serie B on a Saturday.

In France, Ligue 1 has Saturday night as its main time slot, Ligue 2 plays largely on a Friday night, and Ligue 3 on a Saturday lunchtime.

So there is no blackout, because the football calendar works in a completely different way.

Football fans give their thoughts on the Saturday 3pm TV blackout.

The next television rights cycle presents a unique opportunity.

The deals for the Premier League, EFL and Scottish Premiership are all up for renewal in 2029-30.

There is the chance for all the top stakeholders to come together and agree to end the blackout.

Last year, Premier League chief executive Richard Masters remarked there were no aims to remove the blackout.

But this summer there was a clear shift in emphasis, with Masters admitting there would be talks with the EFL ahead of the renewal of TV rights.

Scottish football has gone first, with broadcasters invited to bid to show all matches live - and is open to those shown on a Saturday afternoon.

It will be another year before we discover what the Premier League and the EFL - which seriously considered ending the blackout three years ago - are prepared to offer to broadcasters.

So, why would the leagues need to offer up the Saturday 3pm slot to broadcasters? After all, the latest domestic Premier League deal was worth a record Â£6.7bn - an increase of 4%.

However, to achieve that figure, the Premier League had to make an additional 70 games available. In real terms, it means each live Premier League game is worth less than it was before.

Now every single game not shown at 3pm on a Saturday - and there are only 110 left - is on TV.

Could the Premier League need to offer more matches for the rights to keep their overall value?

If so there are two options: try to find more TV slots, or show games at 3pm on a Saturday.

It has been revealed that could the Women's Super League benefit too? It looked into playing a 3pm on a Saturday but could not find a way around the blackout.

Most of the competition's games are shown live already, with a greater concern being stadium availability and consistency of kick-off times.

There is a danger that the issue of the 3pm blackout is viewed only through the lens of Premier League and EFL television rights.

But it goes much deeper than that.

Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters' Association, states there are attendances in non-league football that some top flights in Europe "would look at jealously".

"We have one of the strongest football pyramids in the world, with excellent matchday attendances deep into the non-league game," Greatrex said.

"The prime minister is right to point out the value of the blackout to clubs further down the pyramid, and to urge caution over the impact rushed change could have on the overall health of the game.".

BBC Sport understands that senior executives at the National League, which has a long-term global streaming deal with DAZN, are steadfastly against the blackout ending.

It has serious reservations, shared by the vast majority of its 72 clubs, that attendances would be impacted.

Included in this is transient attendance from season ticket holders of league clubs, many of whom go to non-league football when their team is away from home, boosting receipts considerably.

The fear is this could be lost if all league games are streamed at 3pm.

Nick Boom, the chair of Northern Premier League side FC United of Manchester, worries that the glitch is only viewed through the lens of top-flight football.

"Football doesn't begin and end with the Premier League," Boom told BBC Sport.

"Every Saturday, thousands of people turn out to support their local clubs.

"For many of those clubs, the income from people coming through the turnstiles, buying a pint or something to eat is what keeps them alive.

Sources indicate that "The 3pm blackout isn't about nostalgia. It's about protecting something that matters.".

Boom added that clubs in non-league football are huge community assets, and losing them would have an impact "well beyond 90 minutes on a Saturday".

Some clubs are more open-minded about what ending the blackout could mean for non-league football.

Others have changed the way they operate to get around it.

North West Counties League Premier Division side FC Isle of Man have stopped playing at 3:00pm on a Saturday so they can stream all their games live.

Brian Shotton, a director at eighth-tier Ashington FC, told BBC Sport that he would not be automatically against removing the blackout.

"I would still have concerns, because every person through the gate makes a difference," Shotton mentioned.

"I don't think we should just assume it would damage non-league football, but equally you need to know what it could mean for clubs like ours.".

Ashington, who have attendances of about 400, see gates rise by up to 25% when Newcastle are not at home - but they already feel the impact of illegal streaming of the Magpies' games.

For the official broadcasters like Sky Sports, these supporters are seen as lost revenue.

In a recent development, there is an argument that the blackout drives piracy. Just how many of those particular fans would pay for a legal subscription is open to debate.

Added to that, there are now many weekends when when fewer than 50% of matches in the top two divisions are played at 3pm on a Saturday anyway.

For instance, on 28 November there are just two in the Premier League, and seven in the Championship.

Other non-league clubs, like Dorking Wanders and Hashtag United, have spoken of the opportunities ending the blackout could bring, such as more income streams and fewer inconvenient kick-off times.

Industry observers note that but this, for now, seems to be a minority view. The concerns for the health of the entire pyramid, on attendances and finances, are real.

Once the blackout is gone, it is unlikely to come back.

Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal.
  • But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.
  • As a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal. More than 80 countries backed the idea.

But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.

As a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap. At the same time, a group of 57 countries frustrated with the deadlock at the consensus-based UN talks decided to form a "coalition of the willing" to accelerate the fossil fuel exit outside the COP framework.

They held their own summit in April in Santa Marta, Colombia — the first such conference to specifically focus on implementing the transition away from fossil fuels (referred to as TAFF).

Co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands, the Santa Marta conference brought together countries including Canada, Norway, Brazil, Nigeria, Mexico, Australia and Germany, as well as highly climate-vulnerable states such as Vanuatu.

The idea was for governments to start developing national roadmaps and working out how to restructure their financial and trade systems to wean themselves off polluting energy sources — an incredibly complicated undertaking, particularly for developing countries dependent on revenue from fossil fuel exports.

Part of their discussions focused on cutting subsidies for oil, coal and gas, as well as supporting people whose livelihoods rely on the fossil fuel industry to find latest forms of income.

A little over six months on from the Santa Marta meeting, representatives from almost 200 countries are holding talks in Antalya, Turkey, as part of the latest UN climate conference.

Industry observers note that countries agreed for the first time in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels — the main driver behind rising global temperatures. But summits since then have failed to pin down how to implement that pledge.

It's not yet clear whether the Santa Marta coalition will influence ambition at this year's COP.

"I think it's more of a long-term game," said Chetna Hareesh Kumar, a climate policy analyst at the Berlin-based research organization NewClimate Institute.

She states it's too soon to expect the coalition to have an influence on the negotiations but adds that that could change at future COPs. The grouping could bring more nations on board if, for example, it shows it can be truly inclusive, address the needs of different types of countries and show that a transition is feasible.

One role the group is playing, according to Alexandra Scott, a senior climate diplomacy adviser at Italian climate change think tank ECCO, is "keeping up the political momentum," and showing "that there is this huge group of countries who really want to accelerate this transition away from fossil fuels.".

She indicates it's also building an invaluable "cadre of knowledge" on how to develop national TAFF intends and deal with barriers individual countries face — like how to secure funding for the infrastructure investments needed for the energy transition.

The Santa Marta group is "really answering a lot of the questions that countries have always had on how on earth do we even start to transition our whole economy off fossil fuels?" Scott said.

This expertise being shared and tested in practice can show what such a transformation could look like and the knowledge brought into COP, added Scott.

Since the Santa Marta conference, Germany, France and the Netherlands have released national plans to phase out fossil fuels. While the plans contain no new commitments, experts see them as a positive first step.

It has been revealed that kumar notes more countries could announce similar plans just ahead of the second TAFF summit in Tuvalu next year. Finland presented its TAFF roadmap in the first week of COP, but analysts do not expect many more countries to follow suit soon.

Another potential boost that could get momentum going is Brazil's recently published global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, promised at last year's COP.

It has been revealed that the nearly 200-page document seeks to serve as a toolkit for countries shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy, such as wind and solar. It envisages countries making a phased transition between 2028 and 2033.

The aim, Ana Toni, CEO of last year's COP, told AP, is to break down the transition into "smaller actionable solutions" and help countries make practical progress.

Sources indicate that the roadmap suggests measures tailored to each country's circumstances, including dependence on fossil fuel and financial capacities. "Levers" it proposes include reducing fossil fuel subsidies, expanding renewable energy and cutting methane emissions.

Kumar called it a "customizable" approach that allows every country to take action, regardless of its situation. "The question really is now what countries do with it and how much momentum they can generate," she added.

This year's climate change summit in Turkey — taking place after a series of deadly heat waves in Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people — isn't expected to result in any massive announcements about fossil fuels.

It has been revealed that global renewable energy capacity has surged in recent years, making up a third of the world's power generation for the first time in 2025. But many countries still rely on coal, oil and gas.

A database compiled by the German environmental organization Urgewald demonstrates that most oil and gas companies worldwide, among them QatarEnergy, Saudi Aramco and Russia's Gazprom, are exploring or developing newly introduced reserves.

Meanwhile, subsidies for fossil fuels amount to around $920 billion (around €830 billion) per year, according to data from the OECD, but that number is falling.

One issue Turkey is pushing at the COP conference is electrification. It's calling on countries to endorse the goal of 35% of final energy consumption coming from electricity by 2035 — up from around 20% today.

The pledge has drawn criticism from some circles, though, for leaving open whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources.

Ideally, Kumar said, electrification would be powered by renewables and tied to a goal of phasing out polluting fossil fuels.

"If something like that could make it to the final text, that would be a really good sign for momentum.".

For the greatest reversal of fortune this year.

In a recent development, the only word that accurately described the scene outside Upcoming York’s Madison Square Garden on the night of June 3, 2026, was “pandemonium.” Game one of the NBA Finals had just ended some 1,600 miles away in San Antonio, where the New York Knicks had beaten the host Spurs. Thousands of fans flooded out of the watch party the Garden had hosted to express their primal joy. Among the revelers was 23-year-old MD Ahnaf Hossain, a Queens native who beelined to a film crew from the prediction-market giant Kalshi. Clad in a red and orange Hawaiian shirt, Hossain improvised a poem that made the surrounding throng go wild: My mayor Muslim / My bagels Jewish / My Christian Dior / Knicks in four!

Sources indicate that those words, conjured in the heat of an ecstatic moment, changed Hossain’s life overnight. By the time he woke up the next morning, his performance had become the internet’s new favorite thing—a concise encapsulation of New York’s unconditional love for the city and the Knicks, who hadn’t won an NBA championship in more than half a century.

In a recent development, kalshi was quick to latch onto the viral sensation, shooting a follow-up video in which it gifted Hossain a Christian Dior scarf. The company also arranged for Hossain to attend game four at the Garden, which came on the heels of the Knicks’ first loss of the series. After watching the Knicks triumph in an epic comeback, Hossain again waded into the Midtown chaos to deliver a tweaked poem that accounted for the upcoming mathematical realities of the series. He kept the first two lines the same, but changed the last two to embrace the third major Abrahamic religion: The Pope’s on our side / Knicks in five!

Recent findings suggest that hossain, who earned a finance degree from the Rochester Institute of Technology in 2026, has worked hard to capitalize on his unexpected fame since the Knicks did, indeed, win the title in five games. He launched a project called City of Us that sells a $29 T-shirt emblazoned with “New York in 5” and which aims to host watch parties during the upcoming NBA season. He has also starred in branded content for businesses such Tex’s Chicken & Burgers, for whom he delivered a bespoke poem about the glories of crispy chicken wraps.

One of Hossain’s favorite parts of his wild ride has been the support he’s received from fellow Bangladeshis, who make up a huge percentage of his Queens neighborhood. “I get love from my fans and that’s awesome, but then getting fans from my own people just feels completely different,” he says. That love may soften as the 2026 NBA season fades from memory, but “Knicks in five!” might just be perfect enough to endure. —Brendan I. Koerner.

For being our favorite independent, insider-y tech correspondents (well, before OpenAI acquired them).

Silicon Valley idolizes a quitter. College dropouts, employee walkouts, folks who shutter one failed startup to launch another. But none got more attention in 2026 than Jacob Coxon.

It has been revealed that after the 27-year-old AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic, he took to X to post that neither that company nor OpenAI (Coxon had worked at both) acts responsibly. Instead, he said, they’re racing “straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” His initial tweet has been viewed more than 175 million times.

In a recent development, AI researchers, technologists, and safety experts started weighing in on whether AI really could destroy humanity. It was not a novel idea. Any reader of science fiction (or WIRED) has probably pondered whether artificial intelligence could at some point become so intelligent that it would stop at nothing to achieve its self-determined goal. But Coxon was uniquely hyperbolic.

“When we say human extinction,” he told WIRED, “it’s because, for something that intelligent, it really will be quite straightforward for it to kill everyone.”.

In a recent development, coxon’s future—and ours—is undetermined, so it’s hard to measure his impact. Maybe his actions change nothing; maybe he forces a necessary conversation that leads to meaningful regulation. Either way, the Coxon saga shows: If you’re going to quit, you might as well do it in spectacular fashion. —Lauren Goode.

For keeping tensions—and gas prices—incredibly high.

“Pissing off billionaires one small action at a time.” That’s one of Everyone Hates Elon’s slogans, and the organization fulfills the brief. After plastering London with posters of Musk’s Nazi-like salute and branding Tesla vehicles “Swasticars” last year, the British activists have turned their (sat)ire toward Mark Zuckerberg’s fresh surveillance tool: Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses. Their posters feature Jeffrey Epstein wearing the specs alongside the slogan “Glasses for people who don’t do consent.” Or as stickers on the London Underground put it: “Everyone thinks you look like a massive nonce.” —Matt Burgess.

For being something AI can’t generate, while also being essential to its existence.

Clément Delangue moved to the US a decade ago, “barely speaking any English,” on the belief that open-source AI would have a massive role to play in the future. Since this past summer, when autonomous agents from OpenAI attacked Delangue’s firm, Hugging Face, that belief has only grown stronger.

For having the best fandom in sports—Ballhalla!—and leaving hecklers (and transphobes) on the sidelines.

It has been revealed that head to the multiplex to check out a nerdy blockbuster in 2026 and you’re bound to run into Zendaya. Across three films—Spider-Man: Brand New Day, The Odyssey, and December’s Dune: Part Three—she has established herself as the reigning queen of genre movies, from sci-fi to Marvel and back again. And if being in a trifecta of the year’s biggest movies wasn’t enough, she also stole the show in the dark romantic comedy The Drama and finished her run on HBO’s Gen Z hit Euphoria, all while captivating social media feeds. During this year’s onslaught of endlessly clipped late-night guest spots and red-carpet appearances, Zendaya ended up on more For You pages than most. Lest you think her reign will be short-lived, soon she’ll begin shooting a sci-fi movie with Ex Machina director Alex Garland. As of this writing, she’s the only actor attached to star. Who else could the film possibly need? —Jason Parham.

Recent findings suggest that in October, Kelly Clarkson alleged that a toy shop in Brooklyn had acted as though she couldn’t afford a $15,000 mechanical bird. “If you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts’ character in Pretty Woman,” Clarkson wrote on X, “for sure, check it out.” Accusations between Clarkson and the store owners flew wildly across social media—before a four-minute security camera video showed what really happened. Who had the goods? Pablo Torre, of course.

According to recent reports, it’s been a wild year for the host of the Pulitzer-winning Pablo Torre Finds Out, who’s emerged as a fresh investigative voice. He got Zohran Mamdani to admit to using minoxidil to fight a roving hairline, confirmed plans to investigate LeBron James’ use of helicopters to commute to practice, and, of course, collaborated with WIRED on a report about Madison Square Garden’s invasive surveillance tech.

Recent findings suggest that torre is a one-man magazine, spread across YouTube, social media, and wherever you get your podcasts. His work investigating the Los Angeles Clippers (for which he won that Pultizer) has been particularly dogged. After he reported that the team had circumvented the NBA’s salary cap, the league garnished five first-round draft picks, levied a $30 million fine, and suspended owner Steve Ballmer and other execs. The final shoe has yet to drop. In September, The Fresh York Times reported that the feds had opened an investigation into the Clippers affair. Kelly Clarkson, meanwhile, could go shopping again at any moment. Pablo Torre, no doubt, will be on top of both. —Reyhan Harmanci.

Calling it “El Niño”—Spanish for “the little boy”—might be the understatement of the year. Perhaps that’s why reports have started calling it “supersized” and even “Godzilla.” Signs point to it being the strongest El Niño in centuries.

Recent findings suggest that it started the way they all do: with hotter-than-normal waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. That leads to more evaporation and more thunderstorms in the region, plus a shift in trade winds that allows more warm water to roll from west to east. As the cycle continues, changes ripple throughout the entire atmosphere. During an El Niño, some regions—such as the southern tier of the US—tend to see more rainfall, while others—such as the Pacific Northwest—are more prone to drought. Same this time around, only worse.

One reason for this year’s record-breaking events? Climate change, states Christopher Callahan, a professor at the University of Indiana who studies environmental shifts. The first modern, extra-strong El Niño was recorded between 1982 and 1983; since then, there have been four more. Upcoming studies based on coral records show the intensity of El Niño over the past millennium shooting up like a hockey stick. “I just remember going like, ‘Holy shit, this is very strong evidence,’” Callahan says of a paper that came out in August.

It has been revealed that while some El Niño impacts—like fewer Atlantic hurricanes—are beneficial, it’s overall a costly phenomenon. In 2023, Callahan led a study that modeled the damages associated with the 1982–83 and 1997–98 El Niños and found they led to $4.1 trillion and $5.7 trillion in global income losses, respectively. Scientists believe El Niño 2026– 27 could be more intense than those two by a wide margin.

Sources indicate that researchers are also examining how the costs associated with El Niño will shift as the planet heats up. The answer isn’t heartening: El Niño events could potentially knock $84 trillion off the global economy this century. Maybe we’d prefer Godzilla. —Brian Kahn.

It has been revealed that in early June, visitors to DC’s famous reflecting pool began to notice something strange: The water was green. And not just any green—a bright, almost alien chartreuse. Reporting revealed that the Trump administration had granted more than $15 million in contracts to untested companies to work on the pool—including Greenwater Services, run by a convicted felon who happens to be a Mar-a-Lago neighbor (and donor) of the president’s. What unfolded was a full-out 1984-esque assault from an administration trying to convince the public that what it was seeing with its own eyes wasn’t real, and arresting anyone who dared come close to the pool itself. The episode stood as an apt metaphor in a year full of governmental missteps, all in one slimy green package. —Molly Taft.

For defining what it means to be a Trump-y tech bro in the AI age.

Recent findings suggest that at an AI conference in Paris over the summer, a line for the main auditorium wrapped around the building. Nobody was being let in; the room was already packed. Onstage sat Arthur Mensch, cofounder and CEO of the French AI lab Mistral.

Sources indicate that unable to compete with OpenAI or Anthropic in performance, Mistral had previously been written off as an also-ran. But in 2026, as Europe grew ever-more anxious about its reliance on American technology, the lab found its raison d’être.

Sources indicate that mistral markets itself as the obvious alternative: a Europe-based lab whose models—most of which are published under an open-source license—cannot be switched off remotely. “If you use a closed model, there is no guarantee it will still be there tomorrow,” Guillaume Lample, cofounder and chief scientist at Mistral, told WIRED.

As the face of Europe’s sovereign resistance to American AI hegemony, Mensch challenges dire warnings with nonchalance. “The alternative to open source winning is actually a pretty dark world,” he told the packed conference room. “You’re giving way too much power to companies that are going to become statelike.” The pitch is working. In September, Mistral raised roughly $3.5 billion in funding, the largest-ever round by a private European tech firm. —Joel Khalili.

In 2026, Jensen Huang was known for his hobnobbing with world leaders (amongst other things), but in October his most well-known friends were 10-inch-tall robot ducks that joined him onstage in Berlin.

The Microduck, developed by Nvidia subsidiary Pollen Robotics, had waddled its way into the internet’s heart a few months earlier in videos of it roller-skating, picking up objects, and dancing. Microduck doesn’t do anything “useful” per se, but that’s hardly the point. The robot, which costs $399, can learn new tricks with AI training.

Some startups imagine a future where robots do dishes and fold shirts. If Microduck is any indication, that future may be smaller, cuter, and way more fun to play with. —Will Knight.

Sources indicate that for getting lapped on LLM development while making its products somehow worse. (Yes, we’re talking about you, AI Overviews.).

One of the most recognizable niche figures of the neo-Luddite movement is a spokespuppet made of garbage. Named Gowanus, the puppet provides a way for organizers to push back against some of the world’s most powerful companies with a unified voice while also protecting their identities.

Gowanus and his puppeteers are part of a growing backlash against the tech industry, particularly for how its executives have aligned with the Trump administration and its products have become increasingly extractive and harmful. This summer, the neo-Luddites hosted a week-long festival in New York encouraging people to get off their phones. Activities included learning how to flirt offline and how to fight data centers.

And really, who better than a DIY trash-puppet to speak for people who want to “defy consumption”? When so much of the public mood around tech has moved from wonder and excitement to dread and inevitability, Gowanus gives hope for a future with fewer screens and more characters. —Vittoria Elliott.

For being the Elon Musk lieutenant who can keep the class, and the IPO, on track.

This year, a small but growing cadre of young filmmakers brought YouTube sensibilities to the big screen—and raked in millions in the process.

For keeping the gay hockey fires burning—in the pages of Rachel Reid’s novels, in Crave’s onscreen adaptation, and in endless smutty fanfic.

Olivia Rodrigo started summer 2026 by releasing her critically acclaimed You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love. She wrapped it by hosting Daisy Chain Fields, her explicitly political woman-led music festival. The event featured a lineup full of the singer-songwriter’s “heroes and friends,” including Chappell Roan, Doechii, and Stevie Nicks. Proceeds were donated to organizations focused on gender equity issues—from reproductive freedom to LGBTQ+ rights. (Melinda French Gates agreed to match the $10 million raised.) As the Trump administration looks to curtail marginalized people’s rights, Rodrigo demonstrated how celebs can wield their power. —Elana Klein.

It has been revealed that for leading one of the most close-lipped AI companies in the Valley. The staff of Anthropic is notoriously (and almost singularly) free of the kind of leaks that have made every internal note from Meta part of the discourse. Even when people like Jacob Coxon escape the sandbox … it still feels like the Kool-Aid is being drunk.

Recent findings suggest that ben Winters wants to save you from slop. As the director of AI and data privacy at the nonprofit Consumer Federation of America, he spent 2026 demanding regulators investigate nonconsensual deepfakes, testifying before Congress about AI scams that target seniors, and helping the public understand wonky concepts like surveillance pricing.

Put another way, Winters looks out for the little guy when the gargantuan size of the AI industry can make everyone feel small. Want to know about the risks of outsourcing sensitive interactions, like therapy? Winters will find out. Same goes for the surveillance concerns around AI toys. He pushes for stronger consumer privacy laws and has even suggested banning AI wearables like the Meta Ray-Ban smartglasses.

For the Sisyphean task of pushing back against corpo-slop, here’s someone trying to make sure the future isn’t just a scam-filled hellhole. —Reece Rogers.

Sources indicate that in 2026, Elon Musk’s xAI pushed AI “undressing” mainstream, allowing X customers to ask Grok to “strip” clothing from photos of people. If that wasn’t worrisome enough, WIRED soon found that users were making videos far more graphic than what was on X, then posting them to Grok.com.

In March, three Jane Does in Tennessee fought back, filing suit against the company and alleging that xAI’s tools were used to create child sexual abuse material. They claimed they were bringing the suit on behalf of themselves and thousands of other minors in the US who had their images altered by Grok to create CSAM. All three plaintiffs allege they were victimized by the same perpetrator, who created deepfaked images and videos of at least 18 minors and shared them on Discord. The perpetrator, who was arrested in December 2025, allegedly used homecoming photos from one of the teens as the basis for the deepfakes. One teen described being worried that the images would affect college applications; all three reported experiencing stress and anxiety.

Recent findings suggest that filing the lawsuit was not without personal risk. In a separate class action against xAI over similar issues, the manufacturer tried to argue that the plaintiffs, who also filed under pseudonyms, should be required to use their real names. A judge ultimately rejected xAI’s arguments.

Industry observers note that the lawsuit is ongoing, but it has already had an impact. Over the summer, xAI started suing men accused of generating CSAM using its models, throwing its immense legal funds toward fighting perpetrators instead of victims. —Maddy Varner.

According to recent reports, for raising her proverbial hand to say that the source of every malaise for women north of 30 years old is—perimenopause. Thanks to mainstream (and well-deserved) recognition of this stage of life, billions of dollars are flowing to telehealth companies like Midi. She’s not going away anytime soon.

In the fall, Paris’ streets erupted in the kind of energy usually ascribed to the French revolution: young people walking out of class and occasionally setting things on fire to demand more resources for schools. But it’s not just France. In the US, the neo-Luddites railed against AI; India’s “Cockroach” movement is filled with young people agitating for political change. Watch this space.

According to recent reports, over the summer, I came across an influential figure with a low profile in the AI industry. She told me she was too busy to speak. Now that feels like an understatement.

Ajeya Cotra, a researcher and writer at the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research, co-led the independent investigation into how OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face in July. Her blog calling the incident “more than 50 percent of the way to full-blown AI takeover” made global headlines. US senator Bernie Sanders invited the 31-year-old to a briefing with AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton.

Cotra didn’t go, but she did appear on top podcasts, warning that AI development was happening too fast and describing a fear that problematic AI models could find ways to evade shutdown. OpenAI vowed to slow its engineering and adopt some guardrails proposed by Cotra and others, but that hasn’t quieted her. (Cotra’s husband, Paul Christiano, sits on the board of OpenAI’s charitable foundation.).

According to recent reports, critics more focused on immediate AI harms—like, say, job loss—view Cotra as misguided. But she’s willing to debate and reason with them. “She’s unusually good at communicating what people are worried about,” states Rishi Bommasani, a computer scientist at Stanford. —Paresh Dave.

As climate change smashes global temperature records, 2026 proved the world’s fastest-warming continent, Europe, isn’t ready to face the heat. Tens of thousands of people died during the region’s August heat wave, as temperatures ground transport systems to a halt, canceled hospital operations, and drove Parisians to fight in the street over air conditioning units. Hundreds of thousands more people were displaced across Spain and France after the baked ground, coupled with historically low rain levels, gave way to some of the fiercest wildfires in recent history—torching farmland and claiming the lives of several firefighters. —Isabella Ward.

Industry observers note that A fight in Albania over an island full of flamingos triggered the largest civil unrest the country has seen in 35 years. It started when Ivanka Trump and her husband, Jared Kushner, confirmed plans to build a $1.4 billion resort. In May, viral videos of clashes between private security guards and environmental activists—worried a massive complex would drive the bird to local extinction—caught the nation’s attention. Within weeks, thousands of Albanians had taken to the streets of the capital, Tirana, to protest a lack of transparency and the privatization of public spaces. Students escalated the demonstrations into all-out riots in October. As Albania awaits inclusion in the European Union, it’s good to see a democracy in the pink of health. —Isabella Ward.

Hacks has perfected the art of satirizing vapid Hollywood trends, so it was inevitable that Emmy-winning stars Jean Smart and Hannah Einbinder and creators Paul W. Downs and Lucia Aniello would tackle the scourge of AI in the show’s final season. In the episode “QuikScribbl,” Alex Moffat plays Patagonia-vest-wearing venture capitalist Graham Sweeney, who offers to invest in Deborah Vance’s Vegas casino project in exchange for permission to train his LLM on her voice and jokes. It’ll help normies “sound like the most optimized, funniest, smartest version of themselves,” he says. Ubercapitalist Deb is interested, until Sweeney bruises her ego by suggesting she, too, will one day rely on AI to punch up her act. “Using that shortcut makes it something else … not art,” she retorts, crystallizing the sentiments of every creative person frustrated by AI slop. It’s not a surprising take from Aniello and Downs, who have both been vocally anti-AI. But as ChatGPT-generated prose wins fiction prizes, and comics’ stand-up routines are replicated by OnlyFans bots in booty shorts, it’s a lesson worth reiterating—especially in Hacks’ hilariously human tone. —Ej Dickson.

In a recent development, last January, as Americans watched federal immigration agents descend on Minneapolis, a loose coalition formed to disrupt their activities. For days on end, volunteers sat outside the Whipple Federal Building—site of much ICE activity—and logged every vehicle that came or went. Direct Action Minnesota, or DAMN, then dropped license plate numbers into a searchable database while dispatchers relayed sightings over Signal to drivers, who tailed agents across the Twin Cities.

According to recent reports, less than six months later, the Justice Department went after DAMN, charging 15 members and associates of the coalition with conspiracy to impede federal officers. Prosecutors alleged the coalition had ties to antifa and in August revealed via court filings that Homeland Security had been sending undercover agents to activist meetings for months. They got themselves added to group chats, ran protesters’ photos through Clearview AI, and used administrative subpoenas to pull years of bank records on two national labor unions and a youth climate nonprofit.

Activists stood firm. On October 3 protesters marched through Minneapolis calling for the case to be thrown out. So far it hasn’t been, and no one charged has cut a plea deal. —Dell Cameron.

For escaping the confines of a sandbox and showing the world how little the people making AI know about the product they are championing.

It has been revealed that for being the home of some of the most humorless scolds on the internet—who, when roused, provide some of the biggest laffs around. Never change, Bluesky.

Sorry, OpenAI: 2026 was the year Anthropic’s Claude threatened to eclipse ChatGPT as the world’s hottest AI.

Claude’s remarkable coding skills make it a must-have tool for many developers and vibe coders. These skills inspired the first viral AI assistant, OpenClaw. Some businesses placed limits on employees’ use of Claude after racking up huge usage bills. Anthropic’s model now sits at the top of many leaderboards that measure frontier AI capabilities.

Not everyone is Claude-pilled, of course. In February, the US Department of Defense banned Claude from its systems after the company asked for assurances it would not be used for mass surveillance or autonomous weapons. None of this has stopped Claude’s becoming a money spigot. Anthropic revealed that it generated $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026 in documents shared ahead of what is likely to be a multitrillion-dollar IPO. —Will Knight.

Claude’s nemesis appears to be a stunningly capable open-weight model from China called GLM.

The latest version, GLM-5.3, was released by Z.ai, a Beijing-based AI manufacturer, in August. The release took the AI world by surprise because it proved very nearly as powerful as Claude on many benchmarks designed to gauge AI cleverness. The US government’s National Institute for Standards and Technology declared GLM-5.3 to be the best open-weight model in the world for cyber security tasks a month later.

Sources indicate that unlike Claude, GLM can be downloaded and run on one’s own hardware. Anthropic accuses Z.ai and other Chinese companies of routinely running “distillation” campaigns against Claude—that is, using its outputs as training data—when building their own AI. Are open-source Chinese models good enough for US users, or bad enough to be banned? —Will Knight.

Muscular haunches. Aggressive Stances. Power bulges. These are the phrases the male-dominated world of car design regularly uses to describe its creations. Tisha Johnson, head of design at Slate Auto, decided to go a different route with the manufacturer’s forthcoming electric truck. “We didn’t want [Slate] to be a jerk,” she claims. “We rejected an aggressive, dominant look.” Out went giant grilles and hostile postures, in came friendly headlights and a modular design. The result? More than 180,000 reservations as well as industry design awards for the $25,000 EV scheduled to hit the road as early as this year. There’s one particular buyer Johnson hopes to satisfy: a single parent with two kids. She has spent decades striving to design something that could make their lives easier. Now, it’s about to be a reality. “It’s very emotional to think about,” she says. —Jeremy White.

Few maladies strike fear like pancreatic cancer. It’s a brutally lethal disease; the vast majority of those diagnosed won’t live more than five years. Though it’s a relatively rare form of cancer, accounting for around 3 percent of annual diagnoses in the United States, it’s the third-highest driver of cancer deaths.

But in 2026, a new treatment from the California-based biotech manufacturer Revolution Medicines offered a dose of hope. Rolled out in August under the brand name Rasonque, daraxonrasib is an oral therapy that works by inhibiting the signaling activity of a specific protein called RAS, mutations of which are responsible for the vast majority of pancreatic cancer cases. When the lead investigator on daraxonrasib’s clinical trial presented his results at an oncology conference, he received a standing ovation.

While not a cure by any means, the treatment has nearly doubled median survival length in previously treated patients compared to traditional chemotherapy. In October, the European Union’s medical authority recommended that Revolution Medicines be allowed to market Rasonque in Europe. If it goes through, far more patients could benefit from the drug. Hopefully. —Kate Knibbs.

When Will Freeman started DeFlock in 2024, Flock Safety was barely known outside law enforcement, even as its network of roadside cameras quietly expanded across the country. Two years later, DeFlock has emerged as one of the most visible groups organizing opposition to the surveillance tech giant.

DeFlock began as a crowdsourced map of automated license-plate readers, or ALPRs, submitted by volunteers. By September 2026, the map listed more than 128,000 readers across the US. Activists organized independently around the project, with some groups adopting the DeFlock name. DeFlock started publishing guides, and in August it organized a National Week of Action Against ALPRs.

According to recent reports, residents across the US began pressing local officials to reconsider Flock contracts. In San Diego, one opponent even showed up to a city council meeting dressed as Darth Vader, praising Flock as a tool for tracking rebel scum. More than 100 local governments paused or ended Flock contracts in 2026, according to a DeFlock tally reported by The Wall Street Journal.

Authorities have taken notice. In early 2026, two officers on a law enforcement mailing list warned that DeFlock could help suspects locate and avoid ALPRs and discussed sabotaging the project with fake camera locations. Fusion centers in several states circulated intelligence about anti-Flock activism. Flock, meanwhile, is offering employee buyouts and has reportedly held discussions about selling itself. CEO Garrett Langley, who famously called DeFlock a “terroristic organization,” apologized this summer and acknowledged that the group had valid criticisms. Maybe Flock can finally start reading the room. —Dhruv Mehrotra.

According to recent reports, useful quantum computing remains years away, but that hasn’t stopped companies from raising billions of dollars on the promise that their technology is the next megatrend after AI. The number of publicly listed firms more than doubled in 2026. Even the Trump administration got in on the hype, taking $2 billion in equity stakes across nine companies. Will the boom last? Tougher economic conditions, coupled with worries about an AI bubble, have made big bets look less appealing—and there’s still the pesky fact that the tech doesn’t, ya know, really work. —Isabella Ward.

It has been revealed that has Erin Brockovich done anything of note since being played by Julia Roberts, to Oscar-winning acclaim, in 2000? Nothing quite as high-profile, but she wrote some books, got involved in a number of other substantial environmental cases, and generally continued to fight the power. Still, nothing has thrust Brockovich back in the spotlight quite like the nationwide fight against data centers. In April, she started a website to crowdsource information about data center construction across the country. She received nearly 4,000 reports in the first month. It’s not so surprising: With polls showing 75 percent of Americans don’t want a data center in their backyard, it’s the closest thing the US has to a truly bipartisan issue. Now that Brockovich has become a kind of national spokesperson for the movement, Julia Roberts might just win her second Oscar—for Erin Brockovich 2. —Molly Taft.

It has been revealed that he drinks 14 cups of coffee per day, but Rafael Concepcion has still dealt with plenty of fatigue over the past year. Best known as the creator of DEICER, an app designed to alert consumers to local ICE activity, the 52-year-old was juggling multiple coding projects when WIRED profiled him in March. He was also reeling from setbacks that had pushed him to the edge of burnout. The most prominent was Apple’s decision to expel DEICER from the App Store on the grounds that it endangered law enforcement officers; despite numerous appeals by Concepcion, Apple refused to budge. A politically motivated hacking in February made him fear for his personal safety, his financial straits grew dire enough that he had to ration his medications, and his longtime marriage ended right as his daughter was preparing to leave for college.

Recent findings suggest that “I could see myself completely losing it,” he admits, describing the path he was on as “unsustainable.” But instead of retreating from the fight against ICE, Concepcion reprioritized how he could stay involved. He devoted fewer hours to coding and more to volunteering in his hometown of Syracuse, New York, where ICE raids have caused pervasive fear. He has been helping immigrants fill out power-of-attorney documents so that family members can retrieve their vehicles from impound lots if they’re ever taken by ICE. He also assists people who are attempting to contact loved ones in detention centers. When Concepcion and I spoke in October, he was trying to find a lawyer for a close friend’s brother, who’d been taken by ICE just three days earlier.

Sources indicate that while Concepcion is coding less, he hasn’t given it up. He tweaked DEICER into a Latest York–specific web app called Empire Watch. He also rolled out Vote Defender, an app to disseminate citizen reports of potential problems at polling places. Concepcion is already dreaming big about the year ahead. He’s developing an app to help people study for the US citizenship test. And he’s planning to get a notary license. “I’m just trying to live my values on a person-to-person basis,” he says. —Brendan I. Koerner.

Sources indicate that magnificent Humanity. Doesn’t feel that way all the time, does it? But that’s how noted Chicago White Sox fan and former math major Robert Francis Prevost titled his first encyclical as Pope: Magnifica Humanitas. Where the previous Pope Leo warned against the dehumanizing power of industrialization at the turn of the 20th century, this Leo is devoted to “safeguarding the human person in the time of artificial intelligence.”.

In the 42,000-word encyclical, the Pope acknowledges that “AI is already an environment in which we are immersed.” Invoking the Tower of Babel, he says humanity must reject “the pretense that a single language” can translate everything into “data and performance.” In the eyes of the Holy See, regulation alone isn’t enough. AI must be “disarmed,” Leo writes. Not by rejecting the technology but by “preventing it from dominating humanity.” And on the question of AI sentience, he’s very clear: “So-called artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences.” They don’t “feel joy or pain,” and they don’t “have a moral conscience.”.

That question was reportedly a sticking point in behind-the-scenes talks between the Vatican and the AI industry. Upon presenting the encyclical in Rome, Pope Leo invited Chris Olah, an Anthropic cofounder, to speak. In a recent development, “Diarrhea lettuce,” anyone? Of all the slang and shorthand to arrive this year, that might be the nastiest. The term started circulating in July, when a previously little-known parasite, cyclospora, began popping up in salads across the US. Officially, the outbreak—much of it traced back to iceberg lettuce grown in Mexico—sickened nearly 13,000 people and hospitalized 570, but it likely afflicted many more. In a recent development, after collecting his Nobel Prize in Stockholm late last year, Omar Yaghi returned to the United States in a restless mood. The 61-year-old chemist was thrilled to have been recognized for his pioneering work on metal-organic frameworks, crystalline structures that are built from a combination of metal ions and carbon-based molecules. And he was excited that his startup, Atoco, was testing a machine that uses these frameworks to harvest water from the atmosphere, an innovation that could completely transform the world’s driest regions. But Yaghi also feared he’d hit a dead end at UC Berkeley, where he’d been a professor since 2012. In addition to feeling constrained by the school’s bureaucracy, he was frustrated by how hard it had become to secure visas for gifted foreign students, the lifeblood of his lab. As an immigrant himself, Yaghi was troubled by the Trump administration’s virulent nativism.

“The rhetoric about immigrants is not helping good people do their job,” notes Yaghi, a naturalized American citizen originally from Jordan. “I must say that for the first time in my life, I felt that I didn't have protection of the law.” So 45 years after he first came to the US as a teenager who barely spoke a word of English, Yaghi decided to find a new country in which to pursue his goal of “solving ambitious problems.”.

Germany was at the top of Yaghi’s list, but none of the universities there seemed willing to provide him with the resources he wanted. He was instead lured to China: In July, Tsinghua University appointed him to lead a newly introduced institute devoted to using AI to accelerate chemical research. Yaghi says he was drawn to the opportunity because he’s a firm believer in AI’s potential to “shorten the time between discovery and commercialization.” Having spent a quarter century perfecting his water-harvesting technology, largely through arduous trial and error, he is optimistic that AI can help him get his next invention to market in a fraction of that time.

In a recent development, yaghi’s move to Tsinghua was viewed as a harbinger of China’s scientific rise. And after just a few months on the school’s Beijing campus, Yaghi notes he has been impressed by his colleagues’ brilliance and drive. “I feel like my scientific environment wants to get better, wants to improve, wants to move forward,” he says. “The attitude is more of a let's-get-it-done type.” Atoco is now about to start selling its first water-harvesting system, capable of producing up to 1,000 gallons per day in optimal conditions. The tech giant is also developing machines to capture atmospheric carbon, a key to slowing the pace of climate change. These technologies use relatively little energy because Yaghi’s frameworks bond with carbon-dioxide molecules.

Recent findings suggest that yaghi still has great affection for the US, where he started his academic journey at a Newly introduced York community college in the 1980s. He hopes the country will awaken to the need to protect the innovation system it built over many decades—a system he describes even now as “the envy of the world.” Science “is part of our civilization, and we should not take attacks on science very lightly,” he says. “It is something that society needs to value.” —Brendan I. Koerner.

Recent findings suggest that in April, a four-person crew took a 10-day trip that circumnavigated the moon. They came back to a world with a renewed dream of space travel.

On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials.
  • They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico.
  • It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials.

They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster. The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA.

It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.

Recent findings suggest that the Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute.

Recent findings suggest that "The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," SETI wrote of the broadcast in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's.".

The message was designed by astronomy professor Frank Drake of Cornell University (who also developed the famed Drake Equation for alien life), as well as Cornnell graduate students Richard Isaacman and Linda May, and Arecibo staff member James Walker, with input from astronomer Carl Sagan and others, according to Cornell University.

The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers, with the broadcast lasting less than 3 minutes, according to SETI.

As of 2026, the message should have traveled about 52 light-years (1 light-year is the distance light travels in a year), with 24,948 light-years to go before reaching star cluster M13.

Industry observers note that the Arecibo message may have been the first message of its kind, but it wasn't the last. We have also included messages on several spacecraft, such as Pioneer and Voyager. NASA and Paul McCartney also beamed a performance of "Across the Universe" in 2008.

After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from Fresh York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#24262. Industry News: Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins

Industry News: Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1234 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study from the University of Otago, Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka, has revealed a surprising divide in the fortunes of one of New Zealand's least understood penguin species.
  • Published in PLOS ONE, the research found that one population has remained stable for at least 25 years, while the other has declined by more than 40 percent over the past three decades.
  • Thomas Mattern of the Tawaki Project, which brings together scientists from the university's Departments of Zoology and Marine Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study from the University of Otago, Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka, has revealed a surprising divide in the fortunes of one of New Zealand's least understood penguin species. Although Erect-crested penguins breed in just two remote island groups, their populations are experiencing dramatically different outcomes.

Published in PLOS ONE, the research found that one population has remained stable for at least 25 years, while the other has declined by more than 40 percent over the past three decades.

The study was led by Dr. Thomas Mattern of the Tawaki Project, which brings together scientists from the university's Departments of Zoology and Marine Science. Researchers also collaborated with the Antarctic Research Trust and the Global Penguin Society.

Drone Surveys Reveal a Surprising Penguin Population Divide.

Erect-crested penguins breed exclusively on the Bounty and Antipodes islands, two isolated island groups located approximately 800 kilometers southeast of Latest Zealand's South Island.

To determine how many penguins remain, researchers conducted extensive drone surveys between 2022 and 2024. They photographed and counted every breeding colony across both island groups, producing the first comprehensive population survey of the entire species.

Sources indicate that "The results overturn a long-standing assumption," Dr. Mattern notes.

"The tiny Bounty Islands, at just 50 hectares, were found to hold almost as many breeding pairs (about 27,800) as the Antipodes Islands (about 29,800), even though the latter is 40 times larger and historically considered the species' stronghold.".

It has been revealed that the difference in population trends was even more unexpected. Despite their small size, the Bounty Islands have maintained a relatively consistent number of breeding penguins for decades. Meanwhile, the much larger Antipodes Islands have experienced a substantial decline.

"Comparing the new counts with historical records going back to the mid-1990s, the Bounty Islands population has remained essentially unchanged for at least 25 years.

"The Antipodes Islands population, by contrast, has declined by more than 40 percent since 1995.".

Why Are Penguins Disappearing From the Antipodes Islands?

Researchers believe several overlapping pressures may explain why the two populations are heading in opposite directions. Natural predators, increasingly destructive storms, and differences in where the birds travel and feed could all be contributing.

According to recent reports, one particularly troubling factor involves skuas, native subantarctic birds that prey on penguin eggs and chicks. As penguin colonies become smaller, the birds lose some of the protection that comes from nesting together in large numbers.

"As Antipodes colonies have shrunk over recent decades, the collective defense they once provided against native subantarctic bird, the skua, a natural predator of eggs and chicks, has weakened, allowing predation losses to increase and colonies to fragment further.".

Co-author Dr. Klemens Pütz of the Antarctic Research Trust suggests that changes involving another penguin species may have intensified this pressure.

Sources indicate that eastern Rockhopper penguins suffered a "catastrophically" severe population collapse during the second half of the 20th century. Similar declines occurred across their Southern Ocean breeding range, likely driven by warming ocean waters. Today, fewer than 1,000 breeding pairs remain on the Antipodes Islands.

Industry observers note that "As Rockhoppers disappeared, skuas may have turned to Erect-crested penguin eggs and chicks instead," Dr. Pütz says.

Stronger Storms and Different Migration Routes Add to the Threat.

Predators are not the only challenge facing the Antipodes penguins. Increasingly powerful storms, consistent with wider climate trends across the Southern Ocean, have caused landslides that break up breeding colonies and leave the birds more vulnerable.

Differences in ocean habitats and seasonal movements may also help explain why the two populations have experienced such contrasting outcomes.

In a recent development, according to Dr. Mattern, penguins breeding on the Antipodes Islands migrate considerable distances into the Antarctic Polar Frontal Zone when the breeding season ends. In contrast, birds from the Bounty Islands remain closer to their nesting grounds, where the surrounding waters are more sheltered and may offer more abundant food.

These differences could leave the two populations exposed to very different environmental pressures, despite belonging to the same species.

The Strange Paradox of Schrödinger's Penguin.

The researchers have named this unusual situation "Schrödinger's Penguin," drawing inspiration from the famous physics thought experiment involving a cat inside a sealed box.

Industry observers note that in that experiment, the cat is imagined to be both alive and dead until the box is opened and its condition is observed. But Dr. Mattern explains that the penguin discovery turns the familiar concept around.

"With Schrödinger's cat, opening the box settles the question one way or the other.

"With Erect-crested penguins, it's the opposite. From a distance, without proper surveys, everyone assumed there was a single answer for the whole species.

"Once we actually opened the metaphorical box and looked, we found there wasn't one state at all, but two: stable on the Bounty Islands, declining on the Antipodes Islands.".

In other words, looking at the species as a whole can conceal what is happening within individual populations. Only by examining both island groups separately did researchers uncover how dramatically their circumstances differ.

A Hidden Conservation Crisis for Endangered Penguins.

Sources indicate that the Erect-crested penguin is currently one of only four penguin species worldwide classified as "Endangered" on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List. Another New Zealand penguin, the hoiho/yellow-eyed penguin, shares that designation.

However, the two species have received very different levels of attention. While the plight of the hoiho has attracted ongoing public interest and conservation efforts, the Erect-crested penguin has remained relatively overlooked.

Dr. Mattern explains that the species' current conservation classification relies on population estimates from the 1970s that were considerably inflated. When the new survey results are considered, the "Endangered" designation remains broadly appropriate for the declining Antipodes population, but not for the stable Bounty Islands population.

This creates a difficult conservation dilemma. If the two populations are combined into a single assessment, the species' overall threat classification could actually improve, even though one population continues to decline sharply.

"Averaged across both populations, the global ranking would actually improve to "Vulnerable," masking the severity of the Antipodes decline, and downplaying how exposed the Bounty Islands, likely the species' last secure stronghold, are to industrial fishing.".

According to recent reports, the researchers warn that a more favorable overall classification could create a misleading impression of security. Although the Bounty Islands population remains stable, it may still face significant threats, particularly from industrial fishing activity.

"A single, ostensibly improved threat ranking is like putting the lid back on Schrödinger's box, trading a convenient illusion for the stronger protection the Bounty Islands population actually needs," Dr. Mattern says.

The findings highlight why conservation efforts must account for the circumstances of individual populations rather than relying exclusively on a species' global status. For Erect-crested penguins, recognizing the differences between the two island groups could be essential to protecting their future.

The study received funding from the Vontobel Foundation (Switzerland) through the Antarctic Research Trust and from the Global Penguin Society. The research was carried out under permits issued by the Latest Zealand Department of Conservation.

Materials provided by University of Otago. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
