📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fiona the Hippo is on the mend.

The Cincinnati Zoo confirmed that its famous semi-aquatic animal, who gained worldwide fame for her premature birth in 2017, is receiving medical treatment after eating a knit hat that was thrown into her habitat earlier this month.

In a recent development, “Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self,” the zoo stated in a statement Nov. 17, noting that Fiona is at the moment getting, “24-hour care and attention.”.

Recent findings suggest that after the zoo consulted with “veterinary and human specialists,” Fiona’s care team concluded that she is unable to undergo surgery to remove the hat. As a representative from the zoo acknowledged, “Our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she can pass it on her own.”.

According to recent reports, so far, Fiona is moving in the right direction. The hippo received a colonoscopy courtesy of The Columbus Zoo earlier this week as well as an ultrasound, which showed that her intestines are bunching, proving that she is working on passing something through.

In the meantime, Fiona is of course receiving all the love and support from her Cincinnati Zoo family, including “all of her favorite foods,” anti-nausea medicine as well as ensuring she stays hydrated.

“Fiona will remain off habitat until this is resolved,” the zoo added in a separate statement. “We will share updates as we have more information. Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats.”.

According to recent reports, this isn’t the first time Fiona has fought an uphill health battle. The now-9-year-old hippo was born six weeks early back in 2017, weighing in at just 25 pounds, the lowest recorded birth weight for her species ever.

Ever since, Fiona has remained beloved in online circles, even participating in a virtual safari show as part of The Cincinnati Zoo’s programming during its shutdown for the COVID-19 pandemic.

As the hippo continues her latest health fight, the Ohio zoo expressed gratitude for all the love and support she’s received.

“As you can imagine, we are rooting for her,” the zoo added in a statement, “and hoping that she proves to be as strong and resilient as she was at the beginning of her life.”.

For a look back at Fiona’s first moments in the world, keep reading….

Industry observers note that the zoo's 17-year-old hippo named Bibi gave birth to little Fiona six weeks early on January 24, 2017. She weighed 25 lbs. less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species, prompting critical care from vet staff.

Sources indicate that fiona's health made steady improvements in the weeks after her arrival, and by mid-March she had reached the 90 lb. mark, was eating hay and enjoying time in the pool!

Ever so curious about her surroundings, Fiona couldn't help but get an up-close look at herself on a computer screen.

By May, Fiona was well into the 200 lb. range and spending plenty of time lounging in her kiddie pool. What. A. Life.

Thanks to Fiona's tireless spirit and determination, she graduated to deeper-level pools after learning how to propel herself through the water.

Recent findings suggest that it wasn't until early June that little Fiona began spending time with her mama. In the beginning, Bifi (as they were so lovingly dubbed) interacted during brief, supervised play dates but have since begun adjusting to life in the outdoor pool enclosure.

Fiona's dad Henry was reunited with his daughter one month later and from the looks of those hippo grins, their first time interacting went swell!

Fiona embraces all her curves and all her edges, and it's a much-needed reminder that we all should too.

Sources indicate that it took much longer than anticipated, but Henry, Bibi and Fiona are finally cohabitating as a happy and healthy bloat. She can't get enough time exploring her dads' mouth, which is apparently normal behavior for a growing baby hippo!

Industry observers note that without a finalized schedule in place, Cincinnati Zoo visitors should cross their fingers in anticipation of seeing Fiona out and about. Here she is laying a wet one on her caregiver. Mwah!

Joint-record six referee errors in last Premier League weekend

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1242 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The failure to award a penalty to Arsenal would have been more controversial had the Gunners not scored a second-half winner.
  • The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel has ruled there were six on-field errors in the last round of games - the joint-highest it has recorded in one weekend.
  • Each week, the five members of the panel assess all the contentious incidents and vote whether both the referee and the video assistant referee (VAR) have got the decisions correct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The failure to award a penalty to Arsenal would have been more controversial had the Gunners not scored a second-half winner.

The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel has ruled there were six on-field errors in the last round of games - the joint-highest it has recorded in one weekend.

Each week, the five members of the panel assess all the contentious incidents and vote whether both the referee and the video assistant referee (VAR) have got the decisions correct.

You have to go back to the early part of the 2023-24 season to find the last time there were six mistakes logged.

The statistic does not include correct VAR interventions to fix errors, such as the red card shown to Brentford's Igor Thiago.

In the last round of games almost every fixture had a contentious refereeing situation which was hotly debated.

It started on Friday with a potential penalty to Coventry City for a hair pull by Everton's James Tarkowski.

Arsenal were denied a penalty following a VAR review after it was deemed Kai Havertz was offside.

Tottenham lodged a complaint over a challenge by Leeds United's Jayden Bogle, who was not shown a red card.

And Liverpool argued against a late Crystal Palace penalty.

But which decisions did the KMI Panel rule were incorrect? Some of the votes might surprise you.

Such was the controversy across the weekend, it may come as a surprise that the KMI Panel ruled only two were missed VAR interventions. There have been six missed overall, the same number as this stage last season.

Incident 1: Coventry's Caleb Yirenkyi appeared to have his hair pulled inside the area by Everton's James Tarkowski. No penalty was awarded.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.

What the KMI Panel said: "Tarkowski had a hold of Yirenkyi's hair and the panel unanimously felt that VAR should have intervened.".

It has been revealed that incident 2: Arsenal's Kai Havertz was pulled down inside the area by Hull City's Nobel Mendy. The VAR, Michael Oliver, sent referee Farai Hallam to the pitchside monitor but it was not given due to an offside offence by the Germany international.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.

What the KMI Panel remarked: "Although Harvertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence.".

Frank Lampard post-match interview - Everton v Coventry.

When the KMI Panel sits down to vote there are two separate considerations.

The first is on the decision of the referee, which is a basic judgement in law and the Premier League's expected interpretation.

The second is on the potential VAR intervention. This takes into account what the referee has said, the available replay angles and the high bar for intervention.

Incident 1: Thierno Barry put Everton in front against Coventry in the 61st minute, but there was a VAR check for a potential handball.

KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "On the balance of probability the ball did accidentally strike Barry's hand. However, the readily available footage did not provide conclusive evidence.".

Incident 2: Crystal Palace were awarded a penalty against Liverpool three minutes into stoppage time for a foul by Milos Kerkez on Dario Osorio. But was it just a clash of heads?

KMI Panel vote: 0:5 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel mentioned: "A penalty was incorrect with the contact being inevitable. However, it was not a clear and obvious error.".

Incident 3: Ipswich were awarded a 72nd-minute penalty against Bournemouth for a foul by Lewis Cook on Abdoul Ouattara.

KMI Panel vote: 1:4 incorrect on the field, but 4:1 no VAR intervention.

It has been revealed that what the KMI Panel noted: "Ouattara made a clear step across Cook who didn't make a challenge and the referee's decision to award a penalty was incorrect. However, it was not a clear and obvious error.".

Incident 4: Potential second yellow card for Bournemouth's Marcus Tavernier.

KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field; no VAR intervention possible.

What the KMI Panel noted: "There was a clear, deliberate action by Tavernier to delay the restart.".

Some of the most high-profile decisions from across the weekend have not yet featured.

That is because they have been voted to be correct on the field and through VAR.

Sources indicate that incident 1: Leeds United's Jayden Bogle caught Tottenham's Mathys Tel on high on his ankle. There was no VAR review for a red card.

KMI Panel vote: 3:2 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel remarked: "The majority felt Bogle was looking to challenge with his right leg and his left leg came down on the back of Tel's ankle without the speed, force or intensity to be serious foul play. Two panellists felt that the challenge was sufficiently dangerous to merit a red card.".

Incident 2: Chelsea's Cole Palmer went down on the edge of the area under a challenge by Sunderland's Luke O'Nien.

KMI Panel vote: 4:1 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

It has been revealed that what the KMI Panel remarked: "Clear contact made by O'Nien on Palmer which the panel felt should have been penalised with a free-kick on the basis that contact was made outside the area. One panellist felt that the foul contact was inside the area.".

Incident 3: Sunderland were awarded a penalty when Levi Colwill was ruled to have tripped Brian Bobbey.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel remarked: "There was upper body holding from both players as they progressed into the penalty area before a careless trip by the Chelsea defender.".

Incident 4: Possible foul by Senne Lammens on Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki before Patrick Dorgu's 96th-minute equaliser.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel noted: "Although Lammens turned away from the ball, the contact he made on Suzuki was not impactful.".

The KMI Panel was scrapped this summer in the Scottish Premiership because clubs became frustrated with the voting patterns of its members.

But it is more important in the Premier League, with the results creating a merit table which contributes to 50% of referees' salaries in bonus payments.

Many fans will feel there should have been more than two VAR errors logged in the last round of games.

Yet the KMI Panel does not exist to mirror the opinion of supporters.

Crucially, it uses the laws of the game and how the Premier League expects its games to be refereed as the barometer.

Still, six on-field mistakes - plus the Thiago red card - is clearly a high number.

And fans struggle to understand why it seems to be OK to have these on-field errors, and not correct them due to the high bar.

It all adds to the frustration of VAR.

Germany dominated neighbor and historic rival the Netherlands in their Nations League quarterfinal match-up at Berlin's Olympic Stadium on Monday evening.

It was the team's sixth game under head coach Jürgen Klopp and the 50th ever between the two sides.

Germany's 5-0 shellacking of the Oranje was their most lopsided victory since 1959, when they won 7-0. In all, Germany have now won 19 of those matches, the Netherlands have won 12, and 18 ended in a draw.

Recent findings suggest that speaking to German broadcaster ARD after the game, attacking midfielder Florian Wirtz — who scored twice in the fixture — said: "We hope that we can make it fun for the fans. It was definitely fun for us, especially in the second half.".

Despite the loss, Xavi Hernandez's Dutch side will reach the final eight alongside Germany.

Prior to the match, Klopp had made it clear that he and his team were approaching Monday's showdown as a final after having lost to Greece 1-0 in his first home game in the job on September 27.

By night's end, Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck each scored once and Brajan Gruda scored once and added two assists on top of Wirtz's double.

Klopp has been high on Wirtz, who has come under fire for not delivering at Liverpool since his arrival there in June 2025, and his bet seems to be paying off with the 23-year-old now scoring four goals in his last four games for Germany.

"We don't care who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly," remarked Wirtz on Monday evening before adding: "We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we've taken some great steps in our development as a team.".

A group of five EU member states, including Germany, have entered talks over a scheme to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.

The proposal to set up so-called return hubs in a non-EU country had been unveiled by the group — which also includes Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark — had first been announced back in September.

Tesla has earmarked some €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its factory in Germany, near to Berlin.

The Grünheide complex will be expanded to start producing the electric car organization's driverless Cybercabs, with output expected to eventually reach 1 million units.

The Elon Musk-owned company remarked construction would begin in 2027, with the first Cybercabs rolling off the line in 2029.

"With this, we are laying the foundations for the world's most technologically advanced Tesla factory here in Grünheide," Tesla said.

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.

Matt Pearson on our sports desk breaks down where the power struggle right now stands, with the deadline for candiates just a matter of hours away now.

Lawmakers in the state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have voted in Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier.

The 52-year-old has been in the role since 2017 and is heading into a third term.

The vote was a secret ballot, but it can still be assumed who voted and how.

She received 39 of the 68 votes cast in the chamber, exactly as many as commanded by Schwesig's three-party coaliton of her Social Democrats (29), the ecologist Greens (5), and the socialist Left Party (5).

While Söder's comments in Munich focused in particular on the policy the coalition in Berlin had not delivered, Merz initiatlly focused on talking up the efficacy of his federal coalition.

"We are aware of the situation. We know that we now need to deliver. And we also know that we face difficult talks within the coalition. But I would also say from the experiences of the last weeks that there are solutions to the problems which we have in Germany," Merz stated.

Merz stated that in the 18 months since last year's election, the coalition "has already successfully implemented many things, not 'set them into motion' as people like to say, but actually implemented.".

He noted a total of 17 bills going through the second and third reading process in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, last week, "including the most comprehensive reforms of our intelligence and security services that we have ever done in [post-war] Germany.".

Among others, he thanked Bavarian Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, a senior member of the Bavarian CSU sister party to Merz's own conservative CDU, for his contribution to this.

Merz also touted the support given to CSU politician Ilse Aigner, not just from his CDU but from the Social Democrat coalition partners and the Greens, to become the next president, calling her a person who would "represent our country very well at home and abroad.".

After hailing these accomplishments, Merz then turned to electricity tax cuts, saying he anticipated talks on the matter on Tuesday that would be "very short.".

He stated that over the weekend, coalition leaders had revisited the figures, and now believed they would be able to "completely" reduce electricity taxes to the minimum European levels in 2027 "also for private households.".

Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has appeared with Friedrich Merz at a press conference during the chancellor's trip to Munich.

It seems Söder, Merz and the CDU/CSU believe they have unfinished business after the budget was finalized in the Bundestag late last week.

Merz had pledged in the run-up to the decision to provide a reduction in electricity tax for all, but the final agreement did not include this step, with the coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) saying it was not adequately costed.

Söder mentioned he and Merz had discussed "backup for the coming days," for Berlin and for a "collective stance, that is really, really notable.".

He stated the coming days were about "demonstrating credibility in politics," seemingly in reference to Merz's promise that the coalition did not ultimately deliver.

According to recent reports, "That's why it's really important to us that we do indeed bring about the reduction in electricity tax," Söder said. "This is important for businesses. It would be a relief for citizens. But it's also a matter of credibility and it's written in the coalition agreement.".

Söder stated that as to the question of "where the money comes from, with a €560 billion (roughly $615 billion) budget, with €200 billion in new debt, nobody can tell me there's no potential within the budgeting process.".

A festive piece of merchandise on the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) "fan shop" website has upset some religious leaders in Germany.

Called a "chocolate Nicholas," it appears to depict a semblance of Saint Nicholas in bishop's regalia and the party's colors and holding a book with "AfD" written on the cover where a Bible might be in more traditional iconography.

The Bishop of Essen, Franz-Josef Overbeck, was highly critical of the promotion in Monday's edition of the Bild newspaper.

"The AfD is appropriating Christian symbols for party campaigning," Overbeck said. "Showing the holy Nicholas in a blue coat with mitre, staff and the gospel with an AfD logo is not in order.".

Overbeck acknowledged that other organizations like football clubs would sell chocolate Christmas figurines in club colors, but he said they would tend to refrain from including overtly Christian symbols when doing so.

Bild quoted an AfD spokesman as saying that as a "liberal-conservative party that clearly associates itself with Christian values," the item fit "particularly well" with the party image.

The main German protestant church group EKD's cultural representative, Johann Hinrich Claussen, mentioned the offer showed the AfD had "no understanding of traditions and no respect" for Christianity.

He described the action as "embarrassing and revealing," and noted that Christianity was "supra-partisan.".

It has been revealed that "The AfD knows little about what is holy to Christians. Otherwise, it would be aware that Bishop Nicholas of Myra, in what today is Demre in Turkey, stood clearly for uniting the occident and the orient. Beyond that, he is the patron saint of rescues at sea," Claussen stated.

The partner of deceased Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger has noted that anybody is welcome at his funeral this coming Saturday.

Aiwanger was the economy minister in Bavaria's state government as the leader of the junior coalition partners to the center-right CSU.

"Hubert was a man of the people and so it stands to reason that anyone who liked or treaasured him is allowed to come to his funeral," Tanja Schweiger wrote on her Instagram profile overnight.

According to recent reports, she was posting after a requiem in the state capital Munich paying tribute to the leader of the Free Voters (Freie Wähler) party over the weekend. Around 1,100 people attended this ceremony.

Aiwanger died suddenly and unexpectedly on November 4 during a working visit to Berlin, aged 55.

Prosecutors have since said he died of natural causes, after he was found dead in his hotel room.

Germany's national men's football team will play neighbors and rivals the Netherlands for the 50th time on Monday night.

And there's quite a lot at stake for Jürgen Klopp's team in the last group stage game of the Nations League competition at Berlin's Olympiastadion.

If Germany win, they will qualify for the knockout stages, but a defeat could lead to potential relegation into the second tier of Nations League football.

Klopp was upbeat in the pre-match press conference at the prospect of playing the Netherlands, who he mentioned play "Xavi football," in the image of the skillful Spanish playmaker and World Cup winner coaching the team.

Sources indicate that "I've always loved playing against teams like this. For all my coaching career," Klopp mentioned. "When someone says, 'hey they can really play football,' then in my mind the party's already started.".

Recent findings suggest that A full house with some 71,000 fans is expected in the capital when the game kicks off. Klopp played on the Dutch reputation for liberal use of bicylces in his comments to reporters, saying he wanted to "put a stick in their spokes" and dislodge them from the saddle.

The notion of a bridge over the valley between Ratingen and Heiligenhaus to the east of Düsseldorf in western Germany as part of the A44 highway is more than half a century old. And the physical bridge itself has stood, complete, ever since 2022.

Yet still the crossing is not connected to any roads at either end.

A construction project to build the last 4.4 kilometers of highway and link the bridge to the A44 highway will formally start on Monday.

State premier Hendrik Wüst, as well as the regional transport and traffic ministers will attend the ground-breaking ceremony.

A project first conceived some 55 years ago has faced repeated delays because of lawsuits, environmental protection studies and onerous planning and permit procedures.

In a recent development, the bridge across the Angerbachtal (Angerbach Valley) should improve the road connection between the North Rhine-Westphalia state capital of Düsseldorf, the Bergisches Land mountain range and the industrial cities in the Ruhr Valley. It's also meant to help remove some strain from the perenially busy A3 highway and to improve the road connections to Düsseldorf International Airport.

The last stretch of highway is expected to cost around €200 million (roughly $220 million), or roughly the annual costs incurred each year by forcing traffic to divert around it, according to estimates from Düsseldorf's IHK industry and trade association.

Construction is expected to take several years, no formal end date has yet been set.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz heads to Munich early on Monday, for a meeting with the leadership of the Bavarian Christian Social Democrats (CSU), the sister party to his conservative  Christian Democrats(CDU).

No concrete details about the talks were made public ahead of time, except for the CSU saying it would serve as a general exchange that had been planned for some time.

The trip comes a week after Merz nominated Ilse Aigner as the next German president, likely paving the way for her to become the first woman and first CSU politician to assume the role.

According to recent reports, it also follows soon after the 2027 federal budget cleared a marathon meeting of the parliamentary budget committee in Berlin. This serves as one of the more conspicuous examples of the frictions and difficulties in the grand coalition between the Christian Democrats and the center-left Social Democrats — with the compromises it contains a point of frustration among the CSU and for state premier Markus Söder.

The northeastern state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will likely vote in Social Democrat (SPD) Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier early in the afternoon.

The 52-year-old, who first stepped into the role in 2017, plans to lead a newly introduced coalition of the SPD, the environmentalist Greens and the socialist Left Party after state elections in September.

The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as the largest single party in the sparsely populated state.

But still, the political calculus that emerged was arguably simpler than in Berlin — where the socialist Left Party is the largest party but could struggle to lead a coaltion — and in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD was by far the largest party but short of an outright majority.

Schwesig's SPD claimed 29 seats, with the Greens and the Left each taking 5, meaning that when combined, they hold a fairly clear majority over the AfD with its 32 seats.

The SPD's relatively successful performance in the state, at least compared to its national struggles, has also led to Schwesig being linked with a possible return to federal politics. The SPD intends to elect a upcoming leadership duo early next year.

Schwesig has already had a spell in Berlin as the federal minsiter for families, pensioners and women, and briefly led the SPD on an interim basis in 2017, but after this she returned to her home state to seek the top regional job instead.

If you hear an emergency broadcast this afternoon, don't panic!

It has been revealed that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) are conducting a scheduled test of the national emergency alert system at 2:20 p.m. ET on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

Industry observers note that the FCC released a public notice about the scheduled test on Sept. 16, but it comes at a moment of high national anxiety, driven by recent tech outages — among other troubling news stories.

First, Microsoft suffered a widespread global outage on Thursday, Nov. 12, followed by a rare FAA nationwide ground stoppage the following day. And on Monday, a JPMorgan Chase outage sparked reports of a major bank outage (the problem was limited to Chase Bank and not a systemic issue or the result of a cyberattack), followed promptly by a United Airlines outage.

None of these outages were directly related to or caused by cyberattackers, but the timing has sparked conspiracy theories and generalized anxiety.

However, the emergency alert was scheduled long before these outages; the FCC also revealed a backup date of Dec. 3, in the event today's test does not occur. So, if your TV or radio suddenly goes into emergency mode today, don't freak out.

FEMA will use the Integrated Public Alert and Warning System (IPAWS) to disseminate a message in both English and Spanish. The message will read, "This is a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, issued by the Federal Emergency Management Agency, covering the United States from 2:20 to 2:50 hours ET. This is only a test. No action is required by the public.".

The test will appear on the following types of media:.

Wired and wireless cable television systems.

Digital television broadcast stations.

Digital audio broadcasting systems.

Recent findings suggest that notably, the emergency alert will not appear on your phone. So, if you do receive an "emergency alert" by text or phone this afternoon, ignore it; scammers may be trying to take advantage of the test.

FEMA tests emergency text alerts, or Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA), separately.

Outside of testing, WEA notifications are used for Imminent Threat alerts, Amber Alerts, Public Safety Messages (PSAs), and National Alerts, which are issued by the president or the FEMA administrator.

Latest Update: Physicists use laser light to unlock a crystal's hidden electrical powers

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physicists at Auburn University have discovered how to use brief bursts of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions hidden inside a crystal.
  • The research was led by Wencan Jin, the Thomas and Jean Walter Endowed Associate Professor in Auburn's Department of Physics, and graduate student Mohamed Kandil.
  • The researchers investigated a modified version of strontium titanate, a material with an unusual combination of electrical characteristics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physicists at Auburn University have discovered how to use brief bursts of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions hidden inside a crystal. Their findings shed latest light on a mystery that has puzzled researchers for decades and demonstrate how lasers can influence the material's electrical behavior. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists explore faster ways to process and store information.

The research was led by Wencan Jin, the Thomas and Jean Walter Endowed Associate Professor in Auburn's Department of Physics, and graduate student Mohamed Kandil. Their paper, "Optical Poling of a Quantum Ferroelectric Metal across the Order-Disorder Phase Transition," received an Editors' Suggestion designation from Physical Review Letters. Scientists at Japan's National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology produced the crystals used in the study.

A Decades-Old Mystery Hidden Inside a Crystal.

The researchers investigated a modified version of strontium titanate, a material with an unusual combination of electrical characteristics. Although electrons can travel through the crystal, it also contains extremely small regions with positive and negative electrical sides. Known as polar nanoregions, these microscopic "islands" can point in different directions or become aligned with one another. Understanding how and why this alignment occurs is essential to explaining the material's properties and learning how to manipulate them.

In a recent development, scientists have spent decades trying to determine what happens when these regions become organized. One possibility is that atoms move together to produce the polarized state. Another is that the tiny electrical islands are already there and simply begin pointing in the same direction as temperatures fall. The distinction is similar to the difference between assembling a group of people and asking people who are already gathered to turn and face the same way. Because the regions are extraordinarily small and produce very weak signals, determining which explanation is correct has been a persistent challenge.

Laser Experiments Reveal How Electrical Order Emerges.

To investigate, the Auburn researchers developed an exceptionally sensitive system that uses lasers to measure subtle changes in the crystal. By studying how the material altered incoming light, they were able to monitor the orientation of its electrical regions while repeatedly heating and cooling the sample.

In a recent development, the measurements revealed a clear pattern. At warmer temperatures, the tiny regions pointed in seemingly random directions. When the crystal cooled, however, they began adopting preferred orientations. This behavior provided compelling evidence that the electrical islands existed before becoming aligned, supporting the explanation that cooling organizes regions already present in the material.

A Flash of Light Creates Order in a Trillionth of a Second.

The team went beyond observing this natural process. Researchers also demonstrated that short laser pulses could temporarily align the electrical islands, even at higher temperatures when the regions would ordinarily remain disorganized. Using an optical measurement, they were able to detect the pattern produced by the laser light.

The effect was extraordinarily brief, lasting approximately one picosecond, or one trillionth of a second. Nevertheless, the ability to create and detect this electrical alignment using light provides a promising approach for studying how information might be controlled at extremely high speeds.

Three Years of Experiments Lead to a Breakthrough.

Achieving these results required considerable patience and technical refinement. The collaboration began at the 2023 American Physical Society March Meeting, where Jin met Japanese researchers capable of producing the specialized crystals needed for the experiments.

Back at Auburn, the team spent almost a year refining its equipment before it could reliably detect the weak optical signals from the tiny electrical regions. The next obstacle was even more demanding: measuring the extremely short interval during which laser illumination caused the regions to align.

Recent findings suggest that "The breakthrough came in 2025, when Mohamed finally observed the disordered polar regions becoming aligned under laser illumination," Jin said. "Seeing that signal emerge was a thrilling moment for the team.".

The achievement also represents an notable personal milestone for Kandil, whose first published research paper reflects three years of dedicated experimental work.

Recent findings suggest that "This experiment has truly been Mohamed's odyssey," Jin said. "It took him three years of dedication to complete the work and achieve his first publication.".

Upcoming Possibilities for Ultrafast Information Technology.

The discovery provides crucial evidence about how electrical order develops in this unusual crystal while also establishing a method for manipulating that order with light. Rather than simply observing the material's internal behavior, researchers can now briefly influence its microscopic electrical patterns and detect the resulting changes.

Although practical applications remain a future possibility, the experiments offer a latest way to investigate the rapid electrical processes occurring inside quantum materials. By revealing how light can control these previously elusive patterns, the Auburn researchers have opened another avenue for exploring technologies that could one day transform how information is processed and stored.

The production from Schirmer Theatrical — part of Wise Music Group and Sony Music Publishing — will follow-up on the 2025 touring production that brought Parton’s songs and stories to audiences around the world.

Recent findings suggest that next year’s run of shows is slated to kick off on Jan. 12 in Rochester, N.Y. at the Kodak Hall at Eastman Theatre, followed by gigs in Seattle and Pittsburgh, before moving to the U.K. in March and April for gigs in Edinburgh, Glasgow, Manchester, Liverpool, Bristol, London and Birmingham. The run will then continue in Chicago and Baltimore in April and May and conclude with two shows in Australia in July.

“From our earliest creative conversations with Dolly, we envisioned Threads: My Songs in Symphony as a musical celebration that could connect audiences across the world,” noted Schirmer Theatrical senior vice president Betsey Perlmutter in a statement. “At its heart, this concert experience captures the warmth, heart and joy of an evening spent with Dolly, centered around her extraordinary songs and singular spirit. Taking Threads to major cities around the world is a natural evolution of that original vision, and we’re beyond proud to bring this one-of-a-kind experience to fans around the globe.”.

Recent findings suggest that tickets for the U.S. dates are available now here and here. Pre-sales for the U.K. shows kicked off on Wednesday (Nov. 18), with a general on-sale slated for Friday (Nov. 20) at 10 a.m. local time here.

Sources indicate that the show premiered in 2025 with the Nashville Symphony before touring 31 cities in North America. The orchestra for the production created and co-produced by Parton will be led by David Hamilton. According to a release, the “innovative multimedia symphonic experience features Dolly’s songs and stories accompanied by original video content, with Dolly herself appearing on-screen to lead audiences through a visual-musical journey.”.

It will also feature a cast of guest vocalists and musicians, selected by Parton, performing such iconic hits as “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors,” “I Will Always Love You” and some of Parton’s personal favorites.

In the meantime, Parton’s Broadway musical, DOLLY: A True Original Musical, is slated to being preview performances at the St. James Theatre in New York on Dec. 7, with opening night scheduled for Jan. 19, which would have been Parton’s 81st birthday. Parton died in August at 80 following a brief battle with cancer.

Breaking: Klopp wants Infantino out as FIFA candidate deadline looms

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has become the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA.
  • "Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job," he said on Sunday.
  • But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for new candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has become the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA.

"Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job," he said on Sunday.

But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for new candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.

"There are people who truly care about the future of football, people who aren't driven by financial interests," Klopp remarked ahead of Germany's Nations League match against the Netherlands on Monday.

"If someone like that were to step up — if someone like that were to become president — I think that would be a significant improvement.".

If that person is waiting in the wings, they're leaving it late to step on the stage. Despite a raft of federations and continental confederations, including Germany, UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia), calling for Infantino's head in the wake of his strategy to sell off part of the World Cup earlier this year, the incumbent appears to have stopped the bleeding.

That blueprint, which involved forming a subsidiary arm of FIFA called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors including Joshua Kushner — brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner — was widely panned before being abandoned.

It followed on from widespread criticism of Infantino's awarding of a latest FIFA Peace Prize to Trump, the overturning of a red card for US national team player Folarin Balogun, and with Trump's involvement, at the World Cup and a host of other controversies.

Since then, though, many public critics have backtracked amid FIFA promising to release an extra $2.7bn (€2.45bn) from its reserves over the next four years to the federations, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn.

Perhaps the most significant of these u-turns came from the AFC, who went from saying Infantino had committed a "fundamental breach of trust" in August, to offering the Swiss its "full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the FIFA president" in October.

Those words were spoken by AFC President, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who ran against Infantino when he first won the top job at FIFA in 2016. He will not run again and said that "my feeling is, I'm sure, the feeling of most of my members," in regard to Infantino.

Proof that the sentiment is not universal comes in the shape of Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA). Tashima is one of only two people to confirm they will oppose Infantino in the March 2027 presidential elections.

The 68-year-old is a well respected figure in Asian football politics and will have no problem meeting the threshold of support from five of FIFA's 211 federations. This is not like the other candidate, former Swiss international player Ramon Vega, who is an enormous outsider. Tashima appears to be running on the basis that he will be able to chart a calmer path at FIFA.

"I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association," Tashima told the Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon. "It's not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world.".

It has been revealed that but the numbers are against him. Though support from within the confederations may not be total, the backing of AFC and the African confederation (CAF) is a huge boost for Infantino, with those two alone making up 101 votes, almost enough for a majority.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, the only real concern remaining for Infantino remains UEFA. The European federation, headed by Aleksander Ceferin, is a major revenue source for FIFA but the two organizations are at loggerheads. As well as a war of words, UEFA are seeking to obtain evidence for a potential Swiss criminal case against Infantino in regards to FFE. FIFA have called this a "smear campaign" and a "fishing expedition".

But, so far, UEFA has not put up a candidate. Former Arsenal coach turned FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger was thought to be a contender but has now ruled himself out. Wenger's compatriot, Philippe Diallo, has since emerged as another option, with The Guardian reporting on Monday that the French Football Federation president could be confirmed on Tuesday.

While Europe is football's powerbase, particularly from a club perspective, UEFA will need Diallo, or any candidate they can convince to run, to win votes from outside its 55 nations to have any chance of success, particularly with Tashima likely to split any challenge. Even if a candidate appears before the November 18 deadline, Klopp's hope for change appears to be a long shot.

#24251. Capillus HairBand Review: Good Looks, Awkward Fit

Capillus HairBand Review: Good Looks, Awkward Fit

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Excepting the few models that look like regular hats, most red-light therapy for hair growth devices look … well, pretty weird.
  • Discreet black, fabric-covered, and sized like a normal hair accessory, the HairBand’s only indication it might do something more than hold back hair is a little 2 x 1-inch battery pack that sits jauntily cocked to one side.
  • Recent findings suggest that interestingly, Capillus makes a series of full-coverage devices with laser diodes built into what looks like a normal black baseball cap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Excepting the few models that look like regular hats, most red-light therapy for hair growth devices look … well, pretty weird. From stormtrooper helmets to headpieces that look like they were designed for Geordi La Forge, these aren’t exactly accessories you’d want to wear in public. Which is why it was nice to unbox the Capillus HairBand and find, at long last, a normal-looking headband.

Discreet black, fabric-covered, and sized like a normal hair accessory, the HairBand’s only indication it might do something more than hold back hair is a little 2 x 1-inch battery pack that sits jauntily cocked to one side. It’s refreshing to finally see a red-light device that doesn’t embarrass the user or frighten animals and young children, but after testing it for over a month, I found the HairBand has its share of shortcomings for the price.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, Capillus makes a series of full-coverage devices with laser diodes built into what looks like a normal black baseball cap. However, the cheapest of these hats runs $1,699, and the most expensive “triple-wavelength” model, with 312 laser diodes, runs $3,299. The 2-inch-wide Capillus HairBand provides a similar laser diode treatment for less, at $599 with only 82 diodes (650 nm). (Capillus says the headband is designed to prioritize areas where hair loss is most noticeable, such as the hairline and temples.).

Unlike straight LED lights, laser diodes provide collimated beams of light that travel in a straight line, allowing for more focused and intense treatment of hair follicles. I actually saw some success with this treatment when I tested the HairBand’s closest competitor, Hairmax’s LaserBand 82 ComfortFlex ($849). It couldn’t help follicles that were scarred or had already died, but studies have shown that red-light therapy can energize follicles that have more recently become dormant.

I did see some growth in the middle of my part with the LaserBand, and while I stopped using it to switch to the HairBand exclusively for the past five or so weeks, I admit this growth did make it difficult to isolate the HairBand’s contribution, especially since the headband’s coverage area is so small. Thus, the following observations are mainly on the wearing experience of the HairBand, not hair growth.

It has been revealed that at only 2 inches wide and five minutes per section, the HairBand took at least 15 minutes to cover my entire part, compared with the 3-inch-wide LaserBand, which also only needs to be used three times per week at 30 seconds per section for a total of 90 seconds. I’m a Type-A full-time working parent in my mid-forties, and let me tell you—15 minutes of doing nothing is a long time in my world.

It has been revealed that the HairBand has teeth and could sit on my head as long as it was in a normal headband position, right in the middle, but the weight of the battery pack pulls it forward ever so slightly, so if I was leaning over or doing anything that didn’t hold my head exactly straight, it would start to slip off. This meant I had to hold it with my hand, which meant no multitasking.

Capillus’ marketing materials use words like “ritual” and feature pictures of twentysomethings admiring themselves in the mirror, but I can’t imagine these women are suffering from the perimenopausal hair loss that would necessitate use of a red-light device in the first place.

According to recent reports, I don’t consider myself to have an overly large head and have never had trouble with hats or other hair accessories, but this headband, which weighs only 6 ounces, felt quite small and somewhat precarious on my head overall. I should note it is also rather overtly feminine in style—my husband and I were able to share “custody” of the LaserBand, but he declined to wear this one, and I didn’t blame him.

There were two other concerns during my testing. One, the back of the box said it contained quick-start instructions, but my box only had the headband and USB-C charging cord—no physical user guide to be found (except online, but I had to do some googling). Not that one is needed, since it’s pretty obvious how it works—push the start button on the battery pack, and it will beep and shut off when the five minutes are up—but it’s an odd omission at this price point.

In a recent development, two, this device is not presently FDA-cleared for treating hair loss or promoting regrowth. This isn’t ideal, but FDA-cleared is much different from FDA-approved; it simply requires the manufacturer to prove its product is “substantially equivalent” to an already FDA-cleared product. (And it doesn’t ensure results, just that it’s safe to use as directed.) Capillus’ rep tells me the brand is currently working on the FDA filing for the HairBand, which was released in September of this year, and intends to have it cleared in 2027. (The brand’s cap-style devices are FDA-cleared.) Even so, the HairBand is a unique device in this space, but if I’m spending that much on a red-light device, I would prefer a little more versatility in the design.

Industry News: Satellites now outnumber the visible stars above most towns

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.
  • That's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that presently circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers).
  • The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 700 satellites are crossing the sky over an average mid-latitude town at any moment of the night, outnumbering in many cases the stars visible to the naked eye.

That's based on an analysis of the trajectories of the 15,833 active satellites that presently circle the planet in low Earth orbit below an altitude of 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers). Analyzing data from Oct. 12 and 18 this year, researchers found that with a completely unobstructed horizon, 710 satellites were crossing the sky in every single moment of the night above an average U.K. town.

The results were published as a non-peer-reviewed study conducted by engineering firm Accu Components, and is based on satellite monitoring data from the U.S. Space Force available through the public website CelesTrak. Although the researchers specifically focused on the U.K., they say that such heavy satellite traffic flows above most of Europe, the U.S. and other mid-latitude regions, especially between 40 and 50 degrees north or south.

Recent findings suggest that "Most Starlink satellites orbit at around 53 degrees to the equator, so the satellites bunch up over the mid-latitudes. These worldwide figures are approximate, based on a global grid over a single day," Accu Components spokesperson told Space.com in an email. "Skies near the equator are the quietest, with around 490 satellites.".

Not all of those satellites are visible to the naked eye, the researchers stated in a statement. Because satellites unlike stars don't produce their own light, they must be illuminated by the sun, while the ground below has already sunk into darkness, to be visible. According to the study, an average of 105 satellites out of those 710 were catching light as they zoomed overhead, shining as bright as stars.

Recent findings suggest that the spokesperson stated that the actual number of visible satellites varies drastically throughout the night. During the hours after dusk and before dawn, a much greater number of satellites can be seen, while in the middle of the night most no longer catch any light.

According to recent reports, "For a typical U.K. town, around 300 satellites are catching the sunlight in the first hour or so after dark," the spokesperson stated. "That falls to fewer than 20 around midnight, then climbs back to around 300 before dawn.".

According to recent reports, for comparison, as little as a few dozen stars are visible to the naked eye in the dead of the night above large, light-polluted megalopolis such as London or Latest York, according to OwnStarMap. In suburban areas and smaller towns, that number grows to a few hundred. To get to a few thousand visible stars, one must retreat into remote countryside or isolated mountain ranges.

The number of satellites orbiting Earth has grown steeply in the past decade, especially since Elon Musk’s SpaceX began launching its internet-beaming Starlink constellation. Satellite companies strategy to launch hundreds of thousands, possibly millions of satellites in the coming decades. If those visions come to pass, the number of passing satellites will vastly outgrow that of stars almost anywhere in the world. The trend especially concerns astronomers who fear the impacts on humankind’s ability to study the Universe.

Satellites crossing the view of ground-based telescopes leave streaks in astronomical images and increase the overall brightness of the sky through the light they reflect down towards Earth. Gradually, even the most powerful telescopes could lose their ability to see the distant stars and galaxies that hold the answers to key questions about the history of the universe.

The study found that throughout the night, an average U.K. town sees 12,891 different satellites passing overhead.

Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

#24248. Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1194 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dinosaurs living along ancient coastlines may have enjoyed an unexpected addition to their diets: seaweed and other food from the ocean.
  • Today, powerful storms frequently deposit seaweed and other ocean material along shorelines, creating opportunities for animals that live on land to find additional food.
  • A new study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution suggests that this relationship between land and sea existed during the age of dinosaurs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dinosaurs living along ancient coastlines may have enjoyed an unexpected addition to their diets: seaweed and other food from the ocean. Latest research suggests that marine resources washed onto prehistoric beaches helped feed dinosaurs and their prey millions of years ago.

Today, powerful storms frequently deposit seaweed and other ocean material along shorelines, creating opportunities for animals that live on land to find additional food. Scientists call this process marine subsidization (MS). It is especially common in coastal environments and can become more vital when food on land is limited, such as during droughts.

A new study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution suggests that this relationship between land and sea existed during the age of dinosaurs. By examining chemical signatures preserved in fossils, researchers found evidence that ocean resources contributed to prehistoric food chains.

Sources indicate that "We show that coastal terrestrial organisms in the greenhouse climates of the Cretaceous relied on marine resources to supplement their diets in a similar way that modern organisms do," said first author Dr. Clayton Forster, a geologist at the University of Arkansas. "We can identify that marine resources are passed along the food chain and incorporated in the minerals of bones and teeth of dinosaurs, crocodiles, turtles, and fish.".

Mysterious Chemical Clues in Dinosaur Teeth.

The discovery helps explain a longstanding mystery involving the chemical composition of dinosaur teeth.

It has been revealed that plants contain two forms of carbon known as isotopes: 'light' (C-12) and 'heavy' (C-13). Scientists can measure the relative amounts of these isotopes, expressed as δ13C, to identify a chemical fingerprint that passes from food into the animals that consume it.

As animals eat, this carbon signature becomes incorporated into their tooth enamel. The δ13C value in enamel is typically higher than that of the food consumed, with living animals generally showing an increase of between 11 and 13 parts per thousand.

However, previous measurements of dinosaur teeth have consistently revealed unusually high values. These readings also exceed what scientists would expect from animals that ate only plants growing on land, which generally have lower δ13C values than most marine plants.

One possible explanation is that dinosaurs, or the animals they consumed, were obtaining some of their nutrients from the ocean.

"By determining the carbon isotope composition of dinosaur, fish, and crocodile tooth enamel, we can determine what their primary dietary source was and if they were different between regions," explained Forster.

Fossils Reveal a Prehistoric Ocean Food Source.

Sources indicate that to investigate, researchers examined fossils from (once) coastal locations bordering the Western Interior Seaway and the ancient coastline of the Gulf of Mexico. Around 100 million years ago, the Western Interior Seaway was an enormous inland sea that divided North America into two separate landmasses.

The team also analyzed fossils from locations farther inland, allowing them to compare animals that lived near the ocean with those that occupied landlocked environments.

The fossil deposits formed during two intervals of the Cretaceous Period: the early Albian (around 113-107 million years ago) and the early Cenomanian (approximately 100-96 million years ago).

It has been revealed that researchers used powdered fossil material to measure carbon isotope signatures from both periods. They also determined the latitudes where the animals had lived to investigate whether geography influenced the results.

A clear pattern emerged. Fossils from coastal environments consistently contained higher δ13C values than those from the inland formation. Remarkably, the coastal signatures remained similar across different locations, regardless of latitude or geological age.

These findings provide the first evidence of marine subsidization in prehistoric ecosystems, indicating that nutrients originating in the ocean were entering food chains on land millions of years ago.

Seaweed May Have Been on the Dinosaur Menu.

The researchers next considered what ocean food source could explain the widespread chemical signatures.

"Coastal-dwelling organisms must have eaten some kind of organic matter from the ocean, or prey that had done so. This pattern is shared from fish to megaherbivores and indicates that the extra carbon source must have been low in the food-chain to affect both aquatic and terrestrial animals," Forster explained.

Sources indicate that for the same chemical pattern to appear in such a wide variety of animals, the marine food source would likely have entered the food chain near its base. It also needed to be something that existed along coastlines but was absent farther inland, while remaining available for millions of years.

Seaweed emerged as the most likely explanation.

Recent findings suggest that "Few organisms meet these criteria besides marine macroalgae or macrophytes - seaweeds," said Forster. "Given the almost ubiquitous behavior of large coastal herbivores today to supplement their diet with seaweeds, it's likely that most of the sampled herbivorous dinosaurs were no different.".

Modern plant-eating animals living near coastlines often consume seaweed to supplement their diets. The fossil evidence suggests that many herbivorous dinosaurs may have behaved similarly, with marine nutrients also passing to other animals through the food chain.

Not Every Dinosaur Had a Taste for the Sea.

Despite the widespread evidence of marine nutrients in coastal food webs, the researchers found that not every dinosaur took advantage of these resources.

One notable exception was Tenontosaurus tilletti, a large plant-eating dinosaur whose fossils have been discovered at numerous locations dating to the Cretaceous Period.

Its tooth enamel contained δ13C values comparable to those of modern animals that feed on plants growing on land. This suggests that Tenontosaurus tilletti did not rely on marine food sources, even though other dinosaurs apparently did.

Recent findings suggest that the difference also strengthens the researchers' interpretation of the fossil evidence. If geological processes occurring after death had altered the carbon signatures in dinosaur teeth, the same unusual values would be expected more broadly. Instead, the variation between species suggests that the elevated readings reflect genuine differences in diet.

An Ancient Connection Between Land and Ocean.

Although the findings provide strong evidence that marine resources supported the coastal ecosystems examined, important questions remain.

The available fossils do not include specimens from polar or equatorial regions during the early Albian and early Cenomanian. As a result, scientists cannot yet determine how widespread this feeding behavior was across different latitudes.

Additional studies will also be needed to establish whether similar relationships existed during other geological periods, including the earlier Jurassic Period and the later early Cenozoic Era.

Beyond revealing a surprising possibility about what dinosaurs ate, the discovery highlights how closely life on land has been connected to the ocean throughout Earth's history.

According to recent reports, "Our study emphasizes the connections between terrestrial and marine ecosystems," concluded Forster. "They are deeply intertwined and have been for hundreds of millions of years. It highlights the importance of environmental linkages across time and space and protecting them where they exist today.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jennifer Lopez knows that sometimes, love does cost a thing.

Nearly two years after the "On The Floor" singer and Ben Affleck finalized their divorce, she reflected on the weight of their breakup—and whether she's ready to dance again with someone upcoming.

"I'm done with that part of my life," Lopez said on the Nov. 17 episode of Benny Blanco and Lil Dicky's Friends Keep Secrets podcast. "It was such a hard, disappointing last situation on every level. On every level, it was so disappointing. I don't ever want to delve into that.".

Though she is focusing on living life single, that doesn't mean she'll never be ready for another great love story, especially after taking a deeper look at her split from the Oscar winner.

Industry observers note that "I'm OK with myself," she explained. "I was a serial monogamist, one after the other, trying to find the thing, hoping that this was it.".

Now, the 57-year-old—mom to 18-year-old twins Max and Emme with ex-husband Marc Anthony—is getting loud with advice for others navigating divorce.

It has been revealed that "Always operate in a way that you'll feel proud of when you look back," she shared. Looking back at her experiences, she added, "Even as painful as some of them were so bad—life-shifting pain and hurt—I can look back and be like, 'I loved completely. I acted in a way that I was proud of as a human. I didn't treat anybody in any way that I would be ashamed of.'".

"I did the best that I could in the moment with what I knew," she continued. "That's my advice for anything because when you go through hard things like that, it's easy to be like, 'F--k this.' You're in so much pain you want to hurt somebody else, or somebody has hurt you so much, but you can't. I've always held myself to that kind of standard.".

Since then, Lopez—who filed for divorce from Affleck in August 2024, exactly two years after they got married—has continued to carry what she learned from their breakup and its aftermath.

Sources indicate that "Be the best person that you can be right now, every single time, especially when it's hard," she emphasized. "When you say you're strong, I think that's part of it. I can look at these things and be like, 'It's OK. These are experiences in my journey.'".

"I don't know why it was my journey sometimes," she admitted. "Then I realized, no, I'm here to learn something. I finally got to a place where I feel like I've learned it, but it took the f--king house to fall down on top of me to do that.".

Looking ahead, the "Let's Get Loud" singer—who was first engaged to Affleck in 2002 before splitting two years later—will be dancing for her papi when the time is right.

According to recent reports, "I'm different," she mentioned. "Because it changed me. Because I allowed it to change me. Because I wanted to learn the thing. I was like, 'It's done. I'm not doing this anymore. What are you going to do different?'".

It has been revealed that "You can intellectually be a smart person and know things," she explained. "But the knowing is not the thing. It's changing the behavior and the patterns. That's the thing. And that is a conscious action that you have to do. You have to change.".

A latest approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine highlights early promise

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.
  • In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.
  • WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

Industry observers note that china and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

Industry observers note that the US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

As long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine.

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, says study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

The immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler remarked.

Mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with fresh variants.

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

In a recent development, “You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler remarked.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

As promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans.

“They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, said Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the new research.

Industry observers note that the study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an upgrade.

It has been revealed that it also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler says they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss company called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

Recent findings suggest that other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland said. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a latest vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

Sources indicate that in reality, Poland noted, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

“That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he noted.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax says it may not survive.

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a firm called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team says it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very important in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler said.

In a recent development, they have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

In a recent development, fluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

Another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler stated, so it would have to be used carefully.

  • The acclaimed Belgian filmmakers, two-time Palme d’Or winners for Rosetta (1999) and The Child (2005), will be feted at the 39th European Film Awards in Athens on Jan.16.
  • Sources indicate that over nearly 50 years, with more than a dozen features and a handful of documentaries, the Dardenne brothers have established themselves as the preeminent humanist filmmakers of our time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sibling directors Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne will be honored with a lifetime achievement award at the 2027 European Film Awards.

The acclaimed Belgian filmmakers, two-time Palme d’Or winners for Rosetta (1999) and The Child (2005), will be feted at the 39th European Film Awards in Athens on Jan.16.

Sources indicate that over nearly 50 years, with more than a dozen features and a handful of documentaries, the Dardenne brothers have established themselves as the preeminent humanist filmmakers of our time. Their work, finely-honed social dramas about the lives of the marginalised, the impoverished and the vulnerable, most of them shot on location in the industrial town of Seraing, where they grew up, have shaped a generation of filmmakers, in Europe and worldwide. Related Stories Music Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Sam Fender Set to Headline Glastonbury 2027 TV 'Intimacy on Prescription' Wins Main Prize at Tallinn's TV Beats Co-Financing Market.

Industry observers note that the brothers began as documentarians, recording the lives and experiences of their local community. Those early films helped shape the directors’ later neo-realistic style as well as their enduring commitment to social issues. Rosetta (1999), the story of a turbulent teenager living in a trailer park with her alcoholic mother, trying to hold down any job she can get, premiered at the Cannes Film Festival and won the Palme d’Or for best film.

Recent findings suggest that every Dardenne film since has premiered in Cannes competition. They won their second Palme d’Or for The Child (2005), the story of two young parents on social benefits who sell their newborn baby on the black market. Lorna’s Silence (2008), about a young Albanian woman caught in a deadly citizenship scam, won Cannes’ Best Screenplay honor, as did their most recent feature, Young Mothers (2025), about a shelter for unwed teenage mums.

It has been revealed that the Kid With a Bike (2011), about an 11-year-old boy struggling with abandonment, took Cannes’ runner-up prize, the Grand Prix. The brothers won the Best Director Award in Cannes for Young Ahmed (2019), about a teenage Muslim boy who is drawn to extremism.

The Dardennes typically work with non-professional actors but made an exception for French star Marion Cotillard, who played a woman struggling to save her job in the workplace drama Two Days, One Night (2014). Cotillard won Best Actress at the European Film Awards for her performance.

Sources indicate that the Dardennes won their first European Film Award for Best Documentary for Gigi, Monica… back in 1997 and took the European Screenwriter Award for The Kid With a Bike in 2011. Surprisingly, given their reputation and the consistent quality of their work, the Dardennes have never been nominated for an Academy Award.
