📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ella Langley’s expected sweep of the 2026 CMA Awards began early, with the announcement of her win for music video of the year for her megahit “Choosin’ Texas.” And Tim McGraw made CMA history, becoming the first five-time winner of musical event of the year for “McArthur,” a collab with HARDY, Eric Church and Morgan Wallen.

The awards were announced live on ABC’s Good Morning America on Wednesday (Nov. 18), with Lara Spencer sharing the news from Honky Tonk Central in downtown Nashville. GMA also took a look inside Bridgestone Arena with Lainey Wilson, who is hosting the show for the third year in a row.

Langley won music video of the year as both artist and director. She shares the award with co-directors Caylee Robillard and Wales Toney. Langley also won in this category last year (again as both artist and co-director) for “You Look Like You Love Me,” her sexy duet with Riley Green.

In a recent development, HARDY, Church, Wallen and McGraw share the award for musical event of the year with producer Jay Joyce. McGraw’s previous wins in the category are for “It’s Your Love” (with Faith Hill); “Find Out Who Your Friends Are (with Tracy Lawrence and Kenny Chesney); “Feel Like a Rock Star” (with Chesney); and “Highway Don’t Care” (with Taylor Swift and Keith Urban).

McGraw’s fifth win in the category allows him to break out of a tie with Brad Paisley, Urban, Chesney and Vince Gill, who have won four times each.

The 60th Annual CMA Awards is a production of the Country Music Association. Robert Deaton serves as executive producer, Alan Carter is director, and Jon Macks is head writer. The awards show will take place in Bridgestone Arena in Nashville on Wednesday night.

Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond has left Google feeling shaken, not stirred.

Following the announcement that Pattinson would be our next 007, Google introduced a new Bond-themed Easter egg. If you search up Pattinson's name, the search results shake a little, and a small twist of lemon falls from the top of the screen to rest daintily on Pattinson's head.

Industry observers note that the Easter egg is a nod to James Bond's classic cocktail order: a vodka martini, shaken, not stirred. Google has essentially turned Pattinson into the cocktail he'll be ordering onscreen.

Pattinson's casting as Bond came after weeks of speculation and reported screen tests for potential Bond candidates, including Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O'Connor, and Nicholas Hoult.

Sources indicate that pattinson will star in the as-yet unnamed 26th Bond film, the first since Daniel Craig took his last bow in 2021's No Time To Die. Dune helmer Denis Villeneuve is set to direct. The pair have also worked together on the upcoming Dune: Part Three. Villeneuve and Pattinson's Bond film does not yet have a release date.

Bond won't be the first franchise Pattinson has led to be commemorated with a Google Easter egg. In 2022, tied to The Batman's release, if you searched terms such as "Bruce Wayne" or "Gotham City," a yellow Bat-Signal would appear alongside the results. Clicking on it turned the page into a moody Gotham night, complete with thunder, the Bat-Signal, and Batman swinging around the screen.

Plus, if you search up "Twilight" now, you'll be treated to a small line of scrolling text that reads "hoa hoa hoa season," flanked by falling leaf emojis. The Easter egg references Twilight fans' loving nickname for fall, drawn from the so-called "hoa hoa hoa" vocals of Blue Foundation's "Eyes on Fire" from the Twilight soundtrack. Those devices aim squarely at Meta’s smart-glasses empire. But the Aura glasses are more like virtual reality headsets, now in a more comfortable, glasses-like design. They go head-to-head with Meta’s VR Glasses, slated for release in early 2027.

The first significant caveat about the Aura glasses is that they’re wired. A long cord hooks onto the end of one of the glasses’ arms via a USB-C cable. That cord connects to an attached compute puck, about the size of a smartphone and weighing a little more than a half-pound. It comes in 12 or 16 GB storage options and has a battery that powers the glasses for roughly four to five hours with constant use.

It has been revealed that when the Aura glasses work, they’re wonderful. The glasses are pretty lightweight, at 95 grams. A four-mic array sits in the arms with Bose EQ tuning that sounds great. (You can also connect wireless headphones.) The display screen has a 1920 x 1200-pixel-per-eye resolution that is noticeably better than other Xreal glasses I’ve worn. A 70-degree field of view means the screens and virtual elements pop up in a wide frame of the wearer’s vision. That means the outer edges of your view will still be the real-life room around you. That can help if you’re trying not to fall over, but it can also be noticeable when trying to feel immersed in a movie.

The substantial thing about Aura is that you can, in theory, run every app that already exists on Android. Xreal has a few primary categories for how it expects people to use its Aura glasses. The big one is entertainment. Like other Xreal glasses, the Aura can project a screen right in your field of vision. You can watch movies, TV shows, or YouTube videos, right in your field of view. The virtual screen stays fixed, or it can follow you around as you turn your head. You can also unplug the glasses from the compute puck and use them as display glasses to extend your Steam Deck’s screen, for example, though I had problems with that when playing more graphics-intensive games like Cyberpunk 2077.

The Aura glasses attach to a compute puck for processing, which also doubles as a battery.

Industry observers note that the other significant use case is productivity. The Aura glasses can host virtual workstations that let you swap between tabs and keep multiple tasks running. So you can have a Google Doc right in front of you, Spotify to the side, and those Slack messages you keep ignoring in the back. If you’ve ever wished you had even more space to stash all your browser tabs, this is the device for you. Pair it with a Bluetooth keyboard, and you’ll have a whole workstation on your face, even on a plane, without having to crane your neck awkwardly at a laptop. I wrote almost half this review with the glasses as my screen, but eventually swapped back to a regular desktop to give my eyes a rest.

There are also augmented reality experiences, like using Google Earth to turn a room into a 3D model of a city that you can stomp around in like Godzilla, plus immersive virtual tours so you can see exotic places like the Galapagos.

Two lenses are set in the frame, one smaller lens behind the other. The smaller lens carries the display and AR elements, popping them up within a 70-degree field of view. The outer lens can go from perfectly see-through to very dark. Turning up the darkness makes it easier to see the projected virtual screens. Turning the darkness down enables a much clearer pass-through, which can help you avoid tripping over things while walking around.

Sources indicate that that remarked, these glasses aren’t really meant to be worn while walking around. Even with no AR elements enabled, the double-lens layout feels distracting. There is also no way around the fact that these glasses are still pretty chunky. If you can rock the thicc fit, then great, but I’ve gotten some pointed stares when I walk around with them.

The compute puck can be used as a trackpad to navigate the interface, and it also has a fingerprint sensor.

Industry observers note that the glasses do feel lightweight, but after a few minutes of use, they start to heat up. When I take them off, they leave red divots on the bridge of my nose. It’s a small price to pay, though, and it doesn’t ruin the experience. Compare that to something like a VR headset, which does offer better immersion but at the cost of being heavy and uncomfortable to wear for long stretches.

The compute puck can be an annoyance. It’s light enough, but using the Aura glasses means you have to carry yet another thing that is strapped to the device on your face. There were some smart choices made on the puck, like a fingerprint sensor for biometric authentication, and the puck’s surface works like a trackpad to move the onscreen cursor. That seems much smoother than reaching out to control the device with hand movements, but the trackpad wasn't very precise either. Which is a shame, as it would be ideal for someone on an airplane, say, who wants to control the device without punching the seat in front of them.

In a recent development, controls are the biggest problem I’ve had with the Aura. The front cameras track your hand movements. Hold out your hand and pinch two fingers together to open up an app or move a window. It works most of the time, but some gestures don’t always register. I find myself trying to open Spotify or switch between titles on Prime Video and have to repeatedly pinch the air in front of me for anything to happen. When people have been around to see me, they’ve told me I look like I’ve gone bonkers, just grunting and wildly pinching thin air.

The Xreal Aura glasses are a stunning display of how far smart-glasses technology has come. But they still feel like a novelty that most people won’t want or need. They haven’t quite solved the core complications facing the product category—looking like a dork or being effortlessly comfortable to wear. But they do feel like a substantial step in the right direction. If only they could get a pinch more usable.

A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly crucial role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections.
  • Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods.
  • Now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly crucial role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that when the body runs low on arginine, a key part of its immune defense system can stop working properly, potentially allowing dangerous cells and viruses to escape detection.

Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods. It is essential for making proteins that perform countless functions throughout the body. Researchers have long known that unusually low arginine levels are associated with several diseases, including colon cancer, but exactly how this shortage affects the body's defenses has remained unclear.

Now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats. In experiments involving mice, increasing dietary arginine reduced the formation of colon cancer tumors and lessened the severity of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infections. Remarkably, providing arginine after mice had already contracted influenza also improved their outcomes.

The findings, published in the journal Cell, raise the possibility that an inexpensive, readily available supplement could eventually become a useful addition to cancer treatments and strategies for combating viral infections. However, further research in humans is needed to determine whether the benefits observed in mice translate into effective treatments for people.

How a Missing Nutrient Could Help Cancer Escape the Immune System.

The research was led by Sohail Tavazoie, who directs the Elizabeth and Vincent Meyer Laboratory of Systems Cancer Biology at Rockefeller University. His team has spent years investigating how arginine influences cancer development and progression.

Recent findings suggest that in 2023, the researchers discovered that depriving colon cancer cells of arginine caused them to accumulate more genetic mutations. These changes can contribute to the unpredictable behavior of cancer cells, raising important questions about how arginine shortages might influence the disease.

The latest study reveals another potentially significant consequence. When arginine becomes scarce, cells struggle to produce enough of a crucial immune system protein known as MHC-1. This protein acts as a warning system, helping immune cells identify potential dangers such as cancerous changes or viral infections.

Without enough MHC-1, abnormal or infected cells may become harder for the immune system to recognize.

Encouragingly, the researchers also found that supplying a moderate amount of arginine, comparable to the quantity available in a couple of over-the-counter supplement tablets, could help restore production of this vital protein.

"Our work reveals how a lack of arginine interferes with the immune system, and suggests that upping arginine intake could prove beneficial," says first author Qiushuang Wu, a postdoc in the lab. "Perhaps that means it could be used in combination with other therapies to treat both cancer and viral infections.".

In a recent development, "Arginine supplementation could be readily tested in patients receiving immunotherapies or given to high-risk populations exposed to viral pathogens," Tavazoie suggests. "Considering that arginine is inexpensive and readily available, we hope that therapeutic and preventative studies could be undertaken soon.".

The Surprising Connection Between Arginine and Immune Defenses.

To understand why arginine has such an important effect, the researchers investigated how cells use amino acids to manufacture proteins.

Proteins are built from amino acids according to genetic instructions encoded in DNA. These instructions are copied into messenger RNA, which carries the information to the cellular machinery responsible for protein production.

Industry observers note that the instructions are read in groups of three genetic letters called codons. Each codon specifies an amino acid or provides another signal needed during protein production. Arginine is unusual in that six different codons can specify it, reflecting the multiple ways its incorporation into proteins can be encoded.

In a recent development, scientists already knew that changes in amino acid availability could affect cellular metabolism and signaling, two processes that help regulate how cells obtain energy and respond to their surroundings. What remained less clear was whether shortages of particular amino acids could directly influence which proteins cells produce.

To investigate, Wu examined the effects of arginine availability across several disease models, including colon cancer, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2. Each of these diseases has previously been associated with abnormal levels of various amino acids.

The research was supported in part by the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Institute for Global Infectious Disease Research at The Rockefeller University and the Weill Cancer East Hub.

"One of the most dramatic patterns to emerge was that arginine was the most depleted amino acid in all of these diseases," she notes.

Why Low Arginine Levels Can Disrupt the Immune System.

In laboratory experiments using cultured cells, Wu examined how arginine shortages affected protein production. She identified 414 proteins whose levels dropped abnormally when arginine was scarce.

Recent findings suggest that many of these proteins were associated with biological functions already known to depend on arginine. However, the researchers uncovered a more unexpected effect involving three genes from the HLA family.

These genes provide instructions for producing proteins associated with MHC-I (major histocompatibility complex class I), an essential component of the immune system's ability to recognize threats.

Sources indicate that MHC-I proteins are displayed on the surfaces of cells throughout the body. They act somewhat like identification displays, presenting small fragments of proteins from inside the cell to immune cells known as T cells.

When these displays reveal suspicious material, such as proteins produced by a virus or abnormal proteins associated with cancer, T cells can recognize the danger and help coordinate an immune response.

But the researchers found that arginine deficiency interfered with the production of these molecular warning signals.

Sources indicate that the reason involved ribosomes, the tiny cellular machines that assemble proteins by following genetic instructions. Because the proteins involved in MHC-I production require arginine at numerous points, the researchers suspected that an insufficient supply could interfere with their assembly.

Further experiments confirmed that suspicion. When arginine was unavailable, ribosomes stalled while trying to manufacture MHC-I proteins. Without enough of the required amino acid, the cells could not efficiently complete the process.

As a result, fewer MHC-I proteins reached the cell surface, reducing the signals that would normally alert T cells to cancer-associated or viral proteins. This created an opportunity for dangerous cells to avoid immune detection.

Industry observers note that "These findings are exciting because they reveal that consumption of a specific amino acid can directly regulate gene expression in an organism by increasing production of a protein enriched in that amino acid," Tavazoie notes. "We believe that such selective translational tuning of gene expression through dietary manipulation likely extends to many other proteins and amino acids.".

More Arginine Meant Fewer Colon Cancer Tumors in Mice.

After identifying the molecular mechanism, Wu investigated whether changing the amount of arginine in an animal's diet could influence disease outcomes.

Recent findings suggest that mice receiving diets low in arginine developed more colon cancer tumors. In contrast, mice consuming higher amounts of the amino acid developed fewer tumors.

These findings provided evidence that arginine availability can influence cancer development through its effects on the immune system, rather than simply changing how individual cancer cells behave.

The results also raised a broader question: If arginine helps immune cells recognize cancer, could it provide similar benefits when the body encounters dangerous viruses?

Arginine Also Improved Outcomes From Influenza and COVID-19 Viruses.

To explore that possibility, Wu collaborated with Heinz-Heinrich Hoffman, a research assistant professor in Charles Rice's Laboratory of Virology and Infectious Disease.

Together, they examined the effects of dietary arginine in mouse models of influenza and SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19.

The findings followed the same general pattern seen in the colon cancer experiments. Mice consuming more arginine experienced less severe symptoms from viral infections, suggesting that adequate levels of the amino acid helped support the body's immune defenses.

The researchers then made an even more surprising discovery.

Recent findings suggest that arginine did not appear to be beneficial only when consumed before an infection. Giving mice additional arginine after they had already been infected with influenza also improved their outcomes.

"Not only did mice with an arginine-rich diet have milder symptoms from viral infections, giving the mice arginine after influenza infection improved their outcomes too," Wu notes. "That was very surprising. From our genetic models, we knew manipulating arginine levels had a strong effect on gene expression, but we didn't expect the dietary manipulation to be equally impactful.".

The observation suggests that changing nutrient availability might influence how the immune system responds even after a viral infection has taken hold.

Could a Simple Supplement Improve Cancer and Virus Treatments?

The discovery has potentially crucial implications for understanding why some people become more vulnerable to cancer and severe viral infections.

Arginine levels naturally decline with age, and inadequate nutrition can further reduce the amount available to cells. The researchers suspect that these changes may contribute to the weakening of immune defenses seen in certain diseases and in older adults.

"Qiushuang's findings illuminate how poor diet and aging -- during which arginine levels naturally decline -- could create the perfect storm for the initiation of colon cancer. Similarly, age-related arginine loss could partially contribute to the greater mortality caused by respiratory viruses," Tavazoie states. "We're also investigating whether making dietary changes in other amino acids has beneficial effects in a variety of disease contexts. There are no doubt more discoveries to come.".

It has been revealed that the possibility of using arginine alongside existing cancer immunotherapies is particularly intriguing. These treatments work by helping the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. If low arginine levels interfere with the molecular signals required for that recognition, restoring the nutrient might help some treatments work more effectively.

The researchers also see potential for investigating arginine supplementation in people at elevated risk of respiratory viral infections.

It has been revealed that for now, these possibilities remain experimental. The findings do not establish that taking arginine supplements prevents or treats cancer, influenza, or COVID-19 in humans.

It has been revealed that nevertheless, the research reveals an important connection between nutrition and immunity. Rather than simply providing the raw materials needed to build proteins, specific amino acids may help determine how effectively the body's immune defenses identify and respond to dangerous threats.

And because arginine is inexpensive and widely available, the discovery could provide a practical starting point for future studies aimed at strengthening the immune system against cancer and infectious diseases.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • At the peak of the shower, observers at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona estimated an astonishing 40 meteors per second streaking across the sky.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that overnight Nov. 17-18, 1966, the Leonid meteor storm thrilled stargazers during one extraordinary night when the stars themselves looked as though they were falling from the sky.

At the peak of the shower, observers at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona estimated an astonishing 40 meteors per second streaking across the sky. That's 2,400 shooting stars per minute, or a staggering 144,000 per hour. It was a spectacle that many regard as the greatest meteor display in recorded history.

Recent findings suggest that it's hard to imagine what it was like to experience such a spectacle. But who better to tell us than those who saw it with their own eyes? To mark the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, we asked those who saw it to share their memories.

"I was around 9 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid storm, living a few miles east of Roxie, Mississippi. We lived in a rural, dark, relatively remote area with almost zero outside lights.

"I and a couple cousins were spending the night at our Uncle and Aunt's house, staying up late, just fooling around outside like young kids do when living in the 'sticks'. As we walked down a road, I remember hearing an almost constant series of little whistling, zipping sounds. The sounds were similar to when you light a nylon rope on fire and as it burns, little flaming droplets drip down with a zippy sound.

"I looked up and the sky was filled with streaks of 'shooting stars' and I realized that was what made the sounds. I yelled at my cousins to look up and we could hardly believe what we saw. We all laid down on our backs and for a couple of hours just watched and listened to what seemed like 1000's of 'shooting stars' zipping and zinging overhead. I could even smell the sulphur-like odor from the burning little bits of space dust.

In a recent development, "I'm nearly 70 years old now but I'll never forget that experience. I always knew what I'd seen that night was special but not until much later in life, after the internet, did I realize just how lucky I was to have experienced that storm. That night was one of the most loved and memorable nights of my life and I'll treasure it forever.".

"I was an astronomy lab assistant at Southwestern College in Winfield, KS, in 1966, majoring in physics and math and the physics professor was sure that the Leonids would be an amazing shower worth the class time.

According to recent reports, "The sky was clear. He called me early the morning of the 17th and told me to get to the campus. I can't remember the exact time as students and faculty were pounding on doors to get people, including neighbors,to watch.

It has been revealed that "We were all lying in an open grassy area because that was the best way to see the whole sky. It was like a humongous fireworks display and lasted even as the sun began to rise.

"As years have gone by, I have felt grateful and privileged to have seen such a wonderful astronomical event.".

"I was 18 and spent the night in El Paso, Texas, lying on the ground in my backyard and watching. It looked like every star in the sky was falling. It was amazing!".

In a recent development, "I was 9 years old and was camping with my dad in the western mountains of California. We were set up to sleep outside, but on this particular night, we saw more meteors than I have ever seen before or since. We watched them all night and didn't get much sleep.".

"Brooklyn Center, Minnesota. 14 years old. Watched in our front yard. The sky was full. It took your breath away".

Industry observers note that "I was 3 years old at the time of the 1966 Leonid meteor shower. I remember very little at that age, but watching the sky fall that night was seared in my memory.

It has been revealed that "My family was living in Troy, Alabama, at the time. My father, a professor of psychology, was a man of science with a special love of astronomy, which he passed onto his young son.

According to recent reports, "He drove us several miles out of town until the skies were dark, without interference from the lights of the town. Troy was much smaller then and it was easy to find dark, clear skies.

Industry observers note that "I remember that it was a little chilly that night. My father and I stretched out on the hood of the car, the warmth of the engine radiating against our backs.

According to recent reports, "That night was my first meteor shower, and only many years later did I learn that year's Leonids were historic. Sadly, though I bore witness to the display, we missed the true event by several hours as I grew tired by 1:00 AM, and my father had to teach class in the morning.

"I remember many bright, colorful, and long-trailed meteors. Some left 'tails' that hung in the sky for several seconds. We only experienced the beginning of the event, but it is a core memory with my father.

"That night/morning spoiled me for future meteor watches; I assumed they would all be as interesting.".

Industry observers note that not everyone was lucky enough to witness the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966. For some, the night was memorable for an entirely different reason.

Space.com columnist Joe Rao was just 10 years old at the time, and despite eagerly anticipating the display, the weather had other ideas.

Industry observers note that "Standing in my backyard late on a Wednesday night in the Throggs Neck section of The Bronx, cursing the heavens. My grandfather stood at my side, just shaking his head and murmuring two words over and over: 'Too bad.'.

It has been revealed that "Clouds covered the midnight sky like a fresh coat of plaster, smearing my view of the Leonids. My mom, sister and grandmother, as well as my neighbors had long since trudged to bed, leaving only Grandpa and I to gaze at a charcoal gray sky totally devoid of stars.".

It has been revealed that rao had been looking forward to the storm ever since a visit to Latest York's Hayden Planetarium, where astronomer Fred C. Hess had encouraged visitors to look out for what could be a spectacular display.

But when Rao and his grandfather ventured outside, there wasn't a single star in sight.

"After a few minutes, I sobbed to my grandfather, 'But they promised it was only going to be partly cloudy tonight.' To which he sadly replied, 'I guess the party is over.'".

The Leonid meteor shower occurs every November when Earth passes through a stream of debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.

As tiny particles of comet dust enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of around 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up and produce brilliant streaks of light we know as meteors, or shooting stars.

Recent findings suggest that most years, the Leonids produce relatively modest displays with around 10 to 15 meteors per hour under ideal viewing conditions. But occasionally, Earth encounters a particularly dense trail of debris, triggering a meteor storm.

Sources indicate that the Leonids have a long history of putting on some spectacular displays, with significant storms recorded in 1833 and 1866. And 1966 wasn't the last time the Leonids put on an extraordinary show. In 1999, 2001 and 2002, the Leonids once again reached meteor-storm levels, producing thousands of meteors per hour at their peaks. The shows aren't over yet! With comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle due to return in 2031, astronomers are already looking ahead to what the following years could bring.

It has been revealed that A study released in August 2026 predicts potentially impressive Leonid displays in 2033 and 2034, with peak rates exceeding 1,000 meteors per hour. However, these forecasts remain uncertain, and a repeat of the extraordinary 1966 storm is far from guaranteed.

For now, we'll just have to wait and see.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

Lee Chang-dong on the Mysteries and Meaning of ‘Possible Love’

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that lee Chang-dong believes in a god of cinema. But like any deity worthy of worship, the celebrated South Korean auteur’s higher power can’t simply be summoned when you feel you need it most.

“All through production, director Lee would talk to me and our assistant director about this movie god,” notes Kim Ji-yong, the cinematographer on Lee’s acclaimed seventh feature and buzzy Oscar contender, Possible Love. “He said the god would only appear after we had tried everything — put all our ideas, all of our energy, into the film. Only then, the god might come down to show us something beautiful — something we never expected or imagined.” Related Stories Movies 'In Starland': How Ray Panthaki, in His Directing Debut, Cast Clarence Maclin in His First Lead Role and Made a Very Personal Film Built on Meritocracy Business Can Peter Rice Fix Netflix? New Content Boss Has a Daunting To-Do List.

According to recent reports, “He really believes this,” Kim adds. “He even told us stories about the handful of times in the past when the movie god appeared on his sets.”.

The most recent visitation came nearly a decade ago, during the tail end of production on Lee’s beguiling 2018 dramatic thriller, Burning.

In the film’s violent, enigmatic climax, the young protagonist, Jong-su (Yoo Ah-in), meets his wealthy rival, Ben (chillingly inhabited by Steven Yeun), on a remote road outside Seoul. Jong-su approaches as if to chat, then plunges a knife into Ben’s stomach. He shoves the body into Ben’s silver Porsche, strips off his bloodied clothes, throws them inside and sets the car on fire. Within the complicated framing of the story, it’s unclear whether this episode actually happened or was imagined.

Sources indicate that “That scene is shot as one long, continuous take during sunset, and they prepared for it very carefully,” Kim claims, recounting Lee’s story. “And if you remember, just as [Jong-su] is walking back to his truck naked, with the burning car behind him, snow starts falling heavily.”.

“This was the movie god, according to director Lee,” Kim adds. “They didn’t plan for it to snow in that moment; they couldn’t have. But it happened, and it’s so cinematic.”.

Within the Korean film industry, it’s no exaggeration to say that Lee himself is regarded as something of a deity, or at least a national treasure.

In a recent development, born in 1954 to an impoverished but educated family in the southern Korean city of Daegu, Lee began his working life as a high school teacher before establishing himself as a fiction writer. He won acclaim for stories delicately attuned to the agonies and ironies of Korea’s tumultuous postwar period, an era of brutal political repression and breakneck economic development. His characters tended to be sympathetic, disadvantaged outsiders — sensitive people placed in impossible predicaments by the wrenching forces of ideology and history.

Recent findings suggest that in the early 1990s, filmmaker friends recruited him to write screenplays, and in 1997 he made his directorial debut with Green Fish, a social critique disguised as a noirish crime movie. The film featured the first performance from Song Kang-ho, who would later become a national treasure in his own right through films like Park Chan-wook’s Joint Security Area and Bong Joon Ho’s Memories of Murder and Parasite.

Earlier this year, Squid Game creator Hwang Dong-hyuk told me that witnessing his favorite novelist — Lee — suddenly become a filmmaker was the moment that made him want to pursue a life in cinema himself.

“I idolized him, and his career pivot kind of gave me courage to go for it,” Hwang stated. “And then when I actually watched [Green Fish], it was stunning — like every film he has done since.”.

According to recent reports, five films followed before Possible Love, each an emotionally searing and intellectually electrifying portrait of people pushed to society’s margins. With Peppermint Candy (1999), Lee issued a devastating state-of-the-nation statement by telling a ruined man’s life in reverse. Moving backward through two decades of political repression, state violence and economic upheaval, the film gradually reveals how an innocent, hopeful young man became both an instrument and a casualty of his country’s corruption. In Oasis (2002), he portrayed an extraordinary romance between a damaged ex-convict and a woman with severe cerebral palsy, reveling in the desires and imaginative freedom that the world around them refuses to acknowledge. The film earned Lee the Venice Film Festival’s best directing prize.

He returned five years later with Secret Sunshine (2007), which follows a bereaved mother through a crisis so harrowing that even the promise of faith and forgiveness becomes a source of existential torment. Secret Sunshine‘s Jeon Do-yeon won the Cannes Film Festival’s best actress award for her powerful performance, a first for a Korean star.

Then came Poetry (2010), which continued Lee’s fusion of generous, humanist drama with challenging philosophical inquiry, following an elderly woman who takes up writing poetry as she confronts the onset of Alzheimer’s and her grandson’s involvement in a horrific crime — her search for beauty becoming inseparable from the obligation to face a truth she would rather not see. Lee won Cannes’ best screenplay prize for the film.

And Burning (2018), finally, transformed a short story by Haruki Murakami into a mesmerizing mystery of class resentment, thwarted desire and the existential angst of Korea’s contemporary youth. It became the first South Korean film shortlisted for the foreign-language Oscar — an embarrassingly late milestone, given how much indelible cinema the country had already produced. But the Academy quickly made up for lost time at the 2020 ceremony, when Parasite, directed by Lee’s friend Bong Joon Ho, won four Oscars, including best picture.

Industry observers note that lee’s legendary status at home also stems from the fact that his contribution to Korean cinema has gone well beyond his own filmmaking. In the 1990s, he became a leading campaigner for enforcement of the country’s screen quota, which required theaters to show domestic movies for a minimum number of days each year. By protecting local filmmakers’ access to audiences from Hollywood dominance, the policy created space for ambitious Korean cinema to flourish throughout the 2000s — a driving force behind the broader Korean cultural wave still unfolding today. From 2003 to 2004, Lee even served as South Korea’s minister of culture and tourism.

Over the summer, I flew to Seoul to meet the mercurial auteur Na Hong-jin at his office on the city’s east side. A favorite of both action fans and art-house aficionados, Na studied under Lee as a graduate student at the prestigious Korea National University of Arts and later became an international cult sensation with a string of singularly twisted genre movies: the serial killer thriller The Chaser (2008), brutal crime flick The Yellow Sea (2010) and the supernatural freakout The Wailing (2016).

Recent findings suggest that the occasion for our chat was the U.S. release of his divisive but wildly entertaining sci-fi action movie Hope. At the time, both his film and Lee’s Possible Love were viewed as leading contenders to represent South Korea in the international Oscar race. (Possible Love was ultimately selected and is now considered a frontrunner in the category.).

Sources indicate that in what I thought would be a light, throwaway question, I asked how it felt to be competing with his former teacher. Na, who has a rather intense, skeptical bearing even when he’s feeling friendly, now grew more serious, and perhaps more skeptical of his interlocutor.

“As a filmmaker, Lee Chang-dong is basically a god to me,” he said, raising his voice a little and staring at me implacably. “I don’t compete with god, do you?”.

Sources indicate that laughing at my startled reaction, he then softened his tone. “For those of us who came of age in the generations after him, Lee Chang-dong represents an older, in some ways better, era. His movies are difficult, but there’s a tolerance and understanding to his work that I find almost healing. I don’t know if this country still produces artists with that kind of depth.”.

Lee’s movie god never appeared on the set of Possible Love — but the production was not without its moments of magic.

The film, which is presently streaming on Netflix globally, reunites Lee with Sul Kyung-gu, the unforgettable male lead of Peppermint Candy and Oasis, and Jeon of Secret Sunshine. Together, thanks in no small part to their performances in Lee’s films, they are now regarded as screen royalty in Korea, having won seven Grand Bell Awards between them, their country’s equivalent to the Oscars.

Sul plays Ho-seok, an autoworker left unemployed and profoundly damaged after a strike at his factory was violently suppressed by the state; Jeon is his loving, resourceful wife, Mi-ok, who works in a mask factory to keep their family afloat.

Recent findings suggest that the drama begins to turn when their lives become unexpectedly entangled with those of an attractive couple from the opposite end of the class divide. Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong, playing another rich wife as she famously did in Parasite) is an aspiring documentary filmmaker working on a project about workers’ rights in Korea, who becomes drawn to Ho-seok’s story. Her husband, Sang-woo (Hope’s Zo In-sung), is a dashing tycoon who seems happy to support her pursuits. The budding friendship among the foursome is warm, awkward and increasingly fraught, with Ye-ji’s attempts at empathy growing difficult to disentangle from her eagerness to make art from the other couple’s struggles.

Recent findings suggest that the film culminates with a group trip to the coast. Hoping to convince Ho-seok to finally sit for a lengthy interview, Ye-ji invites the other couple to her husband’s luxurious seaside family home for a weekend away. (Production designer Jang Min-woo and his team built the house from scratch to Lee’s specifications.) Dinner on the first night becomes a messy drinking session. At dawn, Ho-seok staggers out toward the sea, and Mi-ok, curious about this exit, surreptitiously follows. The camera tracks them into a wind-tossed forest, where Ho-seok’s suppressed rage fully erupts into a PTSD-driven breakdown: Screaming, he thrashes his body against the trees and branches around him, as his wife secretly watches in silence.

As Mi-ok retreats in distress, she encounters Ye-ji in a clearing, attempting to film this painful private moment. The two women stare at each other from opposite edges of the frame as the wind howls and the trees sway behind them. This tableau, which captures so much of the story’s complex meta-fictional pathos, later became one of Possible Love‘s key marketing images.

Originally, in Lee’s script, the sequence was supposed to take place on a calm, clear morning, notes Kim, the cinematographer.

“But on the day of our tech scout to the coast, it was a really windy day, and director Lee and I both thought it looked great,” he recalls.

One of his country’s most in-demand DPs, Kim is perhaps best known internationally for the baroque, highly stylized camerawork he employed on Park Chan-wook’s romantic thriller, Decision to Leave (2022). He also shot the hit second and third seasons of Squid Game. For Possible Love, Kim set aside his impressionistic approach and strove instead for the most naturalistic look he could achieve, shooting nearly the entire film with a handheld camera he carried himself and relying on natural light as much as possible.

“Director Lee agreed it would add a nice layer if we could shoot it in a heavy wind,” Kim recalls. “And since we would be filming at the house for a month, I convinced him we could get all prepped, but then wait to see if we got lucky with a windy day or two.”.

He adds: “And in my head, I thought, ‘Okay, this is where we’ll meet the movie god, right?'”.

According to recent reports, “But then, that whole month: no wind. Not even a strong breeze.”.

Although Lee is famous for the seriousness and solemnity with which he approaches his work, he is also widely admired in the Korean production world for the collaborative atmosphere on his sets.

According to recent reports, many leading auteurs readily discuss matters of craft but resist interpreting their work, preferring to leave its meaning to the audience. Lee believes it’s vital that his collaborators understand the ideas and nuances each scene is intended to convey. His cinema may ask philosophical questions that are ultimately irresolvable, but he is resolutely clear and intentional about how his choices put those questions into play.

Industry observers note that “If someone asks him something about a scene, no matter who it is on the crew — maybe it’s like an assistant set dresser — he will stop and thoroughly explain the scene, his intentions, and how it fits into the whole movie,” Kim indicates. “I’ve worked on a lot of films, but I had never seen a director who is so patient and generous with his thoughts like that.”.

So, when the winds never arrived for Possible Love‘s poignant sunrise moment, Lee’s team resolved to “create a crew god” for him instead.

“More than 100 people — the assistants, some of the cast, and every member of the crew except for three or four of us huddled around the monitor with director Lee — went into the forest and tied ropes to the trees and pulled like crazy so that the whole forest would sway like in a strong wind,” Kim recalls.

He adds: “It wasn’t anyone’s job, but we all did it, because we knew how much that scene meant to him — because he had told every one of us.”.

Possible Love premiered at Venice in September, winning the festival’s Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize. It later screened at the Toronto and New York film festivals, earning rave reviews at every stop. It currently has the highest Rotten Tomatoes score — 97 percent fresh from 112 reviews — of any major global release this year.

Possible Love was fully financed and produced by Netflix, and if the project seems a somewhat out-of-character choice for both Lee and the streamer (as more than a few critics have noted), it is also true that the film is the most critically acclaimed adult drama that the tech giant has ever made — holding higher average review scores than any of the other entries on Netflix’s conspicuously short list of potential enduring classics (The Irishman, Marriage Story, The Power of the Dog, All Quiet on the Western Front and Frankenstein all rank slightly lower, for example, while other lasting favorites, such as Alfonso Cuarón’s Roma, were acquired but not produced by the streamer).

According to recent reports, it is also the best-supported awards contender of Lee’s long but still-too-overlooked career. Netflix is mounting a multi-front Oscar campaign extending beyond the international category to best picture, best director, best original screenplay and the acting categories, with a particularly ambitious push for Jeon.

Netflix had quietly been courting Lee since the manufacturer rolled out operations in South Korea a decade ago.

“One of the top three rumors that’s always floating around the Korean film industry is that Lee Chang-dong has finished a new script,” indicates Minyoung Kim, Netflix’s top content executive in the Asia-Pacific region, who built the streamer’s formidable Korean operations from the ground up.

In recent years, Lee’s output has grown sporadic, with eight-year breaks between each of his last three features.

Industry observers note that “The reason his films take so long is that he deeply, almost painfully, thinks about why a story needs to be told,” Kim explains. “Many directors are happy when they’ve found an entertaining idea that works, or a great piece of IP to adapt; with director Lee, it all starts with an observation about reality, or a question he can’t resolve about life.”.

She says she’s aware of numerous potential projects — all of which sounded, to her creative exec ear, like compelling, ready-to-go premises — that Lee shelved because their themes didn’t feel urgent enough.

“So, every time we heard those rumors about a new script over the years, we checked in — just to be like, ‘We’re here; we’d love to work with you!'”.

“You could even say we were a little clingy,” Kim adds, laughing.

It has been revealed that netflix’s opportunity to partner with Lee came after the auteur struggled to secure the relatively modest budget he was seeking for Possible Love — reportedly around 8 billion won, or roughly $6 million — after the key cast agreed to fee reductions to help him get the project made. South Korea’s prolonged post-pandemic box-office slump has left its major studios increasingly cautious about backing serious dramas, even with filmmakers and casts of this stature. Kim believes Lee would eventually have found a local financier, but the studios’ hesitancy gave Netflix its opening.

Netflix agreed to a larger, undisclosed budget and put its production resources behind the film. The commitment extended to a limited international theatrical release and substantial awards-season support, while leaving all creative decisions — including final cut — in Lee’s hands.

“On a lot of our shows, we try to understand the director’s vision, and become their thought partner. We debate and discuss, and try to make suggestions on what we believe will make the film stronger,” Netflix’s Kim explains. Describing Lee as a maestro, she notes, “he didn’t need our opinions.”.

She adds: “We just tried to understand his vision as fully as we could, so we could support him at every step of the way.”.

The Hollywood Reporter recently spoke with Lee in Seoul about the creation of Possible Love and the ideas behind several pivotal scenes. The conversation includes spoilers.

In a recent development, from what I understand, Possible Love began more than a decade ago as a project about the workers involved in Korea’s real-life SsangYong Motor strike, which resembles the episode depicted in the film. You wrote a script and went into pre-production, then shelved it. What concerned you about that earlier version?

In a recent development, it’s true that the project began for me with the 2009 SsangYong Motor incident, but when I speak about the origins of the story today, I try not to mention the company or the specific year, because I don’t want too much emphasis placed on that particular incident. There have been many similar cases in the Korean labor movement, and I’d like the film to be viewed in that broader context. But yes, about 10 years ago, that case is what got me started. I did a lot of research, wrote a screenplay and went into preproduction. And then I shelved it — for two reasons.

Recent findings suggest that first, I was constantly asking myself: What meaning does it have for me to turn this episode into a dramatic feature? What does it mean to me personally? What will it mean to the audience? And what meaning will it hold as a film in itself? I just couldn’t find answers I had real conviction in. There was already a documentary about the strike and the lives of the workers involved, and I felt it was a very honest and thorough piece of work. [Lee is referring to Seo Seh-chin’s 2009 documentary Before the Full Moon.] Ultimately, I didn’t see how I could add to what the documentary had already achieved simply by turning it into a dramatic feature.

Industry observers note that the second factor was connected to feelings and beliefs I have long held as a creator. I was writing fiction back in the 1970s and 1980s, often about Korean society and the issues within it. Naturally, I wrote about my times, and because of what our country was going through, that meant writing about people who were suffering — people living under our authoritarian military government, factory workers facing hardship, students participating in the democracy movement and those hurting because of our divided nation.

Sources indicate that and I always ended up asking myself, “Am I worthy of telling this story? Does it hold meaning for me to be the one saying this?” I asked these questions because my life and my situation were often very different from those of the people I was portraying. I wasn’t suffering as badly as they were. So what right did I have?

Industry observers note that as I worked on the early versions of Possible Love, all these questions came back to me, and I couldn’t find conviction in any approach. So I shelved it.

Then, as the years passed, the issue of labor itself began to go through big changes. At the time of the strike, the focus was on the direct pain the laid-off workers were suffering as we entered a more global, capital-driven system — the suffering of those betrayed and abandoned. Now, that pain is becoming universal. The issue today is that labor itself is on the verge of disappearing. There is no longer as clear a line between the working class and the nonworking class, because we are beginning to see the disappearance of labor itself, and all the definitions of self that come with it. These shifts got me interested again, but I was still finding it difficult to move forward.

It was only when my co-writer, Oh Jung-mi, suggested placing a documentary filmmaker within the story that I began to see a path with some legitimacy. Now it was also my story, as the creator and teller of other people’s stories. It allowed me to question my own position: What are my attitudes? What’s built into the gaze I direct toward these people? And what should my ethics be?

Industry observers note that that must have been such an exciting discovery — or simply a relief. With Ye-ji as your avatar, you seem able to express your best intentions as a storyteller while voicing your bitterly ironic self-doubts and unresolved questions about such storytelling. As a viewer, it feels like an ongoing, self-aware conversation with you.

You could also say that I gave myself an alibi. But this approach really did free me to tell their story without those earlier questions constantly tugging at my heart. It put me a little more at ease about telling the story of this laid-off worker and his family.

Strictly speaking, is Ye-ji my complete embodiment, my true avatar? Of course not. She and I are very different. But from a larger perspective, you could say that Ye-ji really does embody my best intentions and represents exactly who I am within the structure of this story. I felt this very keenly all over again at the world premiere in Venice. There I was in a very expensive rented tuxedo, walking a red carpet to present the story of a laid-off worker’s pain. I suppose some would say that is simply the nature of things, because filmmaking is married to capital.

Sources indicate that throughout the film, there are moments where characters seem to give direct voice to your self-conscious misgivings, as we’ve been discussing. Other questions are suggested by the plot, but aren’t stated quite so explicitly. One is related to the matter you just mentioned: Does art carry any real power to critique or change the capitalist system, or is the aesthetic itself just another part of the system’s healthy functioning? You certainly seem to be nudging us in the direction of the latter. Ye-ji, the film’s well-intentioned artist, after all, is married to and supported by a capitalist tycoon. The documentary she is making seems entirely genuine — but the fact remains that her real-life husband is executing a private equity deal to sell off the factory at the heart of her story the entire time. By extension, this feels not dissimilar to the fact that increasingly large swaths of the global movie business are owned by some of the very same tech giants and oligarchs that are driving the technological changes that will potentially bring about the elimination of labor you mentioned earlier.

It has been revealed that this question goes to the very essence of the film industry, and art-making in general — and who in this world could give a clear answer to that, right? That said, I have never felt free of this question since the very beginning of my work as a filmmaker. It’s always there.

Sources indicate that one answer, for me at least, is that I believe films must never turn a blind eye to the real world and the people living within it. By “turn a blind eye,” I mean that the lives you portray in your film should never be consumed simply as material or content for making your movie.

Of course, we’re talking about a very fine line. When you are dealing with people in pain — people suffering from the many paradoxes of life — you must ask yourself: Am I only consuming or exploiting their story, or am I really trying to start a conversation with the audience in a meaningful and creative way? That’s a very difficult question to answer with full conviction.

It has been revealed that as a rule of thumb, I believe that the simpler the objective of your story becomes, the further you have probably drifted from reality. I believe that a film exists to ask questions of the audience. If your audience leaves the theater having only experienced catharsis — entertainment or pleasure — then you have probably treated your subject as little more than an exercise in consumption.

Sources indicate that let’s talk about the film’s dual climaxes at the vacation home. How should we interpret Mi-ok’s actions on the beach? I read them as both an attempt to experience the freedom Sang-woo so effortlessly enjoys and a way to reclaim some power over him.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Ho-seok is finally sitting for Ye-ji’s camera. I felt this terrible apprehension — I didn’t want him to give her this, as though she might artistically prey on him in the way you just described. But later I realized he’s doing this for his own reasons: He needs to open up and begin healing for his wife and son. Later, back home, he can finally use the little marble drinking station he built, and he seems a touch healed. So, both moments ultimately felt heroic to me. Am I on the right track?

You’re right that Mi-ok’s actions on the beach are something she chooses for herself in the hope of reclaiming her freedom. But it would be wrong to say she’s only emulating what Sang-woo stated he felt as a child. Of course, his story gave her a hint, or planted the seed, but what she’s actually trying to do is a little different.

In a recent development, I believe what Mi-ok wanted in that moment was to face Sang-woo with nothing between them, not even the clothes on their bodies — simply one human facing another. She realizes that everything she and Ho-seok have endured — all the setbacks, all the pain, all the difficulties — has had everything to do with the distorting power of capital, and nothing to do with their own efforts and worth. And she realizes that this power is wielded by people like Sang-woo.

In a recent development, so she wanted to face the person at the heart of that force with nothing between them, and these are the actions she is able to improvise in that moment. In a way, she also wanted to test the happiness of this other couple a little — to throw a pebble at the glass castle of these people who enjoy all the benefits of such power. She wants to face him as just another naked human, but she also wants to provoke him a little.

As for Ho-seok’s sequence, he decides to sit for Ye-ji’s camera even though he is fully aware that his emotions are going to be used to fulfill her hidden desires. But he also knows he needs to somehow bring it all out of himself — all his deep-rooted rage and sadness. At this point, he knows it can only heal him a little. I also believe Mi-ok knew this from the beginning, and this is why she agreed to her family being part of the documentary in the first place. She wanted Ho-seok to take part in the interview so that he might be healed in some way.

Then, after all is said and done, when they’re sitting together at that marble platform at the very end, there’s a sense that they’ve learned something through all of this.

Sources indicate that that marble platform had been a symbol of Ho-seok’s despair and failure. It’s a place charged with his very Korean sentiments — his sense of responsibility for his family and for the co-workers he tried to treat as brothers. It’s symbolic of his typical Korean masculinity, all of which has been brutally betrayed and taken away from him.

It has been revealed that but now, at the end, he is able to sit in that place again — next to his wife, who has always been there for him — and they look up at the moon and share a peaceful moment together again. The moon, you know, transcends everything — class, capital, even time. Anybody can look up at the moon.

Sources indicate that that’s so beautiful. What does the title mean to you? We’re familiar with the notion of an impossible love — a great romance thwarted by circumstance. Here, you seem to give us a “possible” great love story while also showing what it really takes — the loyalty, strength, sacrifice, wisdom and generosity. Perhaps the film is also saying that even amid the loss of meaningful work and the identity that comes with it, dignity can be found in the work of loving one another? Or could the title refer to love between the artist and her subjects — like the budding friendship between Ye-ji and Mi-ok, which seems genuine despite their class differences? Or is it even broader: the love a more successful labor movement in today’s world would require?

Most simply, I wanted even the title of the film to be a question, and I thought Possible Love could do that. Most of the great love stories we remember are about whether the characters can overcome everything and finally end up together — whether their love comes to fruition. So Possible Love is a sort of paradox. I wanted the audience to ask all the questions you’re asking: What does a possible love mean, and what kind of love is really possible?

I was told by various people that the title was too difficult or confusing. But I think as you grow more familiar with it, it begins to feel just right.

You can say the film is about labor and class, and also the philosophy and ethics of filmmaking. But what it’s really about is human relationships. We live in a time when those relationships are deteriorating and we’re being separated. The nature of human connection is fundamentally changing. There is exploitation and disconnection, and sometimes we intentionally cut people out of our lives.

But I believe human relationships ultimately boil down to a question of love. The only path to healing those relationships is love. It doesn’t matter what kind of relationship it is — within a couple, between an artist and their subject or with the people you meet in everyday life. What is your fundamental attitude toward them? With the title, I wanted to ask: How do we answer the question of love? And what questions should we be asking ourselves about love?

It has been revealed that the second time I watched the film, I noticed more ways in which your fictional drama borrows the formal elements of a documentary. We get classic talking-head sequences by watching Ye-ji shoot her film, and your flashbacks start to feel like documentary reconstructions. I even began to reconsider the rainbow motif: Mi-ok tells that poetic anecdote about her mother’s angry reaction to her picking up a work hose as a child, and later we see her son playing with a servant, spraying water and making a rainbow. This feels like a connection a documentary director might discover in the editing room and use as a visual metaphor to tie together the film’s themes. Am I projecting, or were you deliberately closing the gap between your work and Ye-ji’s via the film’s formal construction?

Recent findings suggest that no, you’re correct. Near the start of the film, after we introduce Ye-ji as a documentary filmmaker, the cinematographer and I were very careful to make it clear whether you were looking through her camera or ours. But as the film goes on, we gradually blur that distinction. If you watch the film again, you might notice shots where you really can’t tell who is supposed to be behind the camera — me or Ye-ji.

In a recent development, but I didn’t only want to emulate a documentary’s structure. I wanted to be intimately connected with the content, too. Through my dramatic feature, I wanted to communicate the pain and suffering of these laid-off workers, which is exactly what Ye-ji wanted to capture. In that sense, I would say there is no demarcation between my intentions and hers.

The clearest example is the therapy session just before they go to the vacation home. We see interviews with four people who are either laid-off workers or their family members. They give their testimony, and it’s done in a very documentary style.

Now, that’s not something you would usually see in a dramatic feature. From a purely filmmaking perspective, the sequence is too long and feels quite out of place. If I had cut it, not only would the pacing have been better, but the story would have been more emotionally effective, because we could have brought the characters to the vacation home sooner, with more momentum. However, I thought the sequence was essential because, above all else, I needed my film to also be loyal to Ye-ji’s intentions. So I felt the documentary style had to be integrated into my film.

It has been revealed that it’s incredible how artfully you pulled all of that off. Changing gears a bit, Korea’s great auteurs seem to have converged lately on the same essential question: what capitalism is doing to society and individual dignity. In the global film-buff hive mind, you, Park Chan-wook and Bong Joon Ho pretty much represent the trifecta of Korean masters. Parasite, No Other Choice and Possible Love share many of the same themes and significant-picture concerns, expressed in your very different cinematic idioms. What do you make of this convergence? Is it simply a matter of the shared history and political tradition from which you emerged, even though you belong to slightly different generations?

This is a question I got quite often in Venice, usually posed in a way that suggested most filmmakers in other countries had moved past this. Why is Korea still making films about class conflict? I gave a pretty general answer that I think is probably true: Because Korea experienced such extreme economic development in such a short period, it touched every aspect of society, and it’s only natural that we continue to suffer from the aftereffects. And the filmmakers that you mentioned, we all experienced those extreme changes when we were sensitive young men. So, I suspect it’s as simple as that.

But while we deal with the same issues, I think what’s most different is our attitude toward cinema, or how we think of our films as we’re creating them. I’m probably quite different from both of them. I might be kind of an oddball compared to most filmmakers.

Many filmmakers love cinema for its own sake, and you can feel that love of moviemaking in their work — and it can be a wonderful thing. But I can only speak for myself. For me, making films is not the most vital thing. I don’t know if this will come across the way I intend, but the reality and the ideas I’m trying to portray are more important to me than the film itself. I think that attitude is apparent in my films. That is why, compared to other filmmakers, my films are not entertaining. They’re difficult.

It has been revealed that my last question isn’t my own. I recently interviewed Na Hong-jin in Seoul about Hope. He holds you in very high esteem, so when I mentioned I’d be speaking with you, I asked if he had a question for you. This was his question: Outside of your work as a novelist and filmmaker, what kind of human being do you think you are?

It has been revealed that I would say that I am a very timid person, and because of that, I tend to spend too much time thinking about how I should live — and it makes me very, very tired. (Laughs).

Lucid misses Wall Street’s earnings expectations, expands loan from Saudi Arabia fund

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (430 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNBC

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lucid Group missed Wall Street's third-quarter expectations as the embattled electric vehicle maker continues an "operational reset" aimed at cutting costs and narrowing losses.
  • The company on Monday also announced a $1.75 billion increase in a delayed draw term loan from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the company's largest shareholder.
  • Lucid stock fell roughly 5% in aftermarket trading Monday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lucid Group missed Wall Street's third-quarter expectations as the embattled electric vehicle maker continues an "operational reset" aimed at cutting costs and narrowing losses.

The company on Monday also announced a $1.75 billion increase in a delayed draw term loan from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, the company's largest shareholder.

Lucid stock fell roughly 5% in aftermarket trading Monday.

Here's how Lucid performed in the third quarter compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:.

According to recent reports, despite the top- and bottom-line misses, the manufacturer's adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of a loss of $726 million beat Wall Street's expectations of a loss of $611 million for the third quarter. Its net loss for the quarter was $830.9 million, down from a loss of $978.4 million a year earlier.

Lucid's 2025 third quarter included revenue of $336.6 million, a loss of $3.31 per share and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $717.7 million.

The quarterly results are the first since Lucid CEO Silvio Napoli, who started leading the company in June, unveiled a restructuring blueprint that included implementing several cost-cutting efforts and delaying the company's upcoming midsize vehicle from the end of this year until the second half of next.

Sources indicate that "Our transformation is beginning to show progress. We are acting with urgency, strengthening the fundamentals and driving greater discipline, while continuing to invest in the priorities to deliver profitable long-term growth," Napoli stated in a release.

The company's turnaround blueprint includes $1.4 billion in cash flow improvements this year as well as focusing attention on a robotaxi program with Uber and Nuro, a factory that's under construction in Saudi Arabia and the midsize vehicle.

Lucid stated the capital from PIF is expected to give the tech giant "additional financial flexibility as Lucid delivers on its turnaround program." It is expected to assist in funding "operations and key investments" into the fourth quarter of 2027, including the start of production for the midsize vehicle.

The additional funds boost Lucid's total liquidity to $3.75 billion, up from $2 billion to end the third quarter.

"We are grateful for the continued financial support from our anchor shareholder, which further energizes us to remain focused on execution and on our commitments as we build a stronger, sustainable Lucid," Napoli stated.

It has been revealed that lucid mentioned Monday that the company expects to communicate its midterm blueprint and targets early next year. The EV maker in May suspended its guidance and many targets, citing latest leadership and time needed to develop a turnaround plan.

Industry News: Should I buy a gaming console just to play GTA 6? That depends on your FOMO.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto VI is out extremely soon, if you hadn't heard.
  • By that, we mean do you have a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series console at the ready for Thursday's significant launch?
  • So, let's lay out the cases for and against doing that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI is out extremely soon, if you hadn't heard. Are you prepared?

By that, we mean do you have a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series console at the ready for Thursday's significant launch? If not, you're going to miss out on the biggest gaming launch of this year and many other years. FOMO is a natural human reaction to these sorts of things, and here at Mashable, we fully understand the pain of not being sure whether or not you should buy a console just for GTA 6.

So, let's lay out the cases for and against doing that.

In a recent development, the primary and most obvious reason to buy a console for GTA 6 is that it's the only real way to play it at launch on Nov. 19. There is technically another way that we'll cover in a little while, but for all intents and purposes, you cannot have the same experience everyone else is having without buying a PS5 or Xbox Series console.

Industry observers note that we don't know this yet for sure, but there's a possibility that GTA 6 is an incredible video game. You probably wouldn't want to miss out on that. What are you going to do while everyone else is having an amazing time parading through Leonida, read books? Come on, that sounds boring.

One thing that's also worth remembering is that other video games exist. A lot of them, in fact. If you buy a PS5 or Xbox Series console, you'll have access to the last six years of current-gen releases, some of which are extremely good. They might even be better than GTA 6! As a fun bonus, through the magic of backward compatibility, ports, remasters, and remakes, you'll also be able to play countless video games from previous generations of hardware, too.

Industry observers note that lastly, both consoles (at least the models with disc drives) work as 4K Blu-ray players, if you're into collecting physical versions of movies. That's cool, too.

Both consoles have been hard to find in stock (thanks in large part to GTA 6), but the Xbox Series S and PS5 Digital Edition are both in stock at Amazon, as of this writing.

First, foremost, in the biggest, boldest font you can imagine: You shouldn't buy a console just for GTA 6 because they're stupid expensive these days.

It has been revealed that both Xbox and PlayStation have recently increased the prices of their consoles due to real-world economic concerns. The cheapest model right now is a $499 Xbox Series S, and Rockstar hasn't shown us that version of the game yet, leading to speculation that the game is better on PS5, which starts at $599. If you want the best possible version at launch, you'll need a PS5 Pro, which costs $899 — and is presently out of stock at most retailers.

In other words, there just isn't a particularly affordable way to play GTA 6 traditionally at launch, unless you already own the hardware.

Recent findings suggest that there are, of course, other reasons to not get a console for GTA 6. There exists a slim likelihood that the game just isn't that good, though again, we have no idea at the time of publication. It also won't have an online component at launch, and no one knows when it will get one. For a lot of people, GTA Online is the only GTA experience that matters, and that audience will have very little to do in the new game until some nebulous point in the future when Rockstar decides to cater to them.

Maybe you just don't care that much about non-GTA video games, either. If that's the case, it's hard to recommend spending this much money on a box that will only play one game.

There are two main ways to play GTA 6 without buying a PS5 or Xbox Series machine. One of them doesn't sound all that great, while the other one will require some patience.

Sources indicate that to be clear, there are multiple massive reasons why you might not want to do this. For starters, it involves a monthly subscription. Beyond that, Microsoft recently imposed strict monthly hour limits on Cloud Gaming. With this system, you will be able to play at most 15 hours of GTA 6 per month. Many people are going to play more than that in the first weekend it's out. Even if those aren't concerns, game streaming is subject to the limits of your home internet, meaning that latency and buffering can and will occur. That version of the game will also be visually downgraded to some degree, per Rockstar.

If game streaming (understandably) doesn't work for you, the last option is to wait for the PC version. Unfortunately, Rockstar has not said anything about when GTA 6 will launch on PC, though a recent report pegged it as coming in early 2027. That will likely be the best version of the game in terms of visuals, but only if you have the requisite hardware. For those who already have capable gaming PCs, this might be the best option for playing GTA 6, provided you're patient enough to wait. For those who don't, this is going to be even more expensive than buying a console, so maybe don't bother.
