📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"I had actually decided to leave Iran back in 2023," a physician in her mid-30s, who wished to remain anonymous, told DW.

Her decision followed the 2022 death in police custody of 22-year-old Iranian-Kurdish woman Jina Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested by Iran's so-called morality police for allegedly violating the country's strict dress code.

Amini's death sparked widespread protests and inspired the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement, which challenged authorities' enforcement of Iran's hijab mandate.

It has been revealed that the physician said that the US-Israel war with Iran ultimately accelerated her looks to leave her homeland. She has been living with her family in a rented apartment in Turkey since early summer. From there, they hope to continue on to Germany.

According to recent reports, "It took two years for my professional qualifications to be recognized in Germany. After that, I applied for an appointment at the German Embassy in Tehran," the physician said.

In a recent development, "Then the 12-day war broke out in the summer of 2025. The embassy closed and suddenly we were all left in limbo, not knowing what would happen next.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

She became concerned after the US and Israel debuted fresh airstrikes on Iran on February 28, 2026 — not just about the escalating conflict, but also about the prospect of internal unrest and political instability.

According to recent reports, "Like many others we encountered during the emigration process, we decided to first move to a neighboring country," she said. "The plan was to stay in a third country for six months and then apply for a visa through the German embassy there. That's why my family and I came to Turkey.".

Turkey is one of the few countries that allows Iranian citizens to enter without a visa for up to 90 days.

Since the latest conflict began, thousands of Iranians have crossed the border into Turkey. Many are trying to secure their stay through residence permits rather than seeking asylum.

Industry observers note that according to official Turkish statistics, nearly 100,000 Iranian citizens were residing there in 2025. Among them are many academics and skilled professionals hoping to settle permanently in Europe or North America, seeing little future for themselves in Iran's war-hit economy.

Recent findings suggest that A US naval blockade of Iranian ports ⁠in ⁠the Gulf over the past few months has disrupted oil exports, trade and government revenues. The turmoil has compounded the impact of decades of sanctions and economic mismanagement.

The situation has put most businesses under pressure by restricting access to foreign currency and raw materials, among other problems, threatening revenues and jobs.

The worsening conditions have left many people struggling to afford food, housing, health care and education.

Industry observers note that the physician mentioned the situation at the German embassy in Tehran, however, has improved in recent months. Some of her unmarried friends, who also initially moved to Turkey and spent substantial sums maintaining their stay there, have already returned to Iran to submit fresh visa applications from home.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

She and her husband, however, have decided to stick to their original initiative and wait out the six-month residency period in Turkey despite the difficulties.

"I can't and don't want to go to Germany without my family. I don't know how long it would take for them to receive family reunification visas," she explained. "And I don't know what might happen in the meantime. A latest war could break out at any moment.".

It has been revealed that the departure of highly qualified professionals and students has become one of the most pressing challenges facing Iranian society. Today, there are few families in which someone has not already emigrated or is not at least considering doing so.

A 2025 study by the University of Guilan in Iran examined the relationship between opportunities for social participation and students' willingness to emigrate.

The researchers found a statistically significant correlation: Students who felt they had fewer opportunities to shape their future in Iran were more likely to consider emigrating.

Sources indicate that economic concerns are only part of the picture. Limited political participation, social restrictions and a sense of powerlessness are also driving many young Iranians to leave.

Mahsa, who is in her mid-20s, told DW that she has already secured admission to a German university.

Ali, meanwhile, dreams of a life outside Iran. The 23-year-old holds a bachelor's degree in engineering and is currently preparing for the entrance exam for a master's program at a public university. His long-term goal is to obtain a stronger qualification and then leave Iran — ideally with a scholarship.

"That's my dream of a better future," he said.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that these days, I spend a lot of my time looking through published papers that I suspect are fraudulent.
  • In a recent development, I retired in 2022 from the University of Oxford, UK, where I worked as a developmental neuropsychologist.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that reworded scientific phrases can thwart publishers’ plagiarism checkers, but, in many cases, the resulting combinations of words only draw more attention from scientific sleuths. Credit: Gregory Dubus/iStock via Getty.

Recent findings suggest that these days, I spend a lot of my time looking through published papers that I suspect are fraudulent. It is a gruelling task. But amid the tedium, there is some light relief, thanks to some hilarious phrases used by authors seeking to avoid detection by plagiarism checkers. It’s hard not to smile when ‘breast cancer’ becomes ‘bosom peril’, or a citation for ‘Baker and Logue’ become ‘Pastry Specialist and Logue’.

In a recent development, I retired in 2022 from the University of Oxford, UK, where I worked as a developmental neuropsychologist. I now track down research fraud as part of a community of scientific sleuths. We work together to identify papers that we consider to be problematic in some way, then send the evidence to publishers or post it on PubPeer, a post-publication peer-review platform. Our aim is for the problematic papers to be investigated and, if appropriate, retracted by their publishers. But, often, publishers are slower and more recalcitrant than many sleuths would like them to be.

‘A waste of time for all of us’: caught in the crossfire of the peer-review wars.

‘A waste of time for all of us’: caught in the crossfire of the peer-review wars.

Many people blame academia’s ‘publish or perish’ research culture for the rise in problematic papers. Without a large number of publications and citations, prospects for employment, promotion and glittering prizes evaporate. Some researchers cut corners, manipulate or fabricate data, or copy the work of other scientists without citing them.

Sources indicate that the demand for desperate researchers to get their name on a publication in any journal has spawned semi-professional organizations known as paper mills. These sell authorship status, with prices that vary depending on the impact factor of the journal. Articles are typically generated using artificial-intelligence tools or plagiarized, and tend to find homes in journals that lack sufficient editorial scrutiny.

According to recent reports, one of the few amusing consequences of these developments is the phenomenon of tortured phrases, first described in 2021 by computer scientists Guillaume Cabanac and Cyril Labbé and software engineer Alexander Magazinov1. They analysed huge volumes of research literature to identify patterns. Tortured phrases arise when someone — or, in most cases, a computer — replaces words in a published article with synonyms to evade plagiarism detectors and ultimately publish the result as their own work.

Authorship for sale: Nature investigates how paper mills work.

Authorship for sale: Nature investigates how paper mills work.

Sources indicate that cabanac and colleagues developed a free website called the Problematic Paper Screener, which documents tortured phrases and other red flags in publications. Detection of tortured phrases has been a communal effort by research sleuths, who document specific articles with tortured phrases on PubPeer.

#24222. A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1469 w)

A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1469 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that an existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for new treatments for chronic neck and back pain.
  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine.
  • In a recent development, although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer new ways to slow spinal degeneration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that an existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for new treatments for chronic neck and back pain. In experiments involving zebrafish, researchers found that the medication prevented abnormal mineral deposits from forming in the spine, a process that can cause spinal tissues to harden and vertebrae to fuse together.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine. Researchers also identified changes in gene activity and metabolism that appear to contribute to this damage, revealing several possible targets for future treatments.

In a recent development, although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer new ways to slow spinal degeneration. The research also demonstrates how zebrafish could help scientists investigate the causes of spinal disease and test potential therapies.

Most people experience back pain at some point in their lives, and one common cause is the deterioration of the spine's natural shock absorbers. These structures, called intervertebral discs, sit between the vertebrae and help the spine absorb pressure, distribute weight, and move comfortably.

Over time, the discs can lose their ability to cushion the spine, a condition known as intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). As the discs deteriorate, they can contribute to pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility.

According to recent reports, despite the widespread impact and substantial economic burden of this condition, no medications are right now available that can stop or reverse the degenerative process. Surgery remains the only established long-term intervention for certain severe cases, creating an urgent need for treatments that address the underlying damage.

Researchers have long known that genetics influences the risk of developing spinal disc degeneration. One gene of particular interest is associated with collagen IX, a protein that helps maintain the structural integrity of spinal discs by supporting the network of fibers that holds them together. Variations affecting this gene have repeatedly been associated with disc problems that develop earlier in life.

In a recent development, to investigate how these genetic changes contribute to spinal damage, scientists at the Universities of Edinburgh and Bristol turned to zebrafish. They studied fish that had been bred without a functioning copy of the gene, allowing them to observe how its absence affected the spine as the animals grew older.

A Hidden Process Causes the Spine To Harden.

The results revealed striking similarities between the genetically altered zebrafish and people with degenerative spinal disease.

As the fish aged, abnormal mineral deposits accumulated in the tissues separating their vertebrae. This process, known as mineralization, involves minerals collecting in tissues where they do not normally belong. In the spine, the buildup can cause normally flexible structures to become unusually rigid, much like unwanted bone forming in the wrong location.

Sources indicate that the researchers also observed spinal fusion, in which neighboring vertebrae become joined together. Such changes can interfere with the spine's normal flexibility and movement.

Importantly, the scientists discovered that the damage began well before the mineral deposits appeared. An underlying layer that provides structural support during spinal development started to break down first, suggesting that deterioration of this protective framework may set the stage for later hardening.

This finding could help explain how genetic changes initiate a chain reaction that eventually damages the spine.

Surprising Links to Fat Metabolism and Vitamin A.

To understand what was happening at the molecular level, the team examined patterns of gene activity in the zebrafish. This allowed them to identify biological processes that had become unusually active or disrupted as spinal degeneration developed.

Several unexpected connections emerged.

It has been revealed that the researchers found alterations in fat metabolism, the processes through which the body breaks down, stores, and uses fats. They also detected disturbances in a cellular signaling system called mTOR, which helps regulate cell growth, metabolism, and responses to nutrients.

Additional changes involved phosphate regulation and vitamin A signaling. Phosphate is an essential mineral involved in building bones and teeth, but its accumulation in the wrong tissues can contribute to abnormal hardening. Vitamin A signaling helps control how cells develop and function.

Recent findings suggest that together, these findings suggest that spinal disc degeneration involves more than the gradual wearing down of tissues. Changes in how cells process nutrients, regulate growth, and handle minerals may also play key roles.

An Osteoporosis Drug Blocks Spinal Mineral Buildup.

One of the most promising discoveries came when researchers tested ways to reduce the spinal abnormalities.

Sources indicate that A medication belonging to a class of drugs called bisphosphonates successfully blocked the abnormal mineral buildup in the zebrafish. Bisphosphonates are already used to treat osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures. These medications help protect bones by slowing the processes that break down bone tissue.

The finding is especially intriguing because it suggests that a treatment already used in patients might also help researchers develop therapies for spinal degeneration.

It has been revealed that the team identified other approaches that reduced spinal damage. Limiting how much food the zebrafish consumed led to fewer spinal fusions, as did medications that suppressed fat metabolism.

These results point toward fat metabolism and phosphate regulation as potentially key targets for future drugs.

It has been revealed that however, the experiments were conducted in zebrafish, not humans. More research will be needed to determine whether the same biological mechanisms operate in people and whether targeting them can safely prevent or slow spinal disc degeneration. The dietary findings also do not establish that restricting food intake can prevent spinal damage in humans.

Upcoming Hope for Chronic Back Pain Treatments.

The study was published in the journal Communications Biology and received support from Arthritis UK and BBSRC.

According to recent reports, dr. Erika Kague, who led the research at the University of Edinburgh's Institute of Genetics and Cancer, emphasized the potential significance of identifying treatments that target the underlying causes of spinal damage.

"For decades, surgery has been the only real answer for disc disease. By understanding the biology that drives the spine to harden, our zebrafish studies point to several ways of slowing it down, including a drug already used safely in patients. There's more work to do, but for a condition that's affected people for generations without a treatment in sight, this is super exciting.".

The findings could be particularly important for the millions of people who live with persistent back pain and have limited options for preventing their condition from worsening.

Dr. Caroline Aylott, Head of Research Delivery at Arthritis UK, highlighted the potential benefits for patients.

"For the 9.5 million people across the UK living with back pain this research brings fresh hope that potential newly introduced therapeutic approaches are on the horizon.

"We are proud to fund research that is unlocking the science behind the processes leading to spinal disc degeneration. Back pain is one of the UK's most common conditions that has blighted millions over generations. Dr. Erika Kague and her team at the University of Edinburgh have uncovered key genetic evidence that could pave the way for fresh treatments, bringing us one step closer to a future where fewer people have to live with the daily pain and challenges that back pain can bring.".

The research also illustrates the broader value of studying basic biological processes to understand diseases that affect large numbers of people.

Dr. Jef Grainger, Executive Director for Bioscience Advancing Knowledge at BBSRC, mentioned:.

"This research reveals how publicly funded discovery bioscience can generate the knowledge needed to address major health challenges. By revealing new knowledge of how healthy biological processes break down in aging-related spinal disc degeneration, the study opens up promising avenues for future treatment development. It's a great example of how BBSRC-supported research helps turn scientific discovery into knowledge and innovations that have the potential to improve people's lives.".

By identifying genetic and metabolic changes that contribute to spinal hardening, and demonstrating that some of the damage can be prevented in zebrafish, the researchers have opened several newly introduced avenues for investigating spinal disc degeneration.

For a condition that affects millions and has no approved drug capable of stopping its progression, these early findings offer an encouraging starting point for developing treatments that could one day protect the spine before serious damage occurs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that ray Panthaki (Boiling Point, Colette, Gangs of London) makes us think about modern culture in his feature directorial debut, In Starland.
  • Maclin is Ernie, 50, who lives a quiet and unremarkable life – until he becomes involved with online content creators in their 20s.
  • Panthaki wrote the script with Jason Kavan and also produced the film with Daniel Khalili, Daisy Allsop and Victor Paul Wajnberg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that ray Panthaki (Boiling Point, Colette, Gangs of London) makes us think about modern culture in his feature directorial debut, In Starland. Clarence Maclin (Sing Sing) stars in his, unbelievably, first lead role. The cast also features Bella Maclean (Rivals) and Miss Benny (Club Kid), among others.

Maclin is Ernie, 50, who lives a quiet and unremarkable life – until he becomes involved with online content creators in their 20s. “Finding a place where he finally belongs, Ernie discovers a world of hedonistic pleasure and voyeurism in which every movement he makes begins to blur the boundaries between performance and reality,” reads a synopsis on the website of the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia, where the film celebrates its world premiere on Thursday, Nov. 19. “As he searches for an identity lost in a mysterious past, fractures begin to appear between his newfound friends and the town of which he has been a part of for so long, and Ernie begins to wonder about the cost of his newfound notoriety.” Related Stories Movies European Lifetime Achievement Award for the Dardenne Brothers Music Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Sam Fender Set to Headline Glastonbury 2027.

Panthaki wrote the script with Jason Kavan and also produced the film with Daniel Khalili, Daisy Allsop and Victor Paul Wajnberg. Jaime Ackroyd is the cinematographer, with editing by Iain Kitching. Le Bateau Lavoir, Archface Films and Christine Vachon‘s Killer Films produced In Starland.

“I haven’t slept properly in years,” Panthaki shares. “But I made a film that I wanted to make with 100 percent creative control. I didn’t want to sell myself out to do the very thing I’m talking about in the movie – about numbers dictating life.”.

When he wrote and directed the short film Life Sentence, Panthaki realized that he loved those behind-the-scenes roles. “That film was about something that was really personal to me,” Panthaki tells THR in Tallinn. “And when it came to getting made, I didn’t want anyone else to make it. I’ve lost someone close to me, so this was a story that I had to tell. It was a five-day shoot on a short film with a minuscule budget, and I realized when I stepped on set that this, in some ways, comes more naturally to me than acting. So I realized it was a massive calling.”.

In Starland is also very close to Panthaki’s heart, comparing it to a child. “I realized that the first feature film, which is why it’s taken so many years, had to be something very personal, something that I wanted to say about the world,” he shares.

And he realized early on that his directorial feature debut came with bigger-picture goals. “I wanted to correct some wrongs that have happened to me as an actor in my career,” he tells THR. “I’ve found it frustrating sometimes that this industry is not a meritocracy. I’ve been offered roles where everyone on the film wants you, and then the head of the studio notes, ‘Oh, actually, we want a bigger name. And so this was an opportunity for me to really get the right people for the right roles.”.

In that context, Panthaki also calls the film “non-dependent because I don’t think independent gives the true story. “If a film that has got public funding is called ‘independent,’ then this has to have a different name, right? So I’ve been calling it non-dependent, which has been hard and frustrating at times. But the payoff for that was that I’m allowed to do things that other films can’t. For example, I was allowed to make this a meritocracy, and I’m so proud of that Clarence was the only actor out of the 11 lead actors whose previous work I had seen [before making In Starland]. When I watched Sing Sing, I was like, ‘This guy is captivating.’ There is something in his eyes that you just cannot deny.”.

Industry observers note that maclin lauds Panthaki for his conviction and vision. “Ray sees the world in his own way, and you can feel that in this film,” the star tells THR. “He knows what he wants, but he’s also open to what you bring to it. He gives you room to be yourself, to try things, to find something you maybe didn’t even know was there. And that’s where the magic happens.”.

In Starland premieres at a time when more of its cast members have broken out. “Miss Benny is, of course, in Club Kid,” notes Panthaki. “Then you got Bella, who is everywhere, and Tai’mua, this amazing Hawaiian actor, was in an Oscar-nominated short [Jane Austen’s Period Drama] playing a lead role. Everyone’s having their moment.”.

Recent findings suggest that while In Starland follows a group of young creators obsessed with views, likes and followers, “I didn’t want to know about the cast’s follower count,” the director recalls. “It was only about whether that person would earn the role in the room, and they did.”.

Sources indicate that and he needed actors happy to improvise. “That is how I like to do things,” the writer-director explains. “Once I have a script, I like to find truth and play around and naturalize things as much as possible. So I needed actors who were able to do that. I needed actors that I work very much on instinct, so I could turn up on a day and say, ‘This doesn’t feel right to me today. We’re going to do something completely different.’ That happened a number of times on set.”.

That and the overall non-dependent nature of In Starland made the experience on set different. “There was something special about making this film,” Maclin shares. “We didn’t have all the things a significant Hollywood production might have, but we had people who believed in what we were doing. And Ray, he wasn’t gonna compromise on what he wanted this film to be. You gotta respect that. When somebody believes in something that much, you wanna be part of it.”.

In Starland leaves certain things open, unanswered or answerable in different ways. “I want people to have different opinions of what happens and instigate conversation,” Panthaki explains.

Industry observers note that “What I love about In Starland is it ain’t trying to give you all the answers,” Maclin also emphasizes. “There’s some funny moments, there’s some painful moments, but there’s a whole lot of humanity in there. It makes you look at people a little differently, maybe think about things you hadn’t thought about before. And to me, that’s what storytelling is about.”.

How did Killer Films end up boarding In Starland? “We asked Christine if she’d take a look and read the script and watch what we shot,” Panthaki says. “We had a conversation with her and over many conversations she just believed in the project. For me, that someone of that clout and and someone who has that amazing body of work believed in it is the biggest seal of approval. I’m so grateful to her and to Mason Plotts [, head of film at Killer Films].”.

Audience will recognize 1980s music throughout In Starland. Given his own love for it, Panthaki says that he simply had to make one of his young characters be obsessed with music from that period. One of the key tunes in the film is the Tears for Fears hit “Everybody Wants to Rule the World.”.

In a recent development, the director recalls reached out to the band himself. “I just wrote a letter, and I just told them why I’m doing this, what I’m trying to say about the world, and I don’t know if they ever read the letter or not,” Panthaki explains. “I actually wrote a number of letters during this process, and they came back and said, ‘Yeah, we’re willing to give the song to you for this amount of money.” I was never asking for it for free. I was asking for it for what we could afford within our means, and and they agreed to it.”.

Sources indicate that asked about the film’s title, Panthaki tells THR: “I wanted something that felt poetic and really explained what the film was in a number of ways, and it just came to me. In Starland was a play on words because if you put those words together, it almost sounds like Instaland, so it has the Instagram element, and Ernie was in starland – but I don’t want to talk about a key twist there. I wanted to have a duality in the title, much like the lives of the people in the film.”.

Industry observers note that could we see another feature directed by Panthaki? “Writing, directing and producing this film has been the hardest thing I’ve ever done in my life,” he shares. “Everything that has happened in this movie over the past seven years has been 10 times harder because we were doing it ourselves. So, will I do it again? I think yes. But I don’t know if I can do it again with so little time and money. I think I’ll need more infrastructure in place to be able to do it again.”.

Recent findings suggest that that said, Panthaki’s passion is coming through again. “I have ideas that are burning in me, and it has to be something I want to say about the world,” he tells THR. “It has to be something important that I can say, and something that I can do well. So I’ve got a couple of ideas that I’m working on. But for right now, get me back to acting!”.

Rob Lowe has stated he asked to star in Ben Shapiro‘s feature film “Confession” despite Shapiro considering him “way too handsome” for the part.

In a recent development, “I read the script, it was written by Ben Shapiro,” Lowe stated on the Second Thought podcast. “I called Ben and said, ‘This is fantastic.’”.

Sources indicate that shapiro, who had met Lowe a couple of times in passing, had sent the script over in the hope the “West Wing” actor could suggest a leading man who wouldn’t be “scared” to work with the conservative writer, who founded The Daily Wire website. Related Stories 'Rings of Power' Season 3 Premiere: [SPOILER] Dies in Shocking Murder, Sauron Assembles Ringwraiths and Jamie Campbell Bower Is Galadriel's Lover Celeborn 'Lord of the Rings,' 'Avatar' VFX House Weta FX Partners With Taiwan’s Moonshine Studio Under AI Pact With TAICCA.

Sources indicate that “And I go, ‘Yeah, me.’ And he goes, ‘You’re good with this?’ I said, ‘I’ve worked with the most left-wing writers in the world. Why wouldn’t I also work with the most right-wing writers in the world?’”.

In a separate interview with writer Coleman Hughes, on his “Conversations With Coleman” podcast, Shapiro recounted a similar story, saying Lowe had been “really deeply affected by the script,” which is set in Stalinist Russia and follows Lowe’s character Alexi, an erstwhile literature professor who is interrogated by a former pupil turned KGB agent Vladimir (played by James Franco) after he is accused of colluding with a dissident priest.

Shapiro noted he told the star: “You’re Rob Lowe. If you ask to play a part, the answer is yes, but I’m just telling you you’re way too handsome for this.”.

According to recent reports, lowe admitted his reps hadn’t been enthused by his decision to work with Shapiro, saying: “There were people who were definitely like, ‘Are you crazy?’ But… I’m old enough, established enough, people know me well enough, to know that I’m not an ideologue at all. I’m not telling anybody how to live, how to think, on either side of the aisle. I’ve campaigned for Republicans. I’ve campaigned for Democrats…. I have my bona fides in both worlds.”.

The film, directed by Václav Marhoul (“The Painted Bird”), also stars Jennifer Jason Leigh, Nick Nolte, Emile Hirsch and Kodi Smit-McPhee. It is being distributed by the Daily Wire.

Lowe said the team had hoped for a traditional distributor or streamer to pick up the film but found every door closed. “It is challenging, it’s a tough watch,” he said of the subject matter. “But I see the movies that are celebrated out there. I see the movies that are picked for film — we got turned down by every single film festival. Summarily frog-marched out of any conversation. Now, this is a movie with me, Nick Nolte, James Franco, Emile Hirsch. I see what they’re picking up. And it’s all political.”.

“The thought would be, we’d play in a film festival, we would get some buzz — never happened — and then Netflix would pick it up… Crickets. Absolute crickets. So then it defaults to the Daily Wire to be the distributor. And I’m like, hell yeah. I want people to see this movie. And good for them for putting it out.”.

It has been revealed that “But that wasn’t originally going to be the life of the movie. My thought would be like, Focus Features would see it in Venice and like it. But people are definitely in a place where a lot of people cannot see a work just for its work. They have to do the math of ‘What does it mean?’ and ‘What will people think?’ and ‘Does that mean I’m on this side or does that mean I’m on that side?’”.

He acknowledged that it was “the greatest irony” given the subject of the movie is about “wrongthink” in the Soviet Union, adding he has friends across the political spectrum. “For every Jane Fonda I have a Ben Shapiro. For every Jimmy Kimmel I’ve got Bill O’Reilly,” Lowe mentioned.

“I feel like that’s what’s lacking,” he added. “People do not have any type of leash for other people in their orbit. But to me, that’s what you want: people who think differently than you. And by the way, I’m not saying I agree with any of these people, but I don’t want to hear the same conversation and the same story over and over. And I really appreciate different opinions.”.

VSCO Is Gunning for Adobe Lightroom With Its Newly introduced Desktop App

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (692 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, new photographers looking for inspiration often start with an app like VSCO.
  • In a recent development, VSCO's pitch is simple: Keep photographers in the ecosystem by building a desktop app to rival Lightroom.
  • Recent findings suggest that “We're helping shape these folks in their formative years,” VSCO CEO Eric Wittman tells WIRED.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, new photographers looking for inspiration often start with an app like VSCO. The popular mobile app, rolled out more than a decade ago, is known for one-click presets that emulate film and make it easy to elevate a photograph before posting it to social media. But as newbie shutterbugs level up their craft, they often graduate to an app like Adobe Lightroom and its more professional tool set.

In a recent development, VSCO's pitch is simple: Keep photographers in the ecosystem by building a desktop app to rival Lightroom. On Tuesday, the manufacturer confirmed that its Studio Pro Desktop app is officially landing on macOS, following the launch of Studio Pro on iOS earlier this year. Neither version is available on Android or Windows, though the San Francisco–based company prepares to port the apps in the future.

Recent findings suggest that “We're helping shape these folks in their formative years,” VSCO CEO Eric Wittman tells WIRED. “We've got to keep giving them more bricks to build upon their own personal, creative journey—not just their creative journey, but also help them build a career.”.

Recent findings suggest that the desktop client is one part of VSCO's growing portfolio that caters to full-time photographers. Subscribing to VSCO One, for example, nets you access to Studio Pro, additional presets, and VSCO Workspace—a customer relationship management tool for handling contracts, booking, and scheduling. It also includes VSCO Galleries to send finished work directly to clients and VSCO Sites, a portfolio website builder to find upcoming clients. All of these apps and services launched in the past year.

Access to the broad suite costs $500 a year, or you can get the Studio Pro mobile and desktop apps alone with a VSCO Pro membership for $5 per month ($60 annually). There is also a free tier, but some tools are locked behind the subscription. (Naturally, the original VSCO app is still around for enthusiasts.).

The Studio Pro Desktop app is speedy, features more than 200 presets, and supports RAW editing for 20 camera brands. Batch editing is the highlight, letting photographers edit up to 500 images simultaneously to speed up workflows while preserving the original files. Previews are rendered in real time, and at the end, customers can export the final images directly to VSCO Galleries (or wherever they'd like).

I've been trying the app for a few weeks, and it is snappy. It loads RAW files quickly, and it even supports keyboard shortcuts. The sheer breadth of presets is also really nice, even if I tend to tweak colors myself. But there's a catch. If you're like me and coming from Lightroom, you'll miss a few features that Studio Pro Desktop doesn't offer yet. For example, Masking, Curves, and the Erase function (aka the spot removal tool) are “coming soon.”.

Sources indicate that “We want to be simple, intentionally, but we want to be powerful with our tools,” indicates Kyle Hale, VSCO's senior product manager. He says the app will feature around 70 percent of what people need for desktop editing, with the rest coming through regular software updates. While he doesn't expect full parity with a competitor like Lightroom by the first quarter of 2027, Studio Pro Desktop will have “the meat of what those programs offer.”.

Companies like Adobe have heavily leaned into generative AI in their creative editing tools. While VSCO uses AI and machine-learning models in some tools like the upcoming Erase and retouch tools, the company says it doesn't train its own models on anything that people post on the VSCO app. VSCO also relies on some third-party models, like those from Black Forest Labs, but it has agreements in place that third parties cannot train on its user data.

Sources indicate that “I don't think all AI is bad,” Wittman states. “But to be very, very clear: Generative AI, or if you're replacing the photographer—like what you're seeing with what Meta is doing, what Adobe's doing, like almost every other manufacturer is doing—we are not doing that. We stand by and champion photographers first and foremost, and that's not going to change.”.

The AfD and neo-Nazi networks: How close are the connections?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1165 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany.
  • This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?
  • Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the electoral successes of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) have brought the party closer than ever to taking power in Germany. For the 2029 federal election, it has set itself an ambitious goal: to see its co-chair Alice Weidel to become Germany's next chancellor.

This raises an even sharper question: what political ideas does the party stand for, which has been classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as a "suspected right-wing extremist" organization and, in several federal states, is already considered "confirmed right-wing extremist"?

Many political scientists have observed that the AfD has become increasingly radicalized since its founding in 2013.

"Viewed as a whole, the AfD is an extreme right-wing party that also displays tendencies associated with a fascist movement," said Fabian Virchow, a researcher on right-wing extremism at Düsseldorf University of Applied Sciences, in an interview with DW.

Virchow identifies different factions and strategic tendencies within the party, some of which are at odds with one another. Party leader Alice Weidel, for example, is generally seen as a proponent of a free-market approach that seeks to keep the state as small as possible. Others, by contrast, favor a strong state shaped by an ethnically homogeneous people, among them Björn Höcke, the influential far-right AfD leader in the state of Thuringia.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that virchow sees a "normalization" of right-wing extremist positions within the AfD. In his view, this has made the party more attractive to neo-Nazi circles: "Today, many people see greater room for ethnonationalist and radical right-wing ideas.".

Support for this observation comes from the latest findings of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study, one of the most widely cited long-term studies tracking right-wing extremist attitudes in Germany. The researchers behind the study have identified a rise in right-wing extremist views within German society, including a growing acceptance of ideologies rooted in the tradition of National Socialism.

Industry observers note that particularly striking is the finding that around two-thirds of people with firmly entrenched far-right worldviews would vote for the AfD. According to the study, the AfD has achieved what earlier far-right parties in Germany never managed: "to unite large segments of the electorate with anti-democratic attitudes behind it.".

In a recent development, the debate has been further fueled by several recent incidents within the party. In 2026 alone, numerous AfD politicians and staff members made headlines over alleged ties to neo-Nazi organizations:.

In August 2026, police carried out a large-scale raid targeting fifteen people. Authorities suspect them of continuing the activities of the so-called "Artgemeinschaft." Before it was banned in 2023, the group was considered one of Germany's largest and most influential neo-Nazi cadre organizations. Particularly explosive was the fact that two of those targeted in the raid are sitting AfD members of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. Their attorneys deny the allegations.

According to reporting by the German daily, Welt, four staff members of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt are former members of the now-banned "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" (HDJ), a neo-Nazi youth organization rooted in National Socialist racial ideology that organized paramilitary camps for young people. Two of the staff members held leadership positions within the HDJ and now work closely with AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who is seeking to become the AfD's first state premier in December.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that remarkably, both organizations, the "Artgemeinschaft" and the HDJ, are on the AfD's so-called incompatibility list, which is intended to draw a line between the party and extremist organizations and movements. In principle, anyone with a history of membership in such groups is supposed to be excluded from the party.

But the list appears to be little more than a dead letter. In 2020, former AfD federal executive board member Andreas Kalbitz was expelled from the party after failing to disclose his membership in the "Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend" on his application to join. Yet according to the news magazine Spiegel, he is once again working for the AfD, this time as a staffer for Saxony-Anhalt state legislator Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, who has since become deputy speaker of the state parliament.

In a recent development, the question of the AfD's relationship to National Socialism has dogged the party since its founding in 2013. Even in its early years, co-founder and first party leader Bernd Lucke sparked controversy when he described democracy and parliamentary politics in Germany as "degenerate," a term the Nazis used to disparage art and culture that did not conform to their ideological worldview.

In Germany, references to the Nazi dictatorship (1933-1945) under Adolf Hitler remain politically taboo because of the country's responsibility for World War Two and the Holocaust, the systematic mass murder of Europe's Jews.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

If AfD members or their staff have come under scrutiny because of past involvement in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations, they have generally sought to distance themselves from those backgrounds or from the ideologies associated with them.

But how credible are these attempts at distancing? Laura Neumann* has worked with many people seeking to leave the far-right scene. She works for "Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts," a network of organizations that supports far-right cadres and activists as they disengage from the movement. "A successful exit is the result of a professionally guided process," she said in an interview with DW.

Neumann describes leaving the far-right scene as a challenging process of self-confrontation. "When it comes to someone leaving the movement, the first question I always ask is: How does that person talk about their past? Have they genuinely come to terms with it?".

Based on the experience of exit counselors, one principle generally holds true: the longer and more deeply a person has been immersed in far-right circles, the more difficult it becomes to distance themselves from those beliefs and affiliations.

DW requested a statement from the AfD's federal executive board regarding its handling of party members who were previously active in ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi organizations. Individual lawmakers and parliamentary staff members were also asked to comment. None responded.

The party's and its politicians' silence in the face of such allegations reflects an observation made by political scientist Fabian Virchow: "Within the AfD, there is no longer a perceived need to distance oneself from radical far-right positions. That is part of this process of normalization.".

Virchow says that right-wing extremism appears to have advanced so far into the mainstream of German society that efforts to scandalize it now remain largely ineffective.

It has been revealed that * Editor's note: To protect the privacy of the staff member of Nordverbund Ausstieg Rechts, we have changed her name to Laura Neumann. Her real name is known to the editors.

This article was originally written in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that alzheimer's disease may begin leaving detectable clues in the brain as much as a decade before memory problems appear. Researchers at Johns Hopkins University have identified two brain regions that show signs of deterioration earlier than the hippocampus, the area commonly examined for evidence of the disease.

The discovery could eventually help doctors recognize Alzheimer's years before symptoms develop, potentially allowing treatment to begin when it has the greatest chance of protecting the brain.

It has been revealed that by examining hundreds of brain scans, the scientists found that the entorhinal cortex and amygdala, two regions involved in memory and emotion, begin losing tissue earlier than the hippocampus. These changes may offer important fresh clues about how Alzheimer's develops and how it could be detected before significant cognitive decline occurs.

It has been revealed that "We have found that there are early changes in the brain manifesting the clinical biomarkers of atrophy as much as a decade before there are clinical symptoms," remarked biomedical engineer and senior author Michael Miller. "It's at least a 5-to-10-year play where your brain is changing. Imagine if we could start to treat the neurodegenerative changes at the 2, 3 or 4-year point rather than after 15 years when the changes are manifesting in memory symptoms. That's the great promise here for your loved ones who are at risk.".

The findings were recently published in NeuroImage Reports and are being presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience.

Detecting Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss Begins.

Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, but the disease does not begin when someone first experiences forgetfulness or confusion. Changes associated with Alzheimer's can accumulate in the brain for decades before noticeable symptoms emerge.

Scientists believe this long period of silent progression may provide a crucial opportunity for treatment. Interventions that begin before extensive damage occurs could potentially do more to preserve memory and other cognitive abilities. However, taking advantage of that opportunity requires reliable ways to identify the disease in its earliest stages.

Recent findings suggest that one promising approach involves biomarkers, measurable biological changes that can indicate the presence or progression of a disease. In Alzheimer's research, these markers could help reveal who is developing the condition before symptoms become apparent.

"Our goal is to be able to treat individuals before the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease develop so that they may delayed or even stopped," remarked Marilyn Albert, co-author and director of the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer's Disease Research Center.

Two Brain Regions Reveal Earlier Warning Signs.

To investigate where the earliest detectable changes occur, the researchers examined hundreds of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) scans collected through two independent research projects: the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and the Biomarkers of Cognitive Decline Among Normal Individuals study.

The scans followed people at different stages of Alzheimer's disease over time, including individuals without symptoms, those experiencing cognitive impairment, and patients who ultimately died from the disease.

In both groups, the researchers observed a consistent pattern. The entorhinal cortex and amygdala, which are located near the hippocampus, highlighted greater relative tissue loss during the early stages of Alzheimer's than the hippocampus itself.

This distinction matters because the hippocampus plays a central role in memory and has traditionally been a major focus when doctors look for Alzheimer's-related brain damage.

Industry observers note that the two newly highlighted regions perform vital functions of their own. The entorhinal cortex helps retrieve previously stored memories, while the amygdala contributes to emotional memory, including how emotional experiences are processed and remembered.

Their earlier shrinkage suggests that examining these structures together could reveal signs of Alzheimer's that might be less apparent when attention is focused primarily on the hippocampus.

Brain Shrinkage Linked to Alzheimer's Tau Protein.

The researchers also found an crucial connection between the loss of brain tissue and tau, a protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Sources indicate that under normal conditions, tau helps maintain the internal structure of nerve cells. In Alzheimer's, however, tau can accumulate abnormally and form tangles that interfere with healthy brain function.

Recent findings suggest that using PET imaging and digital pathology, the scientists found that areas of gray matter shrinkage overlapped with regions showing tau-related changes. Gray matter contains large numbers of nerve cell bodies and is essential for processing information throughout the brain.

This relationship strengthens the possibility that changes in the entorhinal cortex and amygdala could serve as useful indicators of early Alzheimer's disease.

The team believes that measuring tissue loss in both regions, rather than relying primarily on changes in the hippocampus, could eventually improve predictions of who is likely to develop cognitive decline.

Industry observers note that as brain imaging becomes more accessible and less expensive, this approach could also become increasingly practical. For people with a family history of Alzheimer's or other risk factors, researchers envision a future in which doctors might examine these regions as early as a person's 30s or 40s.

"As biomarkers and treatments become increasingly available, knowing who is going to have cognitive decline is going to be really notable," remarked co-author Meaghan Morris, a neuropathologist who studies Alzheimer's and other dementias. "This could really play into better risk stratification for identifying who is going to have cognitive decline in the near future -- and treating people earlier and earlier to hopefully slow the course of the disease.".

A Potential Latest Path Toward Earlier Alzheimer's Treatment.

Although the findings are promising, more research is necessary before doctors can use these brain changes as a reliable diagnostic tool. The study identifies potential early biomarkers, but it does not yet establish a clinical test capable of predicting Alzheimer's years in advance.

The next step is to investigate what happens within these regions at a much smaller scale. The researchers want to understand the molecular changes surrounding abnormal tau accumulation and how those changes contribute to the progressive loss of brain tissue.

Identifying the biological processes involved could eventually reveal upcoming targets for therapies designed to interrupt Alzheimer's before extensive damage occurs.

"Our future work is to better show the molecular neighborhoods associated with these Tau protein changes as localized by these clinical biomarkers of atrophy," Miller said. "Once we know more about the molecular neighborhoods, we can develop therapies.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Skydance is pulling back the curtain on how it plans to achieve at least $6 billion in cost savings in the next three years.

"By combining two global streaming services, two film and TV studio groups, two television portfolios, and overlapping corporate functions, we can reduce duplicative spend across an expense base of more than $50 billion," the manufacturer wrote in a letter to shareholders Monday as part of Paramount Skydance's third-quarter earnings release.

Industry observers note that skydance, the manufacturer formed by the combination of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, stated it projects at least $2.2 billion in cost reductions from eliminating "redundant back-office and corporate functions," including eliminating management layers and ramping the use of artificial intelligence. Those savings also account for "rationalizing" its office footprint.

Skydance expects at least $1 billion in savings from streamlining marketing and promotional spending. And around $1.4 billion in savings will come from unifying its streaming businesses and broadcast architecture and integrating back-end technology.

A final $1.4 billion in savings will be tied to "optimizing third-party spend," eliminating overlapping expenses, and consolidating purchasing decisions to one centralized group, Skydance mentioned.

"We are confident in achieving these savings, drawing on our playbook from Paramount," the manufacturer wrote. "That program is on track to achieve over $2.7 billion in run-rate efficiencies by the end of 2026.".

Some of that cost-cutting has already begun.

According to recent reports, last month, Skydance began offering voluntary buyouts to employees ahead of official layoffs. At the same time, the company adopted a five-day-per-week in-office policy. Additionally, last week saw the departure of eight executives — four from Warner Bros. and four from Paramount.

The firm has previously mentioned it intends to eventually merge the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services into a single platform.

On Monday, Skydance said it would take the first step toward that goal early next year, offering a bundle of the streaming services "at an even greater value.".

Co-CEO Ynon Kreiz told investors during the company's earnings call that Skydance is also looking for ways to optimize its content budget. The company spends more than $30 billion annually on shows and films.

"As one company, we can make smarter choices about how we distribute and monetize both latest content and library content," Kreiz stated.

According to recent reports, skydance noted that it's expecting a $200 million headwind in the fourth quarter from theatrical underperformances at Warner Bros. studio related to already launched titles and upcoming releases.

The manufacturer will also utilize AI to speed up production and decrease costs to make films, co-CEO and chairman David Ellison noted on the call.

"We think these tools will help unlock more original storytelling by being able to make the budget more digestible to be able to take that amount of risk," Ellison said.

The updates came alongside third-quarter results for the legacy Paramount Skydance firm that included revenue of $7.03 billion, which was roughly in line with StreetAccount estimates of $7.04 billion, and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $1 billion, topping StreetAccount estimates of $913.5 million.

However, adjusted earnings per share of 45 cents were not immediately comparable to StreetAccount EPS estimates.

The results don't include the impact of the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, which closed after the end of the third quarter.

Skydance detailed business units of the combined entity, including studios, direct-to-consumer and TV, and said it will provide full-year guidance during its fourth-quarter earnings report early next year.

"Going forward, we will provide guidance on an annual basis, as we prioritize long-term value creation, which we believe will be more consistent with our strategic approach," the company told shareholders. "We will continue to provide quarterly updates, including certain forward-looking commentary where applicable, which will give investors visibility into our near-term progress of the business.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Watkins recently shared a snapshot captured by her crewmate Anil Menon that showcases her experience working on an experiment called InSPA-Auxilium Bioprinter-Cell Printing that takes place inside the station's Life Sciences Glovebox, a contained research space and one of Watkins favorite places to work on the space station, she shared on social media.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronauts get tasked with all kinds of weird science aboard the International Space Station. Recently, NASA astronaut and Crew-13 commander Jessica Watkins got to work supporting an ongoing experiment that includes 3D-printing human cells and tissues in space.

Aboard the space station, astronauts have a multitude of responsibilities ranging from station maintenance and repairs on spacewalks to daily exercise and a wide variety of scientific research.

Watkins recently shared a snapshot captured by her crewmate Anil Menon that showcases her experience working on an experiment called InSPA-Auxilium Bioprinter-Cell Printing that takes place inside the station's Life Sciences Glovebox, a contained research space and one of Watkins favorite places to work on the space station, she shared on social media.

In the image she is gloved-up with both her hands and arms covered in the sealed glovebox while she mixes samples of living cells with a bioink, a mixture she then inserts into a specialized cartridge, NASA shared.

This experiment that Watkins is working on "leverages the microgravity environment of ISS to 3D print cells and manufacture human liver, kidney, and cartilage tissue. Just one of many examples of how we’re using this amazing orbital national laboratory to reshape our understanding of biology, medicine, and engineering, and improve life on Earth!" Watkins shared online.

Sources indicate that this experiment is designed to explore 3D printing human cartilage tissue in microgravity. The experiment aims to one day support future human patients both in space and on Earth.

When you think of the research that happens in space, 3D-printing human cells might not be the first thing to come to mind. But because of the unique microgravity environment onboard the ISS, it is the perfect home for even the strangest of biological experiments.

On the space station, there is still gravity but objects (and people) remain in a sort of constant freefall, leading to total weightlessness that mimics the complete absence of gravity. This weightlessness allows researchers to test, experiment and explore beyond the gravitational confines of Earth.

With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. Industry News: The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.
  • According to recent reports, 'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, fresh report indicates.
  • Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an important purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.

According to recent reports, 'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, fresh report indicates. Here are the key takeaways.

Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an important purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.

This shift in consumer preferences has propelled many beauty brands to set environmental goals: to move away from single-use and virgin plastics, provide recyclable, reusable and refillable packaging and offer more transparency around products’ ingredients so customers can ascertain how “green” their purchase is.

Sources indicate that however, consumers still struggle to understand the sustainability credentials of many products, according to the British Beauty Council. This is because the industry’s clean-up efforts have been inconsistent, and fall short of making a recognizable impact in the absence of collective goal-setting, global strategy and standardized regulations.

There is no international standard for the beauty industry on how much product ingredient information to share with customers — or how to do so. Brands can set their own rules and goals, giving rise to confusion and “greenwashing,” where sustainability claims are often touted but not substantiated.

Companies often use marketing language like “clean beauty” to make it seem like their products are natural, for example, when they may not actually be organic, sustainable or ethically made.

After rebranding in the West, many beauty companies are still offering to 'whiten' skin elsewhere.

Recent findings suggest that “The term ‘clean beauty’ has become quite dangerous. It’s used to sell more products,” according to British Beauty Council CEO Millie Kendall, who added that such buzzwords are losing traction in the UK as British customers wise up to their shortcomings. “Customers need better marketing information and certification information.”.

In a 2021 report calling on the industry to have “the courage to change” their business practices, the British Beauty Council wrote that, all too often, even natural ingredients involved in manufacturing products give way to “over-consumption, non-regenerative farming practices, pollution, waste and neglect.”.

“The only way out of this is transparency,” Kendall told CNN.

It has been revealed that jen Lee, chief impact officer at US-based brand Beautycounter, remarked she continues to see confusion over ingredients among consumers. (In 2013, the company rolled out and published “The Never List,” which currently cites more than 2,800 chemicals — including heavy metals, parabens and formaldehyde — it claims to never use in its products.).

“Natural vs. synthetic ingredients has been a conversation. People think natural is safer, but it’s not always the case,” Lee explained. “Natural ingredients formulated in the industry can have toxic load. Heavy metals can occur in natural components of the earth.”.

Mother loses peripheral vision from apparent exposure to mercury in beauty creams. Toxic levels in her home put family at risk, say experts.

“We used to be more natural and organic,” added Sasha Plavsic, founder of makeup brand ILIA Beauty. “What was challenging is (that) raw materials were difficult to source or would come in inconsistently or products wouldn’t perform.”.

Industry observers note that most makeup is created and molded at high temperatures, Plavsic explained. Purely organic materials often fall apart in this heat, leading to inconsistent results and subpar product performance. “Not every synthetic is bad,” Plavsic said. “Sometimes, it helps create the best in class formula.”.

The industry’s plastic packaging is a particular sustainability challenge — 95% is thrown away and the vast majority is not recycled, according to the British Beauty Council.

The cosmetics business is the fourth biggest plastic packaging user globally — after food and beverage, industrial packaging and pharmaceuticals — and plastic is about 67% of the industry’s packaging volume, according to Vantage Market Research. Beauty giant L’Oreal used 144,430 metric tons of plastic in its packaging material in 2021, for example, according to the Ellen Macarthur Foundation (EMF). Estee Lauder Companies reported its brands produced 71,600 metric tons of plastic in product packaging that same year.

And only 9% of the global plastic waste is recycled, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The United States only recycles 4% of its plastic waste.

Industry observers note that single-use plastic is wreaking havoc on the planet. Here's what you can do to minimize your impact.

In a recent development, many brands are trying to phase out harmful plastics from their operations and adopt post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastic. (L’Oreal has set a target of 50% PCR plastic usage by 2025, while Estee Lauder is targeting 25% “or more” PCR plastic — but both are far from achieving their targets.).

Recent findings suggest that “Between 60-70 major global brands have made unprecedented progress” in PCR plastic usage across industries, EMF’s Plastic Initiative Lead Sander DeFruyt told CNN. But DeFruyt stressed that PCR plastic must be adopted in conjunction with brands removing single and virgin plastics from their usage cycles to truly make a difference.

In a recent development, however, PCR plastic is not easy to find — low recycling rates around the world mean there is limited supply. Meanwhile, demand for it is growing demand across industries, DeFruyt noted. This competition hikes up its price, which is already higher than virgin plastic.

Hair care brand FEKKAI claims that it used up to 95% PCR content in its packaging, but pricing and supply challenges posed a challenge, forcing it to currently aim for containers and packaging that feature at least 50% PCR in its packaging.

It has been revealed that “PCR plastic is more expensive than stock plastic. The cost is hard and then sourcing it is too,” founder Frédéric Fekkai told CNN. “PCR is close to our heart, but there is a massive demand, so finding recycled plastic is difficult.”.

Beauty retailers plays a pivotal — and under-utilized — role, with control over stocking decisions and supply chains. But many vary when it comes to the standards they set for brands they sell.

“Smaller businesses do more, full stop,” said Jessi Baker, founder of the technology platform Provenance, which helps brands display their sustainability credentials for customers. “They move more nimbly. Some of them are born-good brands — climate friendliness was part of their setup. They don’t need to restructure their entire supply chain. Their culture already has it compared to the larger brands who need to work hard to change.”.

A history of beauty trends -- and the standards that shaped them.

In a recent development, sephora launched its “Clean + Planet Positive” initiative in 2021, which labeled products that met its set criteria. (This is separate from the French retailer’s “Clean at Sephora” program, which is currently facing a consumer lawsuit alleging it carries a significant percentage of products understood by customers to be harmful.) Target launched a similar program in 2022, featuring a “Target Zero” icon for both online and in-store offerings that either have reusable, recyclable, compostable or reduced plastic packaging, or feature waterless or concentrated products.

Still, many steps taken by brands and retailers do not even begin to touch on the waste and pollution generated throughout supply chains, manufacturing and shipping, all huge problems for the industry to grapple with.

The gaps in standardization in the beauty ecosystem can, to some extent, be filled by certifications such as the US-born B Corporation, or B Corp. This accreditation, one of the most well-known in the beauty space, is issued by the non-profit B Lab, which scores a company on a variety of criteria around ethics and sustainability. However beneficial it may be among eco-conscious consumers, though, it is at the moment completely voluntary for brands to apply for.

Governments and multinationals enforcing regulations and setting a base line for brands to operate from when making sustainability claims would go a long way to making change, many experts and business leaders believe.

Susanne Kaufmann, founder of her namesake beauty brand, says her efforts in Austria would reap better results if more countries around the world had stricter, more uniform garbage disposal laws.

A trash heap 62 meters high demonstrates the scale of India's climate challenge.

According to recent reports, “I package our product in a recyclable material,” Kaufmann said. (Her products’ packaging, which is refillable and reusable, is made from 75% recycled plastic — and is 100% recyclable.) If I send this to the US, the garbage is not separated… and it’s not recyclable,” she explained, referring to inconsistencies in recycling laws across the United States.

And when it comes to ingredients, the European Chemicals Agency lists 2,495 substances banned from use in cosmetic products marketed for sale or use in the bloc. But the US Food and Drug administration only lists 11, making it more challenging for American consumers to find safer, greener options. The Environmental Working Group, a non-profit watchdog, studied lab tests of 51 sunscreen products in 2021 and found that only 35% of products met the EU standard, compared with 94% that passed the US standard.

However, while government can set minimum requirements, Mia Davis, vice president of sustainability and impact at beauty retailer Credo Beauty, says the needle will move in the private sector.

Sustainable ships: The world's most eco-conscious cruises.

“Regulation can raise the floor a bit. A person who doesn’t know about any (sustainability issues) should still be able to walk into a bodega and get clean products… But that’s never going to be what the market can do,” she said. “Market leadership is key.”.

Sources indicate that in the absence of bold regulations or global standards on sustainability practices, this “leadership” — undertaken both by brands and customers in the beauty marketplace — is likely to be the most immediately impactful vector for addressing the industry’s climate shortcomings. It will take continued collective advocacy and initiative to see meaningful climate-conscious change.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Sony Future Filmmaker Awards revealed on Wednesday the jury panel for its 2027 edition on Wednesday.

The jury members include Sony Pictures Animation director Alan Hawkins (“The Haunting of Hotel Transylvania,” head of character animation on “Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse,” “The Mitchells vs. the Machines”), film and television producer and founder of Vertigo Entertainment Roy Lee (“The Ring,” “The Departed,” “Weapons”), cinematographer Christopher Ross (“Shōgun,” “Yesterday,” “The Day of the Jackal”), filmmaker Dana Adam Shapiro (“Murderball,” “Monogamy,” “Better Angels”) and director Justin Chadwick (“Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom,” “The Other Boleyn Girl,” “Brothers Under Fire”), who returns as jury chair for the fifth consecutive year. Related Stories Macaulay Culkin Returns as Kevin McCallister in McDonalds' 'Home Alone' Christmas Ad.

“Every year, the shortlist reminds us of the remarkable filmmaking talent out there waiting to be uncovered,” Chadwick said in a statement. “Last year’s filmmakers arrived in Los Angeles from every corner of the world and left with relationships and insights that will continue to shape and further their careers for years to come.”.

This year’s awards are introducing a fresh Immersive category, presented by Meta, open to short films in 3D, 180° and 360° video, in any genre, fiction or non-fiction, live-action or animation.The awards will also partner with Snapdragon for the Snapdragon Shorts Award, which will award $10,000 each to five shortlisted filmmakers, along with a Snapdragon-powered filmmaking kit (smartphone, PC and smart glasses) to make an original short.

It has been revealed that the 2027 Sony Future Filmmaker Awards will include a four-day program at the Sony Pictures Studios in Culver City from June 7-10 giving recognizing filmmaking talent, giving their work a global stage and connecting them directly with the industry. Submissions for the 2027 edition close on Dec. 15. Filmmakers can enter short films across six categories: fiction, non-fiction, immersive, animation, student and future format. The Awards shortlist will be announced in the spring.
